title: Meta-Analytic Evidence of Clinical, Cognitive, Biological and Treatment Characteristics of Bipolar Spectrum Disorder in Children and Adolescents: Results From an Umbrella Review
journal: J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To comprehensively synthesize the meta-analytic evidence regarding bipolar spectrum disorder (BSD) in children and adolescents.

METHOD: PRISMA-compliant umbrella review (PROSPERO:CRD420250651065) across multiple databases to identify meta-analyses involving children and adolescents with BSD. Literature search, screening, data extraction, and quality assessment (via AMSTAR-2) were performed independently. Findings were synthesized and grouped according to key clinical, cognitive, biological and treatment domains.

RESULTS: Fifty-two meta-analyses were included (k=754, N=59,967, age=13.0 years, 44.8% female participants). Most reported symptoms were increased energy (79%, 95% confidence interval (CI)=61-93%), irritability (77%, 95%CI=64-88%), and mood lability (76%, 95%CI=55-92%). Psychiatric comorbidities were common, with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder being most frequent (53%, 95%CI=36-70%). Treatment delay was longer in children and adolescents than in adults with BSD (SMD=0.39, 95%CI=0.15-0.64). 26.2% (95%CI=24.4-28.0) of children and adolescents with BSD attempted suicide at least once, with higher risk vs. children and adolescents with depression (OR=1.59; 95%CI=1.24-2.05) and adult-BSD (OR=1.68, 95%CI=1.29-2.18). Compared to healthy controls (HCs), children and adolescents with BSD showed neurocognitive impairments. Abnormalities in neuroimaging markers were significant in children and adolescents with BSD vs. HCs, children and adolescents with depression and adult-BSD. Second-generation antipsychotics (SMD=0.68, 95%CI=0.51-0.86) and mood stabilizers (SMD=0.61, 95%CI=0.40-0.82) were superior for mania vs. placebo. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) was associated with improvements in manic and depressive symptoms.

CONCLUSION: BSD in children and adolescents is linked to illness severity, cognitive deficits, and neuroimaging abnormalities, requiring integrated pharmacological and psychosocial interventions (e.g. CBT). SGAs effectively treat mania, but options for depression remain limited. More prognostic and long-term studies are needed.

title: Cariprazine in the Treatment of Pediatric Patients With Irritability Associated With Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Randomized Controlled Trial
journal: J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of cariprazine in youth with irritability associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

METHOD: This 8-week, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, controlled trial compared age- and weight-dependent flexibly-dosed cariprazine (0.75-3 mg/day) versus placebo in youth (5-17y) with ASD and irritability. The primary efficacy endpoint was week 8 change from baseline in caregiver-rated Aberrant Behavior Checklist-Irritability subscale (ABC-I) score. The first key secondary endpoint was the week 8 proportion of participants who were responders for clinician-rated Clinical Global Impressions-Change (CGI-C) in irritability ("much improved" or "very much improved").

RESULTS: 155 participants (mean age 10.6y, 70% male participants) received ≥1 study dose; 152 had baseline and ≥1 postbaseline ABC-I or CGI-C scores (n=74 cariprazine, n=78 placebo), with 81% completing the treatment period and 3.9% discontinuing due to treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs). The cariprazine group had significantly greater week 8 ABC-I improvement than placebo (least square mean difference [95% CI] = -3.7 [-6.75, -0.57], Cohen's d effect size = 0.42, p = 0.0205). A significantly greater percentage of cariprazine-treated participants were CGI-C Irritability responders at week 8 than placebo (68.9% vs. 38.0%, odds ratio [95% CI] = 3.6 [1.7, 7.8], p = 0.0012). Overall, 51% of participants had TEAEs (1.3% had severe TEAEs); most commonly, somnolence and headache. TEAEs, laboratory values, and vital signs were consistent with cariprazine's known adult safety profile.

CONCLUSION: Pediatric patients with ASD treated with cariprazine demonstrated significantly greater improvement in irritability than placebo.

title: Adverse childhood experiences and child executive functions: influences of deprivation and threat in a Brazilian birth cohort
abstract:
BACKGROUND: A large proportion of children in low- and middle-income countries are exposed to adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), increasing the risk of poor physical and mental development. The Dimensional Model of Adversity and Psychopathology proposes that deprivation and threat have distinct effects on child executive functioning (EF), but longitudinal evidence, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, remains limited. We examined associations between deprivation, threat and their subtypes with child EFs in Brazil.

METHODS: We analysed data from over 2,000 children aged 4 and 6-7 years from a population-based birth cohort in Pelotas, Brazil. ACEs were assessed at age 4 using caregiver questionnaires and filmed observations. Composite exposure scores for deprivation, threat and their subtypes were generated using principal component analysis. Composite EF outcome scores were similarly derived from measures of inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility and working memory at ages 4 and 6-7. Associations were estimated using adjusted linear regression models.

RESULTS: Total deprivation was associated with lower EF scores at both ages, as were separate indices of material and interactional deprivation. Children in the highest versus lowest tertile of total deprivation had EF scores 0.67 standard deviations lower at age 6-7 years (β = -0.67; 95% CI: -0.78, -0.56). Total threat (highest versus lowest tertile: β = -0.28; 95% CI: -0.39, -0.17; 6-7 anos) and direct threat were also associated with lower EF scores at both ages, whereas household threat showed no evidence of association.

CONCLUSIONS: Deprivation and threat in early childhood were both associated with lower executive function scores at school entry, with material deprivation and direct threat showing the strongest associations within their respective domains. These findings extend the Dimensional Model of Adversity and Psychopathology and highlight the importance of socioeconomic and trauma-informed strategies to support children exposed to adversity.

title: Glymphatic dysfunction in early-onset schizophrenia: DTI-ALPS index reduction tracks illness burden and is independently associated with cognitive performance in treatment-resistant patients
abstract: Early-onset schizophrenia (EOS) is associated with greater cognitive impairment than adult-onset disease, and many patients also develop treatment resistance. Glymphatic dysfunction has been described in adult schizophrenia but not in EOS or in relation to treatment resistance. We used diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) to assess glymphatic function in 30 adolescents with EOS (15 treatment-resistant, TRS; 15 non-treatment-resistant, nTRS) and 29 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HC). Participants completed a neuropsychological battery covering verbal memory, processing speed, executive function, working memory, verbal fluency, and social cognition. ALPS differed across groups (F(2,56) = 34.66, p < 0.001, η² = 0.553), with values decreasing from HC (1.625 ± 0.072) to nTRS (1.501 ± 0.098) to TRS (1.439 ± 0.048); the TRS-nTRS difference was not significant (d = 0.81, p = 0.066). Patients showed broad cognitive deficits relative to HC, but nTRS and TRS did not differ on any measure after FDR correction. ALPS showed a nominal inverse association with the number of psychotic episodes (ρ = -0.391, p = 0.033) but was unrelated to PANSS scores or antipsychotic dose. Within TRS, ALPS was independently associated with phonemic verbal fluency (COWAT: β = +0.74, p = 0.003); a parallel association with categorical fluency (β = +0.88, p < 0.001) was partly driven by an influential observation and is exploratory. Glymphatic dysfunction appears to be a disease-intrinsic feature of EOS, lowest in TRS, possibly linked to cumulative episodes rather than current symptoms, and may contribute to cognitive impairment in treatment-resistant patients.

title: Mental health-related service contact amongst young people with a possible eating problem in the English national child mental health surveys
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To describe patterns of service contact among young people screening positive for possible eating problems and their characteristics.

METHODS: Secondary analysis of the Mental Health of Children and Young People in England 2017 survey, a national stratified probability sample. Possible eating problems were identified using Development and Wellbeing Assessment (DAWBA) eating disorder screening items in young people aged 11-19. Individuals answered questions regarding contact with sources of help for any mental health concern.

RESULTS: Overall, 36.4% of young people screened positive for a possible eating problem, of whom 60.7% reported no contact with sources of mental health support. Among those reporting contact with formal and specialist services, a substantial proportion screened positive for possible eating problems, including half of those reporting contact with mental health specialists. In weighted multinomial logistic regression restricted to screen-positive young people, older age (17-19 years) and presence of a DSM-5 diagnosis on the DAWBA were associated with higher likelihood of contact across informal, formal, and secondary healthcare sources. Young people from minoritised ethnic backgrounds were less likely to report secondary healthcare contact than White peers.

CONCLUSION: Despite high numbers of young people screening positive for possible eating problems, rates of help seeking for any mental health concerns in this group were low. Within this subgroup, service contact varies by age, ethnicity, and psychiatric morbidity. Differences in service contact in this subgroup should be further explored.

title: Early predictors of the childhood dysregulation profile from ages 5 to 8: evidence from the UK household study
abstract: Childhood dysregulation profile (DP) involves co-occurring difficulties regulating emotions, behaviour and cognitions, and is associated with adverse outcomes. However, its early predictors are not well understood. We examined child- and family-related predictors of borderline and clinical DP symptoms at ages 5 and 8 years. Participants were 3,467 children from the UK Household Longitudinal Study. Parents reported on early child-related factors (infant regulatory problems, age 3 temperament and screen media use), prenatal exposures (smoking, alcohol) and postnatal family factors (parental psychological distress, stimulating home environment), and DP symptoms at ages 5 and 8 years. Hierarchical logistic regression analyses were conducted to examine predictors of borderline and clinical DP symptoms and their persistence over time. Negative affect at age 3 predicted borderline and clinical DP symptoms at ages 5 and 8 years, as well as symptom persistence. Other child-related predictors included impulsivity, impatience and irregularity, whereas family-related factors were not consistent predictors. These findings highlight the role of child temperament, particularly negative affect, in the development and persistence of dysregulation symptoms. Early identification of temperament-based risk factors may support targeted interventions to strengthen children's self-regulation skills before dysregulation difficulties become more persistent and difficult to modify.

title: Mobile Subthreshold Exercise Program (MSTEP) for Youth With Prolonged Concussion Recovery: A Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract:
Key Points Question Does a virtually delivered aerobic exercise program (Mobile Subthreshold Exercise Program [MSTEP]) improve recovery for youth with persistent postconcussive symptoms? Findings This randomized clinical trial found that MSTEP (aerobic exercise administered virtually) resulted in more rapid recovery and greater improvements in symptoms and health-related quality of life at 3 months compared to a stretching control. Benefit was only seen for those in an acute or subacute time window (<3 months from injury). Meaning Aerobic exercise following concussion can be effectively delivered virtually but only appears to provide benefit for individuals with acute or subacute symptoms.

Importance Research suggests that aerobic exercise improves recovery for youth with concussion; however, prior studies primarily focused on acute concussion and required multiple in-person visits. Objective To determine whether a virtually delivered aerobic exercise program improves recovery following concussion compared to a stretching control and examine potential moderators. Design, Setting, and Participants A randomized clinical trial was conducted from 2021 to 2025 comparing the Mobile Subthreshold Exercise Program (MSTEP) to a stretching control for 11- to 18-year-olds with concussion up to 1 year from injury. Participants were recruited from a variety of outpatient locations in 4 US states (Washington, Utah, Wisconsin, and Oregon). Recruitment and data collection occurred from March 2021 until October 2025, and data analysis occurred from November 2025 to April 2026. Interventions Youth randomized to MSTEP were provided activity trackers and an aerobic exercise program initiated at 60% of heart rate maximum. Exercise was advanced in intensity and duration over 6 weeks through weekly videoconferencing calls. Youth in the control group were given stretching exercises and similar weekly calls. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcomes included (1) concussive symptoms and (2) health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Secondary outcomes included sleep, depression, and anxiety. Moderation by sex, age, and time since injury was examined. Patients were followed up for 6 months. Results The sample included 210 participants, among whom 122 (58.1%) were female, mean (SD) age was 15.1 (2.2) years, and mean (SD) time since injury was 73.3 (63.3) days. Covariate-adjusted regression analysis showed significant improvement in concussive symptoms and HRQoL at all time points, with greater improvement in MSTEP compared to control at the 3-month time point for both concussive symptoms (β, −3.15; 95% CI, −6.05 to −0.25; adjusted P = .04) and HRQoL (β, 4.15; 95% CI, 0.64-7.66; adjusted P = .04). No significant differences by group were seen at 6 months. Nonlinear mixed-effects modeling with exponential decay showed significantly faster symptom recovery in MSTEP compared to control (difference in rates, −0.68; 95% CI, −2.22 to −0.04; P = .002). Secondary outcomes (sleep, depression, and anxiety) improved in all participants but were not different by group. Benefit of the intervention was only significant for individuals less than 3 months from injury (concussive symptoms: β, −4.44; 95% CI, −7.99 to −0.90; unadjusted P = .01; HRQoL: β, 6.64; 95% CI, 2.55-10.72; unadjusted P = .002). No evidence was found for moderation by other factors. Conclusions and Relevance Per the results of this randomized clinical trial, an aerobic exercise program improves speed of recovery following concussion for youth compared to stretching and can be delivered remotely. However, this type of program appears to be most beneficial for individuals with acute or subacute injury (<3 months since injury). Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04688255

This randomized clinical trial determines whether a virtually delivered aerobic exercise program improves recovery following concussion in youth compared to a stretching control and examines potential moderators.

title: Multimodal Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Relapse in Major Depressive Disorder
abstract:
Key Points Question Does machine learning–based integration of multiple data modalities, relative to single data modalities, improve relapse prediction in major depressive disorder? Findings In this prognostic study, depressive relapse within 2 years was predicted among 564 patients with major depressive disorder, with a highest classification accuracy of 64.43%. The best-performing classification model relied solely on 1 modality including few clinical features; integrating additional modalities of structural and functional neuroimaging, genetics, neurocognition, blood markers, and gut microbiome did not improve relapse prediction. Meaning Multimodal models did not improve prediction beyond a unimodal clinical model, while overall prognostic value for individual-level relapse remained limited.

Importance Early identification of patients at high risk of relapse is key to personalized preventive strategies in major depressive disorder (MDD). However, current predictive models do not adequately account for the multimodal factors contributing to MDD relapse and fail to provide clinically meaningful predictions. Objective To predict relapse within 2 years in patients with MDD by using a comprehensive machine learning pipeline that integrates an unprecedented set of multimodal data. Design, Setting, and Participants This naturalistic longitudinal prognostic study used data from the Marburg-Münster Affective Disorders Cohort Study, with baseline assessments collected from October 2014 to May 2019 and follow-up approximately 2 years later, between October 2016 and June 2021. Data analysis was conducted between July 2024 and June 2026. The study was performed at 2 sites in Germany (Marburg and Münster), with participants recruited from psychiatric inpatient and outpatient departments and the general population. Patients meeting diagnostic criteria for current or lifetime MDD without history of neurological or severe somatic conditions were included. Exposure Natural course of illness in patients with MDD. Main Outcomes and Measures Balanced accuracy (BACC) for binary prediction of relapse vs no relapse during 2-year follow-up served as the primary outcome. Baseline features comprised 9 modalities including clinical and psychometric data, 4 structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging modalities, genetics, neurocognition, blood markers, and gut microbiome. Results A total of 564 patients with a current or lifetime MDD diagnosis were included (367 female [65.1%]; mean [SD] age, 37.34 [13.38] years). A total of 270 patients relapsed during the 2-year follow-up, while 294 did not. Mean (SD) BACC for the prediction of relapse ranged from 47.21% (5.85%) to 64.43% (6.63%). The best-performing model was solely based on few clinical relapse risk factors, while multimodal data integration did not improve performance. Conclusions and Relevance In this prognostic study, the models achieved moderate accuracy, yet the results suggest limited scope for guiding individual-level clinical decision-making. Predictive performance was largely driven by established clinical risk factors, indicating limited incremental value of multimodal measures when assessed at a single time point. Future advances may instead benefit from dynamic modeling approaches that more closely align temporally evolving multimodal markers with longitudinal clinical outcomes.

This prognostic study evaluates whether relapse within 2 years can be predicted among patients with major depressive disorder by using a comprehensive machine learning pipeline that integrates an unprecedented set of multimodal data.

title: [Training teams in suicide risk assessment: the role of advanced practice nurses]
abstract: Suicide risk encompasses a variety of complex clinical situations that require specific skills on the part of nurses. A process of reflecting on past experiences provides a better understanding of the role of advanced practice nurses in their interdisciplinary collaboration and clinical leadership responsibilities. The implementation of a training program on suicide risk prevention at a medical-psychological center concretely illustrates their contribution to enhancing team competencies.

title: Media-based surveillance of suicide in Türkiye: a mixed-methods analysis of epidemiological patterns, homicide-suicide events, and contextual factors
abstract:
Background Suicide remains a major public health concern worldwide, yet official mortality statistics often provide limited information regarding the contextual circumstances surrounding suicide events. Media reports provide insights into demographic characteristics, suicide methods, homicide–suicide incidents, and the social contexts associated with these events. This study aimed to examine suicide cases reported in Turkish media using a mixed-methods approach with epidemiological surveillance and qualitative document analysis. Methods A convergent mixed-methods design was employed. Suicide-related news reports published in Turkish media between January and December 2025 were prospectively monitored and screened. After removing duplicate reports, 688 suicide cases were included in the quantitative analysis. Descriptive and inferential statistical analyses were conducted to examine demographic characteristics, suicide methods, geographic distribution, and homicide–suicide patterns. Qualitative document analysis was performed on contextual narratives from 179 suicide cases. Quantitative and qualitative findings were integrated during interpretation. Results Among the 688 media-reported suicide cases, 76.7% were male, 15.7% were female, and sex was not reported for the remaining 7.6%. Firearms (43.2%) and hanging (30.4%) were the most frequently reported suicide methods. Homicide–suicide was identified in 16.1% of cases and was significantly more common among males than females (20.3% vs. 2.8%, unadjusted OR = 8.90, 95% CI: 2.77–28.58, p < 0.001). Suicide method was significantly associated with homicide–suicide status ( p < 0.001). Among suicides involving firearms, 30.6% were classified as homicide–suicide. Within the media-reported sample, the proportion of cases classified as homicide–suicide differed significantly across regions. Qualitative analysis identified one descriptive event/legal category—violence, homicide–suicide event characteristics, and legal circumstances (31.8%)—and four contextual themes: physical and psychological health problems and addictions (26.3%); family and intimate relationship conflicts (24.6%); economic and occupational difficulties (15.6%); and social exclusion and social vulnerability (1.7%). Integration of findings indicated that homicide–suicide events were frequently embedded within narratives of domestic violence, relationship conflict, and legal problems, whereas psychological distress and economic hardship emerged as common contextual factors across suicide cases. Conclusion Media-reported suicide cases in Türkiye demonstrated distinct epidemiological and contextual patterns that should be interpreted within the context of media reporting rather than as representative of all suicide deaths in the country. Combining epidemiological surveillance with qualitative analysis provides complementary contextual information that may inform suicide prevention policies, responsible media reporting practices, and future research integrating official mortality data.

1 Introduction Suicide remains one of the most significant public health challenges worldwide, accounting for substantial mortality, disability, and social burden across populations. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), approximately 727,000 people died by suicide in 2021, representing more than one in every 100 deaths globally. Suicide is also among the leading causes of death among young people aged 15–29 years, highlighting its profound impact on individuals, families, communities, and healthcare systems ( 1 , 2 ). Despite advances in mental health care and suicide prevention initiatives, suicide continues to pose a major global health concern, reflecting the complex interaction of individual, social, economic, and environmental factors. Suicide is increasingly conceptualized as a public health outcome influenced not only by psychiatric disorders but also by broader social determinants of health, including unemployment, income insecurity, housing conditions, childhood adversity, social exclusion, and access to healthcare services ( 3 , 4 ). Although mental disorders remain among the strongest risk factors for suicidal behavior, growing evidence suggests that broader structural factors—including socioeconomic disadvantage, unemployment, debt burden, social isolation, relationship breakdown, exposure to violence, and limited access to support services—also play critical roles in suicide risk ( 3 , 5 ). Recent studies have highlighted the role of socioeconomic disadvantages, occupational vulnerability, and financial hardship in shaping suicide risk. Men experiencing socioeconomic adversity appear to be at particularly elevated risk, while debt burden has been consistently associated with suicidality and poor mental health outcomes ( 6 , 7 ). Consequently, understanding suicide requires approaches that extend beyond individual-level explanations and incorporate the broader social and contextual environments in which suicidal behaviors occur. Although global age-standardized suicide rates have declined in many regions over recent decades, important demographic and geographic disparities persist. Men consistently die by suicide at higher rates than women, and considerable variations exist across countries with respect to suicide mortality, age distributions, and associated risk factors ( 8 ). Access to lethal means remains an important determinant of suicide mortality, with firearms, hanging, and poisoning among the most commonly reported methods worldwide ( 2 ). These variations underscore the importance of country-specific surveillance systems and context-sensitive suicide prevention strategies that are informed by local epidemiological patterns and social contexts ( 2 ). In Türkiye, suicide has emerged as an increasingly important public health issue. According to the Turkish Statistical Institute (TURKSTAT), 4,460 individuals died by suicide in 2024, corresponding to a crude suicide rate of 5.22 per 100,000 population. Like global trends, males account for the majority of suicide deaths in Türkiye. Previous national studies have identified significant associations between suicide mortality and factors such as gender inequality, socioeconomic conditions, family structure, and regional disparities. Furthermore, recent research has emphasized the growing importance of suicide prevention among children and adolescents, drawing attention to the need for evidence-based interventions tailored to different population groups ( 9–11 ). Recent analysis of official Turkish Statistical Institute (TURKSTAT) mortality data (2007–2022) demonstrated sex-specific trends in suicide mortality, with increasing rates among males and a recent increase among females after 2019. The same study also reported rising suicide mortality among young adults aged 15–29 years ( 12 ). Reliable surveillance systems constitute a cornerstone of effective suicide prevention. Official mortality statistics provide essential information regarding suicide rates, demographic characteristics, and temporal trends ( 2 ). However, these databases often provide limited information regarding the social and contextual circumstances surrounding suicide events. Factors such as interpersonal conflicts, intimate partner violence, economic difficulties, legal problems, family disputes, and other precipitating life stressors are often not systematically documented in routine mortality statistics, highlighting the value of complementary data sources such as media reports ( 13 , 14 ). In recent years, media reports have increasingly been recognized as a valuable supplementary source of information for suicide surveillance. News reports frequently contain detailed descriptions of the circumstances surrounding suicide events, including information regarding family relationships, economic stressors, legal issues, mental health concerns, and social contexts that are often unavailable in official datasets. Consequently, media-based surveillance may contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of suicide by capturing contextual information that complements traditional epidemiological data. Media reports are increasingly used as secondary data sources to examine suicide patterns and contextual characteristics, particularly when timely surveillance data or detailed case-level information are unavailable. Although official mortality statistics remain the primary source for monitoring suicide epidemiology, media reports can provide complementary information on the circumstances surrounding suicide events. However, media coverage reflects journalistic selection and reporting practices rather than the complete epidemiology of suicide. Therefore, findings derived from media-based surveillance should be interpreted as reflecting reported cases and contextual narratives rather than the full distribution of suicide characteristics in the population ( 1 , 15 ). Beyond their role as information sources, media reports may themselves influence suicidal behavior. A substantial body of evidence has demonstrated associations between suicide reporting and subsequent suicide rates. Detailed descriptions of suicide methods, sensationalized headlines, repetitive coverage, and prominent reporting have been associated with increases in suicidal behavior, a phenomenon commonly referred to as the “Werther effect” ( 13 ). Conversely, responsible reporting practices that emphasize coping strategies, recovery, resilience, and help-seeking behaviors may contribute to protective effects, known as the “Papageno effect” ( 16 ). In response to these findings, the World Health Organization and other international organizations have developed evidence-based guidelines for responsible suicide reporting and have emphasized the importance of monitoring media coverage of suicide-related events ( 14 ). The role of media reporting is particularly relevant in Türkiye. Recent evaluations of Turkish media have indicated that suicide-related news reports frequently contain explicit descriptions of suicide methods, sensationalized language, and limited information regarding prevention resources or mental health support services. Such reporting practices may not fully align with international recommendations and may contribute to potentially harmful reporting effects. Moreover, analyses of high-profile suicide incidents and suicide clusters in Türkiye have raised concerns regarding possible contagion and copycat effects associated with intensive media coverage ( 15 , 17 ). These findings underscore the need for continued examination of suicide reporting practices within the Turkish media landscape. An especially severe but understudied form of lethal violence is homicide–suicide, defined as the killing of one or more individuals followed by the perpetrator’s suicide. Homicide–suicide events frequently occur in the context of intimate partner violence, family conflicts, firearm access, and severe psychosocial stressors ( 18 ). These incidents represent a unique intersection between suicide prevention, violence prevention, and public safety and often generate considerable public and media attention. Despite their public health significance, homicide–suicide events remain insufficiently investigated in many countries, including Türkiye, and are not routinely examined within official surveillance systems ( 18 ). Although previous research in Türkiye has primarily focused on official mortality statistics and quantitative analyses of suicide trends, relatively little is known about the epidemiological characteristics and contextual narratives of suicide cases reported in the media. Furthermore, few studies have integrated quantitative epidemiological analyses with qualitative exploration of contextual factors associated with suicide events. A mixed-methods approach may therefore provide a more comprehensive understanding of suicide by combining epidemiological surveillance with qualitative examination of the social, economic, psychological, and relational circumstances described in media reports. Specifically, the combination of prospective daily media monitoring, quantitative characterization of homicide–suicide events, and qualitative analysis of case-level contextual narratives remains underexamined in Türkiye. Therefore, this study aimed to examine suicide cases reported in Turkish media using a convergent mixed-methods design. Specifically, the study sought to (1) describe the epidemiological characteristics of suicide cases, including demographic features, suicide methods, geographic distribution, and homicide–suicide patterns, and (2) identify and analyze contextual factors associated with suicide through qualitative document analysis of media reports. By integrating quantitative and qualitative findings, this study aims to contribute to suicide prevention research, public health surveillance, and the development of evidence-informed recommendations for responsible media reporting in Türkiye. 2 Methods 2.1 Study design The present study used a convergent mixed-methods methodology to analyze suicide instances reported in Turkish online news media in 2025. Quantitative studies were used to describe the epidemiological characteristics of suicide cases, demographic factors, regional distribution, suicide methods, and homicide-suicide events. Qualitative theme analysis was also conducted to analyze the contextual elements and stories of suicide as reported in the media. The results of the two components were merged in the interpretation process to reach a thorough understanding of suicide instances in the Turkish news coverage. 2.2 Data collection Data were collected through daily monitoring of Google Alerts using the Turkish keywords “İntihar” (“Suicide”) and “Kendini Öldürdü” (“Killed Himself/Herself”). Google Alerts notifications were checked daily from January 1, 2025, to January 15, 2026. Data collection continued until January 15, 2026. Only suicide episodes that occurred between January 1 and December 31, 2025, were included in the study. title: The effectiveness of meaning-based interventions in reducing suicide-related vulnerability: A systematic review
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Existential factors such as loss of meaning play a central role in suicide-related vulnerability, yet most prevention interventions target symptom reduction. We aimed to systematically review the effects of meaning-based interventions on suicide-related outcomes and characterize the mechanisms through which these effects operate.

METHODS: A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Six databases (PubMed, Web of Science, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Research Information Sharing Service, and Korean Studies Information Service System) were searched from inception to April 2026. Studies were included if they evaluated meaning-based interventions and reported suicide-related outcomes. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 for randomized trials and RoBANS for nonrandomized studies. Given heterogeneity across populations, interventions, and outcomes, findings were synthesized narratively by domain.

RESULTS: Ten studies were included (7 randomized controlled trials, 2 quasi-experimental studies, and 1 secondary analysis). Meaning-based interventions most consistently improved existential outcomes, including meaning in life, spiritual well-being, and quality of life. Emotional outcomes showed partial and heterogeneous effects. Suicide-related outcomes, including hopelessness, demoralization, and suicidal ideation, generally showed reductions, although effects varied across studies. Mechanistically, most studies showed patterns of indirect pathways, whereby improvements in existential variables co-occurred with reductions in emotional and suicide-related outcomes.

SIGNIFICANCE OF RESULTS: Meaning-based interventions may reduce suicide-related vulnerability primarily by enhancing existential resources rather than directly targeting symptoms. These findings support integrating meaning-centered approaches into suicide prevention strategies and highlight the need for longitudinal and mediation-based studies to examine causal mechanisms.

title: Bipolar Disorder and the Risk of Cardiovascular Diseases: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Observational Studies
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a chronic psychiatric illness characterized by recurrent manic and depressive episodes, affecting 2% of the global population. It is associated with premature mortality, including cardiovascular disease (CVD)-related mortality. Although clinically important, the absolute burden and incidence of cardiovascular outcomes in BD remain incompletely characterized. This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized observational evidence on CVD prevalence and incidence in adults with BD.

METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines and prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD42023484712), we searched PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Scopus, and PsycInfo, screening 11,909 records. Thirty-two observational studies in adults with BD were included after Newcastle-Ottawa Scale assessment. Data were extracted on overall CVD, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, peripheral arterial disease, comorbidities, and psychotropic exposure. Pooled prevalence and incidence rate ratios were calculated using random-effects models when data were comparable.

RESULTS: The pooled CVD prevalence in BD was 7.70% (95% CI: 5.07-11.52), with coronary artery disease at 6.89% (95% CI: 4.05-11.47), cerebrovascular disease at 4.45% (95% CI: 2.13-9.05), and peripheral arterial disease at 3.30% (95% CI: 1.66-6.45). However, prevalence estimates showed extreme heterogeneity and should be interpreted as broad indicators of absolute burden rather than precise estimates for a single BD population. In controlled incidence studies, BD was associated with increased CVD incidence (IRR 1.66, 95% CI: 1.32-2.08), with elevated coronary and cerebrovascular estimates. Clinical variable analyses involving medication use, lifestyle factors, and cardiometabolic comorbidities were not feasible because reporting was insufficient and noncomparable.

CONCLUSION: Adults with BD show substantial cardiovascular burden and increased incidence. However, extreme heterogeneity, limited incidence data, observational designs, and insufficient moderator reporting limit the precision and generalizability of pooled estimates. These findings support integrated cardiovascular screening in BD populations and future prospective studies.

TRAIL REGISTRATION: PROSPERO CRD42023484712.

title: Digital Therapeutic Interventions for Suicide Prevention: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Their Effectiveness in Reducing Suicidal Ideation and Suicide Attempts
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Although digital interventions show potential for reducing suicidal ideation and behavior, the evidence base is mixed and characterized by methodological variability. This study synthesizes randomized clinical trials that have evaluated their effectiveness.

METHOD: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Seventeen studies ( N  = 5.089) met the inclusion criteria. Effect sizes were estimated using random-effects models, and we conducted analyses for type of control group (traditional vs. active), moderators (age, delivery setting, and intervention format), and follow-up. Heterogeneity and publication bias were also examined.

RESULTS: Digital interventions significantly reduced suicidal ideation ( g  = -0.61), with effects maintained at follow up ( g  = -0.77). Significant effects were observed with respect to both traditional and active controls. There was a moderate reduction in relative risk of suicide attempts, although it was not statistically significant. Moderator analysis indicated a greater effect for clinical populations, self-guided interventions, and younger participants. There was no robust evidence of publication bias.

CONCLUSIONS: Digital interventions may represent a promising complementary approach for reducing suicidal ideation and potentially lowering suicide risk. However, the findings should be interpreted cautiously given the heterogeneity of the studies and the limited evidence regarding suicide attempts.

title: Suicide mortality among survivors of first primary thyroid cancer: a population-based competing risk analysis
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Thyroid cancer is associated with favorable survival, yet suicide risk during long-term survivorship remains incompletely characterized, particularly in the presence of competing mortality.

METHODS: We identified 178,014 patients with first primary thyroid cancer from the SEER 17 database between 2000 and 2022. Suicide mortality was quantified using standardized mortality ratios. Risk factors were evaluated using cause-specific Cox models and Fine-Gray competing risk regression, with non-suicide deaths treated as competing events.

RESULTS: During 1,566,507 person-years of follow-up, 165 suicides occurred, corresponding to 10.53 deaths per 100,000 person-years. Overall suicide mortality was comparable to that of the general population. In cause-specific Cox models, older age, no surgery, and chemotherapy appeared associated with suicide risk. These associations did not reach statistical significance in the Fine-Gray model. Male sex, single status, and separated/divorced status remained independently associated with higher suicide incidence, whereas the highest area-level median household income category was associated with lower suicide incidence.

CONCLUSION: Sociodemographic factors were associated with suicide incidence in the Fine-Gray model, supporting attention to psychosocial vulnerability alongside disease-related needs. These findings support incorporating social vulnerability assessment, psychosocial screening, and referral pathways into supportive care for patients with thyroid cancer.

title: Identifying capacity building priorities for implementation science in suicide prevention: a concept mapping study in Australia
abstract:
Abstract Background Capacity building in the science and practice of implementation is critical for driving and evaluating meaningful change. However, capacity needs of stakeholders to effectively apply implementation science in suicide prevention remain unclear. Purpose To address this gap in Australia, we conducted a concept mapping (CM) study to identify and prioritize stakeholder capacity-building needs in this area. Methods Diverse stakeholders: practitioners, lived experience advocates, researchers, public servants, and clinicians working within the suicide prevention sector in Australia participated in the study. Using CM, participants individually brainstormed statements representing capacity-building needs for implementation science for suicide prevention. These statements were then organized in clusters and rated on importance and feasibility. Data were collected, analyzed, and visually represented using the groupwisdom™ platform. Results In total, 52 stakeholders participated in at least one stage of the study (i.e. brainstorming, sorting and/or rating). Brainstorming generated 59 statements, which were synthesized into 53 distinctive statements and supplemented with 13 statements from the literature. A multidimensional scaling and hierarchical cluster analysis generated many cluster solutions, out of which an eight-cluster solution was chosen as the most meaningful. Knowledge dissemination and lived experience integration clusters were rated highest on importance and feasibility. Conclusions This study provides a snapshot of implementation capacity-building needs and priorities within the suicide prevention sector in Australia. The identified priorities can help inform future sector capacity-building initiatives for implementation.

Teaser What does it take to build implementation capacity in suicide prevention? Our study shows that training alone may not be enough; highlighting the need for coordinated, system-level initiatives to meet diverse stakeholder needs and drive meaningful impact.

Implications Practice: Programs to strengthen capacity for implementation in suicide prevention must be conceptualized and delivered across multiple system levels. Such programs must move beyond individual training and extend their reach beyond academic and research audiences. Policy: Concerted efforts toward incorporating diverse perspectives of stakeholders in the sector are needed to foster partnerships, collaboration, and enable policy environments that strengthen sector-wide evidence translation. Research: The study highlights gaps in stakeholder-specific capacity needs and tailored implementation strategies to effectively deliver these targeted initiatives. Introduction Suicide is a complex, multifaceted issue, making its prevention particularly challenging [ 1 ]. Recently, there is an emphasis on a public health approach to prevention, recognizing that risk factors are rooted in broader social determinants [ 2 ]. However, despite growing investment, there remains limited translational evidence to guide policy and practice [ 3 ]. Significant methodological challenges hinder understanding of what works, for whom, and in which contexts [ 4 ]. Implementation science is “the study of methods to promote the systematic uptake of evidence-based interventions into practice and policy to improve health” [ 5 ] (p. 1). The field has two key focus areas: implementation research and implementation practice. Implementation research seeks to understand and evaluate approaches used to translate evidence to the real world [ 6 ]. Implementation practice seeks to apply and adapt these approaches in different contexts and settings to achieve positive outcomes [ 6 ]. Despite its growth and integration across multiple disciplines, implementation science continues to face limitations in its broader applicability [ 7 ]. The use of implementation research and practice in suicide prevention remains inconsistent and under-prioritized [ 8 , 9 ]. Contributing factors for this challenge arise from both suicide prevention and implementation science. These include methodological challenges, limited translational examples, inadequate stakeholder collaboration [ 3 , 10 , 11 ]; disciplinary silos [ 12 ]; limited guidance on co-production and stakeholder engagement [ 13 , 14 ]; and rigid adherence to evidence-related paradigms [ 7 ]. Beyond a paradigmatic shift, strengthening implementation science in suicide prevention may require building capacity across the spectrum, from general awareness to advanced application and training of implementation science [ 7 , 15 , 16 ]. Capacity building for implementation science has been described as activities (e.g. training, identification of alternative resources, building internal assets) that build durable resources and enable the recipient setting or community to continue the delivery of an evidence-based intervention [ 17 ]. Six strategies for capacity building have been identified: training, tools, technical assistance, assessment and feedback, peer networking, and incentives. Capacity for implementation research and practice is specialized and multidimensional, requiring not only knowledge of implementation theory and methods but also competencies in stakeholder engagement [ 18 ]. Identified competencies span setting-specific knowledge, research methodology, management, communication, and collaboration [ 6 , 18 , 19 ]. Although stakeholder needs for capacity building have been explored through interviews, surveys, and concept mapping (CM) [ 19–21 ], gaps remain in understanding practical skill development and the “art and craft” of implementation [ 22 ]. Although recognition of implementation science in suicide prevention is increasing [ 23 ], its inconsistent application [ 8 ] suggests a significant capacity gap within the sector. This issue has attracted growing attention from policymakers and sector leaders, alongside broader efforts to strengthen the translation, implementation, and sustainability of suicide prevention initiatives. Our previous work has highlighted the limited and variable use of implementation science approaches in suicide prevention and identified a need to build implementation capacity among stakeholders [ 8 ]. Our international Delphi study with stakeholders across the sector further identified capacity building as a key strategy for advancing the use of implementation science in suicide prevention, highlighting the need to better understand stakeholders’ ability to apply these approaches and address the evidence–practice gap [ 24 ]. Despite growing interest in this area, there remains limited research examining implementation science capacity-building needs specific to suicide prevention. This study therefore builds on this emerging body of work by identifying and examining stakeholder capacity-building needs and priorities in Australia to support the effective use of implementation science in suicide prevention. Methods The study adopted a CM approach, a systematic participatory approach that integrates qualitative data collection with quantitative analytical techniques [ 25 ]. Unlike surveys and interviews, CM moves beyond the identification and examination of perspectives by enabling participants to generate, organize, and prioritize ideas [ 26 ]. Moreover, rather than encouraging convergence towards consensus, as is the aim of Delphi methods, CM accommodates diverse perspectives and provides a structured means of understanding both common priorities and differing perspectives across stakeholder groups [ 27 ]. This is particularly important in suicide prevention, a multidisciplinary field characterized by a diverse range of stakeholders whose differing roles, experiences, and priorities may influence perceptions of implementation science capacity-building needs. Data collection comprises two primary activities: (i) brainstorming responses that characterize the issue of interest, which are based on a focus prompt (“To build capacity for implementation research and practice in suicide prevention, we need…”); and (ii) sorting the statements generated during brainstorming into groups of conceptually related ideas, followed by rating them on relevant scales (e.g. importance and feasibility). Although the literature recommends a minimum sample size of 10 participants each for sorting and rating, many studies comprise samples of 20 or more participants [ 28 ]. Data analysis involves multidimensional scaling (MDS) and hierarchical cluster analysis to position each statement as a point that can be visually displayed across a series of conceptual maps. These visualizations illustrate the relationships among statements [ 27 ]. Recruitment of participants Participants were recruited using purposive and snowball sampling to ensure the inclusion of individuals with relevant expertise and experience in suicide prevention and implementation science. Consistent with CM methodology, the aim was to capture a breadth of informed perspectives on the topic rather than achieve population representativeness [ 29 ]. Participants were recruited using the Australian Institute for Suicide Research and Prevention’s email distribution list, social media links, and via a newsletter from the LIFEWAYS project. Additionally, members of the research team shared a study flyer on social media. Potential participants were provided with an overview of the study with links to an online participant information sheet and consent form. They were encouraged to share this invitation with others who may be interested in the study. After participants completed the consent form, they were directed to the Concept Systems groupwisdom™ data collection platform to create an account. Participants completed the five socio-demographic questions: the role(s) they identified with (researcher, practitioner, clinician, lived experience, public servant); the primary role they identified with; their primary work setting (university, research institute, not-for-profit organization, health authority, government, private sector, other); age; and gender. Data were collected from October to December 2025, with a three-week gap between the brainstorming and sorting tasks. Member checking was not undertaken, considering the participatory nature of the CM process with participants contributing directly to the generation, structuring, and interpretation of ideas. All the data collection and analyses were conducted using the groupwisdom™ Group Concept Systems platform. Griffith University Human Research Ethics Committee approved all procedures for this study (2025/764). Brainstorming The following definitions were used to prepare participants for the brainstorming task: Implementation: Involves efforts to put evidence-based programs or practices into use by applying effective strategies for change [ 30 ]. Implementation research: Studies how to move evidence into real-world use to achieve desired outcomes [ 6 ]. Implementation practice: Focuses on applying and adapting these evidence-based approaches in different settings to achieve desired outcomes [ 6 ]. Capacity building: Involves activities that strengthen skills, resources, and support to enable an individual, community, or organization to continue delivering an evidence-based program [ 17 ]. Participants were directed to consider these definitions and provide responses to the focus prompt: “To build capacity for implementation research and practice in suicide prevention, we need…”. There was no limit to the number of responses/statements that could be provided. This task was open for three weeks with two reminder emails sent to participants about completing brainstorming. Members of the research team (S.K., L.T.B., L.R., K.K.) reviewed and synthesized the resulting statements over two meetings until these were distinct and clear. The original wording of statements was retained as much as possible. Complementary statements ( n = 13) were added from research literature on implementation science-related capacity-building initiatives to ensure that important aspects identified in prior research were represented in the study. Statement sorting and rating The sorting task asked participants to “Sort the statements into piles in a way that makes sense to you. Group the statements on how similar in meaning or closely related they are to one another.” The participants were presented with the statements in random order and were instructed to create between 5 and 15 groups of statements, assigning descriptive names to each group. They were advised to avoid grouping statements by priority or placing unrelated statements into a generic “other” category. Participants were then asked to rate each statement in terms of importance and the feasibility of accomplishing the activities. Specifically, participants were asked to rate, on a five-point scale, the importance of each statement as an activity/strategy for capacity building in implementation research and practice in suicide prevention (1 = less important; 5 = more important), and the feasibility of addressing each activity/strategy (1 = less feasible; 5 = more feasible). Data analysis After all activities were completed, the data were reviewed to confirm usability. Participants with incomplete submissions (e.g. completion of only one of the two rating tasks) were prompted to finish the remaining activities through personalized emails. Participants who sorted fewer than 75% of the statements into meaningful categories were excluded from analysis. The 75% completion threshold represents a pragmatic data quality criterion commonly used in CM practice. To minimize the influence of uniform response patterns (i.e. the tendency to assign similar ratings across all statements), participants were informed that the rating scales should be interpreted as relative rather than absolute measures and were encouraged to use the full range of response options available. Participants’ rating data were excluded if their responses did not span at least three of the five available scale points (i.e. 1–3, 2–4, 3–5) [ 31 ]. This was applied to ensure sufficient discrimination between statements and meaningful contribution to the prioritization analyses [ 26 ]. Statistical analyses began with the construction of a similarity matrix, which served as input for nonmetric MDS to generate a two-dimensional point map. The MDS procedure produced a stress value (0–1) to evaluate the goodness of fit between the point map and the original sorting data. Hierarchical cluster analysis using Ward’s method was then applied to the point map to derive a cluster solution consisting of nonoverlapping clusters. Because there is no established mathematical criterion for determining the optimal number of clusters in CM, we followed recommended practice by first identifying the maximum number of clusters deemed interpretable [ 32 ]. title: [Efficacy and tolerability of co-administration of clozapine with atypical antipsychotics in patients with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, comorbid with chemical addictions]
journal: Zh Nevrol Psikhiatr Im S S Korsakova
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To compare the efficacy and tolerability of combination therapy with clozapine and atypical antipsychotics for patients with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, comorbid with chemical addictions.

MATERIAL AND METHODS: A clinical study was conducted from 2018 to 2026 in various psychiatric departments in the North-Western, Siberian, and Ural regions of the Russian Federation. The study included a total of 470 male and female participants diagnosed with therapeutically resistant paranoid schizophrenia, comprising individuals with and without concomitant chemical addictions:  n= 80 without addictions;  n= 390 with unrelated chemical addictions (opioid, cannabinoid, psychostimulant, and ethanol dependence). Participants were randomly allocated into six treatment groups receiving distinct combinations of medications: clozapine with cariprazine ( n= 84), lurasidone ( n= 84), aripiprazole ( n= 78), risperidone ( n= 84), olanzapine ( n= 70), or brexpiprazole ( n= 70). The clinical status of patients was assessed at weeks 2 and 6 of the therapeutic regimen.

RESULTS: A comparative analysis of treatment efficacy indicated significant differences between therapy groups across various psychometric scales ( p <0.05). The co-administration of clozapine with cariprazine, and to a lesser extent with lurasidone, demonstrated the most pronounced therapeutic effect within a 42-day treatment period ( p< 0.05), specifically in alleviating psychotic symptoms and reducing the negative symptoms characteristic of schizophrenia, as compared to alternative combinations, thereby extending the duration of outpatient treatment.

CONCLUSIONS: A comprehensive treatment strategy for therapeutically resistant schizophrenia, irrespective of concomitant addictions, is the combination of clozapine with cariprazine; lurasidone serves as an alternative option. The selection of an effective adjunctive therapy should consider the specific type of addiction: lurasidone or aripiprazole is recommended for cannabinoid, psychostimulant, and alcohol dependencies; risperidone or olanzapine is advised for opioid and alcohol dependencies. The combination with brexpiprazole is deemed ineffective. Notable advantages of this approach include a marked effect on negative symptoms and an extension of the outpatient treatment period. No adverse events associated with the combination therapy were reported.

ЦЕЛЬ ИССЛЕДОВАНИЯ: Сравнить эффективность и переносимость комбинированной терапии клозапином с атипичными антипсихотиками при терапевтически резистентной шизофрении с коморбидными химическими аддикциями.

МАТЕРИАЛ И МЕТОДЫ: В течение 2018—2026 гг. осуществлялось клиническое исследование в условиях психиатрических отделений Северо-Западного, Сибирского и Уральского регионов РФ. В работе приняли участие 470 молодых мужчин и женщин с диагнозом «терапевтически устойчивая параноидная шизофрения» без сопутствующих зависимостей ( n= 80) и с наличием химических аддикций ( n= 390), характеризующихся различными формами зависимости (от опиоидов, каннабиноидов, психостимуляторов, этанола). Пациенты методом случайных чисел распределялись в одну из 6 групп комбинированной медикаментозной терапии: клозапин в сочетании с карипразином ( n= 84), луразидоном ( n= 84), арипипразолом ( n= 78), рисперидоном ( n= 84), оланзапином ( n= 70), брекспипразолом ( n= 70). Клиническое состояние пациентов оценивали на 2-й и 6-й неделях проводимой комплексной терапии.

РЕЗУЛЬТАТЫ: Сравнительный анализ эффективности терапии показал различия между терапевтическими группами по ряду психометрических шкал ( p <0,05). Совместное использование клозапина с карипразином, в меньшей степени с луразидоном в рамках 42 дней терапии демонстрирует наиболее заметный эффект ( p <0,05) в отношении купирования психотической симптоматики и смягчения негативных симптомов шизофрении по сравнению с другими комбинациями, увеличивает период амбулаторного лечения.

ЗАКЛЮЧЕНИЕ: Универсальная стратегия в лечении терапевтически резистентной шизофрении вне зависимости от коморбидности с аддикциями — сочетание клозапина с карипразином, альтернативой является луразидон. Выбор эффективного адъюванта должен осуществляться с учетом аддикции: луразидон или арипипразол — при каннабиноидной, психостимуляторной и алкогольной, рисперидон или оланзапин — при опиоидной и алкогольной. Комбинация с брекспипразолом малоэффективна. Преимуществами подхода являются выраженное воздействие на дефицитарную симптоматику, увеличение амбулаторного периода. Нежелательных явлений, ассоциированных с комбинированной терапией, не зарегистрировано.

title: Age-specific profiles of suicide warning signs among Korean suicide decedents, 2013-2020
abstract:
Introduction Suicide warning signs may provide important opportunities for early recognition and intervention, yet their presentation may vary across the life course. However, population-level evidence on age-specific patterns of suicide warning signs remains limited. This study examined age-group differences in the presence and types of suicide warning signs among suicide decedents in South Korea. Methods We analyzed data from the Korean National Investigations of Suicide Deaths Through Police Records, 2013–2020. The analytic sample included 96,501 suicide decedents with valid information on age group and warning sign status. Participants were categorized as children/adolescents, young adults, middle-aged adults, or older adults. Chi-square tests were used to examine age-group differences in the presence of any warning sign, and binary logistic regression was conducted to assess age-group differences in any warning sign. Separate item-level logistic regression models were used for specific warning signs. Results Overall, 92.9% of suicide decedents had at least one warning sign. The proportion was highest among older adults (95.1%) and lowest among children/adolescents (87.4%). Compared with older adults, all younger age groups had lower odds of having any recorded warning sign. The types of warning signs also differed by age. Verbal warning signs, particularly complaints of physical discomfort, were more characteristic of older adults, whereas emotional warning signs were more prominent among children/adolescents and young adults. Behavioral warning signs were more frequently observed among younger and middle-aged adults than among older adults. Conclusion Suicide warning signs vary substantially across age groups, suggesting that a uniform approach to warning sign recognition may overlook age-specific patterns. These findings may inform future age-sensitive recognition strategies and improvements in suicide mortality surveillance.

1 Introduction Suicide prevention requires attention not only to who is at risk, but also to how suicide risk becomes observable before death. Although psychiatric disorders, previous self-harm, substance misuse, and adverse social circumstances are well-established risk factors for suicide mortality, these factors do not always indicate when a suicidal crisis is becoming imminent ( 1 , 2 ). In addition, many people who die by suicide have limited or no contact with mental health services before death, reducing the effectiveness of prevention strategies that depend primarily on clinical detection ( 3 ). These limitations highlight the need to examine warning signs that may be observed outside clinical settings, including by family members, peers, neighbors, community workers, and other people who encounter individuals in their everyday lives. Suicide warning signs are conceptually different from distal risk factors. Risk factors indicate vulnerability over time, whereas warning signs refer to observable verbal, behavioral, or emotional changes that may suggest more immediate suicide risk ( 4 ). Such signs may include communication about death or suicide, marked changes in behavior, withdrawal from others, emotional instability, substance misuse, or other deviations from usual functioning. Because warning signs are closer to the suicidal crisis, they may provide practical opportunities for earlier recognition and timely intervention. Despite their prevention relevance, warning signs have received less systematic attention than broader suicide risk factors. Prior research has shown that warning signs can be difficult to recognize because they may be indirect, context-dependent, or interpreted as ordinary distress rather than as indicators of suicide risk ( 5 ). Korean studies using psychological autopsy or police-record-based data have also shown that warning signs are frequently documented before suicide and may vary by timing, psychiatric history, and observability ( 6–8 ). These findings suggest that warning signs should not be treated simply as a single yes-or-no phenomenon; rather, their specific forms and meanings may differ depending on the characteristics and life context of the decedent. Age is one of the key contexts that may shape how suicide warning signs are expressed and recognized. Across the life course, individuals differ in developmental tasks, social roles, health status, interpersonal relationships, communication patterns, and help-seeking behavior. These differences may influence whether suicide risk becomes visible through verbal expressions, behavioral changes, emotional symptoms, physical complaints, or disclosure of suicidal intent. Recent studies support this age-sensitive perspective. Research on Korean adolescents has shown that warning signs may be difficult to recognize when emotional distress is concealed or when outward school and peer functioning appears relatively preserved ( 8 ). Studies of adult and older adult suicide decedents have also found that suicidal intent disclosure and its correlates differ by age group, with age-related variation in the roles of relationship problems, health problems, suicide means, and other contextual factors ( 9 , 10 ). Together, these findings indicate that suicide warning signs may be better understood as age-specific profiles rather than as uniform indicators that appear similarly across all decedents. Korea is an important setting in which to examine age-specific warning sign profiles. Suicide remains a major public health concern in Korea, and recent OECD data indicate that Korea continues to report suicide rates above the OECD average ( 11 ). However, large-scale national evidence on how warning signs differ across age groups among Korean suicide decedents remains limited. Most previous work has focused on the overall presence of warning signs, specific clinical subgroups, or selected age groups ( 1 , 12 , 13 ). Less is known about how verbal, behavioral, and emotional warning signs are distributed across adolescents, young adults, middle-aged adults, and older adults within the same national dataset. Therefore, this study examined age-specific profiles of suicide warning signs among Korean suicide decedents using data from The Korean National Investigations of Suicide Deaths Through Police Records from 2013 to 2020. Specifically, this study compared the presence of any warning sign across children/adolescents, young adults, middle-aged adults, and older adults, and examined age-group differences in specific verbal, behavioral, and emotional warning signs. 2 Methods 2.1 Study design and reporting framework This study used a retrospective secondary data analysis design. The manuscript was prepared with reference to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) recommendations for observational studies ( 14 ). The study examined age-specific profiles of suicide-related warning signs among Korean suicide decedents. 2.2 Data source and study population Data were obtained from The Korean National Investigations of Suicide Deaths Through Police Records, a nationwide database based on police investigation records of deaths officially concluded as suicide in Korea. The database was coded by trained investigators at the Korea Foundation for Suicide Prevention, an agency under the Ministry of Health and Welfare. The present analysis used data from suicide decedents recorded between 2013 and 2020. The original dataset included 102,922 suicide decedents. User-defined missing values were treated as missing in all analyses. No weighting, filtering, or split-file procedure was applied. Because missingness differed across variables, analyses were conducted using analysis-specific valid cases. The primary cross-tabulation of age group and the presence of any suicide warning sign included 96,501 valid cases; 6,421 cases were excluded from this analysis because age group or warning sign status was missing or coded as unknown. The primary logistic regression model including age group and sex included 96,487 valid cases; 14 additional cases were excluded because of missing sex. For item-level logistic regression models, analytic sample sizes varied by warning sign item because of variable-specific missingness. 2.3 Measures The main independent variable was age group. Age was originally recorded in 5-year categories and recoded into four life-course groups: children/adolescents aged 19 years or younger, young adults aged 20–39 years, middle-aged adults aged 40–64 years, and older adults aged 65 years or older. These cutoffs were selected to distinguish minors and school-age youth, early and established adulthood, midlife adulthood, and later life. Because the source data were provided in 5-year age bands, the <=19 years group included preadolescent children as well as adolescents. In the logistic regression analyses, older adults served as the reference group. The primary outcome was the presence of any suicide-related warning sign before death. Warning signs were conceptualized as observable verbal, behavioral, or emotional indicators that may suggest more immediate suicide risk, distinct from more distal suicide risk factors ( 4 ). Warning sign information was coded from police investigation reports that had been prepared based on sources such as statements from bereaved family members, acquaintances, and coworkers, as well as suicide notes when available. The Korea Foundation for Suicide Prevention provided standardized coding training to investigators, and investigators who completed this training coded the police investigation reports. The original warning sign variable was recoded into a binary variable, with cases coded as 1 if at least one warning sign was present and 0 if no warning sign was identified in the record-based coding framework. Thus, a code of absence indicates that the warning sign was coded as absent based on the available police investigation report, while still reflecting the inherent limits of retrospective record-based ascertainment. Specific warning signs were examined in three domains: verbal, behavioral, and emotional warning signs. Verbal warning signs included statements about suicide, homicide, or death; complaints of physical discomfort; and self-deprecating statements. Behavioral warning signs included indifference to appearance management; self-harm, suicide attempts, or substance misuse; and apathy, interpersonal withdrawal, or loss of interest. Emotional warning signs included depressed mood, elevated mood, and anxiety. In the original coding framework, elevated mood referred to a state that included mood that was unusually elevated compared with the decedent’s usual state, emotional elevation, excitement, or agitation before death. Each warning sign item was coded as present or absent within the standardized record-based coding framework. Because multiple warning signs could be recorded for the same decedent, the specific warning sign items were analyzed as non-mutually exclusive indicators. Sex was included as a covariate in the primary adjusted logistic regression model for the presence of any warning sign, with female decedents serving as the reference group. 2.4 Statistical analysis All statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS. First, frequencies and percentages were calculated to describe the distribution of suicide warning signs by age group. The presence of any warning sign was summarized as a binary outcome, and the composition of verbal, behavioral, and emotional warning sign occurrences was described within each age group. Second, chi-square tests were conducted to examine whether the presence of any warning sign differed across age groups. The primary cross-tabulation compared warning sign presence versus absence among children/adolescents, young adults, middle-aged adults, and older adults. Third, binary logistic regression was performed to estimate age-group differences in the presence of any warning sign. The primary adjusted model included age group and sex as predictors. Odds ratios (ORs), 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and p -values were reported. Finally, separate binary logistic regression models were conducted for each specific verbal, behavioral, and emotional warning sign item to examine age-group differences in specific warning signs. Older adults were used as the reference group in these models. These item-level models included age group only and were not adjusted for sex because their purpose was to describe age-specific warning sign profiles rather than to estimate sex-adjusted independent age effects for each item. Accordingly, they were interpreted as descriptive age-group comparisons rather than causal or fully adjusted estimates. Analytic sample sizes were 82,795–82,813 for verbal warning sign models, 76,912–76,918 for behavioral warning sign models, and 76,232–76,255 for emotional warning sign models. Together, the descriptive comparisons and item-level regression analyses were used to characterize age-specific profiles of suicide warning signs. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. For descriptive analyses of warning sign domains, percentages were calculated based on warning sign occurrences rather than mutually exclusive person-level categories, because a single decedent could have more than one warning sign. Accordingly, these percentages describe the composition of warning sign occurrences within each age group and should not be interpreted as person-level prevalence of each domain. 2.5 Ethical considerations This study used de-identified secondary data derived from police investigation records. The study was granted an exemption from institutional review board review (IRB No. E2509/003-010). Data access and analysis were conducted in a secure data environment managed by the Korea Foundation for Suicide Prevention. Export of raw data was restricted, and only approved statistical output files were released for research use. 3 Results 3.1 Presence of suicide warning signs across age groups Among 96,501 suicide decedents with valid data on age group and warning sign status, 89,668 (92.9%) had at least one suicide warning sign. As described in the Methods, this variable was derived from standardized coding of police investigation reports and should be interpreted within the record-based ascertainment process. The proportion of decedents with warning signs differed significantly across age groups [ χ 2 (3) = 433.202, p < 0.001]. Warning signs were most frequently observed among older adults (95.1%), followed by middle-aged adults (92.9%), young adults (90.9%), and children/adolescents (87.4%) ( Table 1 ). In the adjusted logistic regression model including age group and sex, all age groups younger than older adults had significantly lower odds of having any warning sign.
