title: The interaction between progesterone and glucocorticoid signaling on pregnancy-related mood symptoms
abstract: Postpartum depression (PPD) is a heterogeneous disorder whose biological basis remains incompletely understood. Although the rapid postpartum decline in progesterone and its neuroactive metabolite allopregnanolone has been implicated in PPD, this hormonal transition occurs in all pregnant individuals, whereas only a subset develop depression. This review proposes a two-hit framework in which early-life adversity establishes persistent, maladaptive stress-system vulnerability and pregnancy-related progesterone exposure subsequently interacts with that altered system to increase depression risk. Adverse childhood experiences may dysregulate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis through genetic and epigenetic mechanisms involving stress response genes. Progesterone and glucocorticoid signaling may converge because their receptors, which are structurally similar, recognize related hormone-response elements and regulate overlapping gene networks. In other words, progesterone may contribute to psychiatric symptoms by activating stress response genes. Associations between progesterone exposure and depression, prospective evidence linking progesterone levels with subsequent PPD and the efficacy of the gamma-aminobutyric acid. A receptor modulator allopregnanolone further support investigation of progesterone-related mechanisms. However, current evidence does not yet establish progesterone as a causal second hit. Longitudinal and mechanistic studies integrating early adversity, steroid trajectories, neuroactive-steroid metabolism, HPA-axis function and stress response gene regulation are needed to test this model.

title: The role of distress tolerance and adverse childhood experiences in depression and suicidal ideation among Latinos: A moderation analysis
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Rates of mental health challenges are rising among Hispanic communities in the United States, yet research examining factors that shape the relationship between depression and suicidal ideation relationship in this population remains limited. The present study investigated whether adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) and distress tolerance, both well-documented factors in mental health risk, moderate the association between depressive symptoms and suicidal thoughts.

METHODS: Data were collected from 800 Latino adults in Texas who completed validated assessments of depression, suicidal ideation, ACEs, and distress tolerance. Using a dual-moderation analysis, we examined interaction effects of ACEs and distress tolerance on the relationship between depression and suicidal ideation, while accounting for age, sex, and acculturative stress.

RESULTS: Depression, ACEs, and distress tolerance each demonstrated significant direct associations with suicidal ideation, with distress tolerance negatively associated. Only distress tolerance significantly moderated the depression-suicidal ideation relationship, and this association was most pronounced among participants with lower distress tolerance relative to those with higher levels. Additionally, acculturative stress was positively associated with suicidal ideation, whereas age was negatively associated, and males reported higher levels of suicidal ideation relative to females.

DISCUSSION: Findings highlight a complex interplay between depression, distress tolerance, and suicidal ideation among Latino adults. The interesting result that lower distress tolerance amplified the depression-suicide association, indicates distress tolerance may function as a protective mechanism. These results emphasize the importance of continued investigation of these dynamics within a population experiencing significant mental health challenges.

title: Associations between adverse childhood experiences and breastfeeding initiation and duration: a longitudinal birth cohort study in Pakistan
abstract:
Rationale Prior studies have found that a history of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) is associated with breastfeeding initiation and duration, but the evidence is inconsistent. ACEs are associated with poor maternal and infant health outcomes. Despite low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) carrying a disproportionate amount of poor maternal and infant health outcomes and despite evidence that breastfeeding could alleviate some of these outcomes, little research has assessed the relative impact of ACEs on breastfeeding initiation and duration of exclusive breastfeeding in LMICs. Objective The study investigates whether maternal ACEs are associated with breastfeeding initiation and exclusive breastfeeding at 3 and 6 months postpartum among a cohort of women from rural Pakistan. Methods The prospective cohort analysis included 869 women 18–45 years of age from the Bachpan Cohort Study. Multivariable modified log-Poisson regression models were used to assess the relationship between any ACE exposure with breastfeeding initiation ( n = 755) and exclusive breastfeeding at 3 ( n = 758) and 6 months ( n = 809). Models were adjusted for known confounders. Results 58% of participants reported experiencing at least 1 ACE. 17.5% of women with a history of at least one ACE reported initiating breastfeeding within an hour of childbirth. 43.8% of women with at least one ACE reported exclusively breastfeeding at 3 months postpartum and 7.6% of women with at least one ACE reported exclusively breastfeeding within the last 24 h at 6 months postpartum. There was no significant difference between groups for initiating breastfeeding. However, women who had experienced ACEs were less likely to recall exclusively breastfeeding at 3 (RR = 0.8; 95 CI = 0.7, 1.0) and 6 months (RR = 0.7; 95% CI = 0.5, 1.2) postpartum compared to women with no self-reported history of ACEs. Conclusion Our findings indicate that ACEs may contribute to differences in exclusive breastfeeding. Understanding the long-term effects of ACEs on breastfeeding is important to help inform the design of intervention programs to prevent or mediate the negative repercussions of ACEs. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-026-28648-8 .

Introduction The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends breastfeeding as the ideal form of nutrition for infants [ 1 , 2 ]. WHO recommends initiating breastfeeding within one hour of birth [ 3 ]. Initiating breastfeeding within one hour of childbirth is pivotal because it guarantees that infants receive colostrum— the first breast milk produced for 2–4 days after childbirth [ 4 ]. Compared to other stages of breast milk, colostrum is concentrated with antibodies that provide passive immunity for babies [ 4 , 5 ]. Initiating breastfeeding within one hour of childbirth has also been shown to be associated with the continuation of exclusive breastfeeding practices [ 6 ]. Breastfeeding has been shown to enhance infant health in many ways. In low- and middle-income countries (LMIC) such as Pakistan, exclusive breastfeeding until six months can be particularly protective against malnutrition [ 7 – 10 ]. More broadly, breast milk has been associated with lower rates of a variety of childhood illnesses, such asthma and wheezing [ 11 , 12 ]. Breastfeeding is also associated with mental and emotional health benefits, such as maternal-child attachment and reduced physiological stress, anxiety, and postpartum depression for breastfeeding mothers [ 9 ]. Breastfeeding initiation and duration of exclusive breastfeeding vary widely across LMIC [ 13 ]. The World Health Organization defines exclusive breastfeeding as an infant receiving no liquids besides breastmilk, including water “with the exception of oral rehydration solution, or drops or syrups of vitamins, minerals or medicines” [ 14 ]. Between 2010 and 2018 in LMIC, only 45.1% of infants were breastfed at 6 months. One in five babies born in Pakistan is breastfed within one hour of birth and 48% are exclusively breastfed at six months old (based on 24-hour recall) [ 15 ]. Infant mortality has been declining in Pakistan over the past decade, reaching 62 deaths per 1000 live births in 2018 [ 16 ]. Child malnutrition is the cause of nearly 50% of these deaths [ 17 ]. Exclusive breastfeeding can reduce infant deaths up to 10 percent [ 18 ]. While many birthing people are aware that breastfeeding provides optimal nutrition benefits for infants, qualitative studies have consistently demonstrated that most are unable to identify the specific benefits associated with breastfeeding [ 19 ]. In Pakistan, 52% and 54% of women received antenatal counseling about the initiation of breastfeeding and exclusive breastfeeding, respectively [ 16 ]. Counseling rates were highest in urban areas and among women who had relatively high education status [ 16 ]. Many therefore use cultural practices known to reduce hunger and respiratory illnesses in their infants [ 17 ]. For instance, mothers sometimes discard colostrum in Pakistani villages because they perceive it as not having value for a child’s wellbeing [ 20 , 21 ]. In one study, 14% of mothers in urban and semi-urban Pakistan discarded colostrum [ 22 ]. Many Pakistani mothers complementary feed their infants during the first three days of life with water, ghee, animal milk, and herbal tea, which many Pakistani mothers believe optimizes newborn nourishment and health outcomes [ 20 , 21 , 23 ]. This is referred to as prelacteal feeding [ 24 ]. Among children who were breastfed, 76% received pre-lacteal feeds within the first three hours of life [ 16 ]. Pakistani mothers also face the wide variety of common barriers to breastfeeding such as: time management, physiological changes after delivery, perception of insufficient breast milk, high maternal work load, additional maternal stress from initiating breastfeeding early, cesarean section deliveries, employment, and limited workplace support [ 20 , 25 ]. Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), categorized as abuse, neglect, and household challenges, are important determinants of maternal and infant well-being [ 26 , 27 ]. Several studies suggest that the prevalence of ACEs is consistently highest among LMIC countries [ 28 – 31 ]. ACEs have been found to have an enduring effect on maternal health prior to and during pregnancy [ 28 ]. Evidence suggests that ACEs induce physiological changes that lead to increased risk of poor health and behavioral outcomes [ 32 , 33 ]. An increase in the number and severity of ACEs also appears to be linked to worse health outcomes throughout the life course, indicating the existence of a dose-response relationship [ 34 – 36 ]. Evidence suggests that conditions associated with ACEs, such as substance use and intimate partner violence, can reduce the initiation and continuation of breastfeeding, due to higher rates of chronic health conditions and psychosocial difficulties with pregnancy [ 25 , 37 , 38 ]. Several studies have examined the association between ACEs and breastfeeding outcomes; however, results of these studies vary and few have been conducted in LMIC [ 39 , 40 ]. One study reported that ACEs are associated with an increased likelihood of exclusive breastfeeding, but not breastfeeding initiation, while another found an association between experiencing child sexual abuse and a higher breastfeeding initiation rate [ 26 , 41 ]. Another reported a significant association between ACE count and an increased likelihood of initiating breastfeeding, but not continued breastfeeding at two months postpartum [ 42 ]. To our knowledge, no research has assessed the relationship between ACEs and breastfeeding outcomes in Pakistan. This study investigates whether experiencing ACEs is associated with breastfeeding initiation and exclusive breastfeeding at 3 and 6 months among a cohort of women from a rural subdistrict of Pakistan. Our study tests the associations between ACEs and breastfeeding outcomes in LMIC. Given evidence that breastfeeding can contribute to maternal and infant health, particularly in resource-strained contexts, investigating early-life exposures that may hinder breastfeeding uptake may have significant public health impact. Methods Study design and participants Data come from the Bachpan Cohort Study, which enrolled women from rural communities in Kallar Syedan, a subdistrict of Rawalpindi, Pakistan [ 43 ]. The Bachpan Cohort Study is an ongoing prospective pregnancy-birth cohort study designed to investigate the effects of depression on child health and development [ 43 ]. Eligibility criteria for the Bachpan Cohort Study included being married, in the third trimester of pregnancy (≥ 28 weeks’ gestation), at least 18 years of age, intending to remain in the study area, not requiring immediate inpatient care for medical or psychiatric reasons, and being able to speak Urdu, Punjabi, or Potohari [ 43 ]. Within the Bachpan birth cohort is the Thinking Health PLUS Program (THPP), a cluster-randomized trial evaluating a peer-delivered psychosocial treatment for depression [ 43 ]. Researchers screened all eligible pregnant women residing in the study area at the time of recruitment for depression using the Urdu validated Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) [ 44 ]. The study defined women from each of the 40 village clusters who scored a PHQ-9 score ≥ 10 as screening positive for depression. These women were invited to join the Bachpan Cohort, while one of every three women who did not meet the threshold was invited to participate as the non-depressed reference group [ 43 ]. Researchers used the ≥ 10 threshold to enroll pregnant women into the trial portion of the cohort. A total of 1154 pregnant women enrolled into the cohort and completed baseline screening between October 2014 and February 2016 [ 43 ]. For the present study, the study team analyzed data from 869 participants related to ACEs, breastfeeding initiation, and breastfeeding continuation. Data from the following timepoints were utilized in this analysis: third trimester during pregnancy (baseline), 3 months, 6 months, and 36 months postpartum. Fewer women participated in the 3-month study point than the 6-point. This can likely be explained by the Pakistani custom of chilla, in which postpartum women return to their maternal home for the first 40 days following birth [ 45 ]. This could have made them unavailable to participate in the study due to a temporary change in physical location. Measures Outcomes The three primary outcomes of interest originate from the World Health Organization breastfeeding recommendations to initiate breastfeeding within the first hour of birth and exclusively breastfeed for the first 6 months of life. These include: (1) time of breastfeeding initiation (“When was the baby’s first breast milk feed?”) and exclusive breastfeeding at 3 and 6 months (“What has the child had in the last 24 hours? )” [ 3 ]. 24-hour recall is a WHO-accepted indicator for retrospective questions about breastfeeding exclusivity at 3 and 6 months [ 46 ]. In addition, we incorporate data from 3 months postpartum to help us better understand breastfeeding practices between birth and 6 months. Children who were only fed breast milk in the last 24 hours (no reported feeding of ghutti, herbal water, water, or tea) were categorized as having been exclusively breastfed. We inquired about these three liquids, because they are the non-breastmilk liquids most commonly given to infants in Pakistan. The study team treated each of the three outcome variables as binary variables (yes/no). The breastfeeding questionnaire is included as an appendix file. Exposure We used the ACE questionnaire to measure experiences of abuse, neglect, household dysfunction, and community dysfunction during childhood [ 27 ]. We measured ACEs using the 12-item ACE-IQ at 36-months postpartum, which retrospectively asks about an individual’s exposure to adverse experiences prior to the age of 18. This questionnaire has been validated for use in international settings and was additionally adapted for use in the Bachpan Cohort Study [ 27 , 47 ]. Our team removed sexual abuse questions because of the high probability of underreporting due to stigma and fear in the community [ 27 ]. We operationally defined ACEs in three ways [ 27 ]. ACEs variables included (1) a binary yes/no variable for any ACE reported, (2) a continuous variable for number of experiences, and (3) a binary indicator for each of the four ACE domains (neglect [emotional neglect; physical neglect], family psychological distress [alcohol and/or drug abuser in the household; incarcerated household member; someone depressed, mentally ill, institutionalized or suicidal], home violence [physical abuse; emotional abuse; household member treated violently], and community violence [bullying; community violence; collective violence]. We coded binary variables for each ACE domain ‘yes’ if a woman experienced any of the ACEs within the domain. Because there is no agreed-upon standard about how to present ACEs, presenting them from several angles allows for the data to reveal nuances and patterns that might be missed if choosing only one method. Control variables We adjusted all statistical models described below for mother’s age at baseline, education level (> 5th grade) as a proxy for childhood socioeconomic status [ 48 ], trial arm (control, intervention, non-depressed), and assessor. We considered age, education, and trial arm to confound the relationship between ACEs and breastfeeding given their associations with both exposure and outcomes. Assessor was not a theoretical confounder but was included to control for potential variability in data collection across interviewers. Statistical analyses We calculated descriptive statistics for sociodemographic variables by whether an individual experienced any ACE. Descriptive statistics for each ACE operationalization were calculated by breastfeeding outcomes. To examine whether missingness differed by key demographic factors, we compared baseline characteristics across three groups: participants present at 36 months with complete ACE data ( n = 869), those lost to follow-up ( n = 265), and those present at follow-up, but missing ACE data ( n = 20; Supplementary Table 1). To account for potential bias from missingness, we used inverse probability weighting (IPW) in all models. We included the marginal probability of being observed in the numerator of the IPW to stabilize weights. title: Associations between dysfunctional parental discipline and parent-reported mental health outcomes in preschoolers: a cross-sectional study
abstract:
This study explored the association between parental discipline and mental health in a sample of 21,366 Chinese preschool children (mean age = 4.82 ± 0.89 years; 51.77% boys, 48.23% girls). Parenting practices were measured as overall parenting scores, laxness, overreactivity, and verbosity, and children’s mental health was assessed by the official simplified Chinese version of the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ). Both outcomes were dichotomized using validated cut-offs for Chinese preschoolers, and odds ratios are reported as the odds of meeting these cut-off definitions (Total Difficulties Score > 14; adequate Prosocial Behavior Score ≥ 6). The results indicated that higher parenting scores (for total difficulties: AOR = 4.03; 95% CI: 3.64–4.46; for prosocial behavior: AOR = 0.48; 95% CI: 0.45–0.51), particularly in laxness (for total difficulties: AOR = 1.28; 95% CI: 1.23–1.34; for prosocial behavior: AOR = 0.88; 95% CI: 0.85–0.91) and overreactivity (for total difficulties: AOR = 1.83; 95% CI: 1.76–1.90; for prosocial behavior: AOR = 0.66; 95% CI: 0.64–0.68), were associated with higher odds of a Total Difficulties Score > 14 (i.e., risk of mental health difficulties) and lower odds of an adequate Prosocial Behavior Score (≥ 6), while verbosity (for total difficulties: AOR = 0.80; 95% CI: 0.77–0.84; for prosocial behavior: AOR = 1.23; 95% CI: 1.19–1.27) was associated with lower odds of a Total Difficulties Score > 14 and higher odds of an adequate Prosocial Behavior Score (≥ 6). Subgroup analyses suggested potential effect modification by education level and child age, but most interaction effects were not significant after multiple comparison correction. The findings emphasize the need for balanced parenting and interventions targeting both discipline and parental well-being to enhance children’s mental health.

1 Introduction Mental health problems represent a considerable public health challenge, significantly contributing to the overall global disease burden ( 1 , 2 ). In this article, “mental health problems in children” refer to problems involving emotional, behavioral, and social interaction abnormalities ( 3 , 4 ). An increasing volume of literature indicates that mental health disorders, such as hyperactivity, attention deficits, and emotional or behavioral dysfunctions, impact a substantial proportion of children globally. Studies from different countries have reported varying prevalence rates: approximately 0.7–3% in some European populations ( 5 ), up to 12–39% in rural China ( 6 ). Mental health problems in children may persist into adulthood ( 7 ), leading an increased risk of chronic issues like depression, anxiety ( 8 ), and substance abuse ( 9 ). Over time, they also increase the risk of unemployment, criminal behavior ( 10 ), emphasizing the need for early intervention to prevent long-term negative outcomes ( 11 ). Parenting young children can be highly demanding, requiring parents to regulate their emotions, cognition, and biology in order to manage daily stress and meet the evolving developmental needs of their children ( 12 ). Previous researches showed that dysfunctional parental discipline behavior increased the risk of children developing externalizing and internalizing problems, as well as social problems ( 13–15 ). However, these outcomes are conceptually multifaceted, and the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) assesses five domains of child mental health: emotional symptoms, conduct problems, hyperactivity/inattention, peer relationship problems, and prosocial behavior. Feng et al. ( 16 ) found a nonlinear dose–response relationship between maternal depressive symptoms and children’s mental health outcomes among 17,115 mother–child dyads, with turning points at CES-D scores of 17 (total difficulties and internalizing problems), 21 (externalizing problems), and 14 (prosocial behavior problems). According to Arnold et al. ( 17 ), dysfunctional parental discipline behavior can be divided into three categories: laxness, overreactivity, and verbosity. Laxness is marked by permissive discipline, where parents may give in, neglect to enforce rules, or unintentionally reward misbehavior. In contrast, overreactive caregivers tend to manage their children through anger, harshness, and irritability. Verbosity refers to caregivers who rely on lengthy verbal responses and excessive talking, even when it proves ineffective in addressing the child’s behavior ( 17 ). These categories laid the foundation for the development of the Arnold-O’Leary Parenting Scale, a tool designed to evaluate dysfunctional parental discipline across various cultural contexts. Research has demonstrated that different forms of parental discipline to which young children are exposed have different associations with their mental health problems ( 18–21 ). Kiel et al. ( 19 ) found an adverse association between maternal overprotectiveness and children’s inhibition and shyness. Similarly, Lovato et al. ( 18 ) found that elevated levels of parental laxness were related to diminished childhood negative affectivity. Research also showed that uncaring parental behavior was linked to both mental health problems and a higher likelihood of injury in children ( 22 ). Despite the existing literature detailing the connections between parental disciplinary styles and children’s well-being ( 23 , 24 ), previous studies have used relatively small sample sizes, with some being qualitative research, and there is currently a lack of large-sample empirical studies. We aimed to address these limitations by using a large population-based cohort of preschoolers in a city in China. Employing a stratified cluster sampling approach across multiple districts and encompassing a diverse array of child and family characteristics, this research endeavors to deliver a thorough analysis of the relationship between parental discipline and mental health among children aged 3 to 6 years. Theoretical Framework: This study is grounded in Bandura’s Social Learning Theory, which posits that children acquire behavioral patterns, emotional regulation strategies, and social competencies through observational learning and modeling of parental behaviors ( 25 ). Parents’ disciplinary practices serve as behavioral models that children internalize, influencing their subsequent emotional and behavioral development. Additionally, the ecological systems theory ( 26 ) emphasizes that parenting practices operate within multiple contextual systems - including family dynamics, parental stress, and child characteristics - that collectively shape child development outcomes. Dysfunctional disciplinary practices, such as overreactivity and laxness, may disrupt children’s development of self-regulation and social competencies, thereby increasing the risk of mental health difficulties. Conversely, adaptive disciplinary strategies may promote protective factors such as prosocial behavior. 2 Methods 2.1 Study population The research was carried out in partnership with the Education Bureau and local schools in a western Chinese city. A stratified cluster sampling method was employed to obtain a representative sample of preschoolers. Initially, the city was divided into 13 districts and counties for stratification. Next, public kindergartens were randomly selected from each district using an official list of kindergartens. To account for differences in the total number of children across the districts, proportional allocation was applied to determine the required number of participants from each district, based on the proportion of children relative to the overall population. In total, 189 kindergartens were selected as recruitment sites, and all children and their parents from the chosen schools were invited to participate. The recruitment period spanned from February 28 to March 5, 2025. The study included preschool children aged 3 to 6 years enrolled in junior, middle, and senior kindergarten classes. Written informed consent was acquired from parents prior to participation. The questionnaire was completed by one parent per child. A total of 25,017 parent–child pairs participated in the survey. After excluding responses with outliers in the form filler’s age (n = 517), responses where the form filler was not the parent (e.g., other guardians; n = 2,408), and outliers in the child’s age (n = 726), the final analysis included 21,366 parent–child pairs. 2.2 Exposure The primary exposure variable assessed in this investigation was parental discipline, which was evaluated utilizing the Parenting Scale developed by Arnold-O’Leary ( 17 ). This Parenting Scale consists of 30 items aimed at measuring dysfunctional disciplinary behaviors of parents toward children aged between 2 and 16 years. The responses are rated on a 7-point Likert scale, where a score of 7 indicates a greater propensity for disciplinary mistakes, whereas a score of 1 signifies a higher likelihood of employing effective, alternative disciplinary methods. Consequently, higher overall scores represent a more dysfunctional disciplinary style. Factor analysis of the Parenting Scale identified three dimensions: overreactivity, laxness, and verbosity. The scale demonstrates strong internal consistency and has been validated for use with parents of preschool-aged children and young adolescents ( 27 ). Additionally, it has proven applicable to assessing parental disciplines in families with children experiencing developmental and behavioral challenges ( 28 , 29 ). 2.3 Outcome The primary outcome measure for this study was the mental health of children, assessed via the official simplified Chinese version of the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) ( 30–32 ). The SDQ comprises 25 items, each rated on a scale ranging from 0 (indicating “does not apply”) to 2 (indicating “completely applies”). Reverse scoring is applicable to items 7, 11, 14, 21, and 25. The questionnaire is partitioned into five subscales: emotional symptoms, conduct problems, hyperactivity, peer problems, and prosocial behavior. According to the recommended cutoff values for the SDQ in Chinese preschoolers ( 31 , 33 ), a total difficulties score exceeding 14 suggests a risk of mental health issues. A prosocial behavior score ≥ 6 indicates adequate Prosocial Behavior. For the multivariable logistic regression analyses, the binary outcomes were coded as follows: total difficulties, 1 = Total Difficulties Score > 14 and 0 = score ≤ 14; prosocial behavior, 1 = adequate Prosocial Behavior Score (≥ 6) and 0 = score < 6 (indicating prosocial deficits). The SDQ has demonstrated strong internal consistency and validity for assessing mental health in Chinese children aged 3 to 17 years ( 30 , 31 ). This study utilizes both the total difficulties score and the prosocial score as dependent variables. 2.4 Covariates To mitigate the influence of confounding variables and to enhance the comprehension of the relationship between parental discipline and children’s mental health, we collected and adjusted for potential confounding variables related to parental gender (male/female), parental age (as a continuous or categorical variable: < 30, ≥ 30 to 45 and ≥ 45), child age (as a continuous or categorical variable: < 4, ≥ 4 to 5 and ≥ 5), child gender (boys/girls), education level (≤ junior high school, high school diploma and junior college and ≥ undergraduate degree), employment status (working/not working), annual family income (< 30, ≥ 30 to 100 and ≥ 100), smoking status (no/yes), alcohol intake status (no/yes), marital status (married/living with partner/others). From a family systems and ecological perspective, these covariates represent key demographic and contextual characteristics that may influence both the exposure (parental discipline) and the outcome (child mental health), and thus need to be controlled to reduce confounding. 2.5 Statistical analysis Continuous variables were presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) for descriptive purposes. Because the distributions of some continuous variables deviated from normality (as indicated by Shapiro–Wilk tests), the Kruskal-Wallis test was used for group comparisons, as it does not assume a normal distribution. Participant characteristics were categorized based on the total difficulty scores, with scores greater than 14 and less than or equal to 14. Categorical variables were compared using Fisher’s exact test, rather than Pearson’s chi-square test, because the expected cell counts for some categorical variables were below 5, violating the assumption of the chi-square test. To assess potential multicollinearity among the covariates included in the multivariable regression models, we calculated the variance inflation factor (VIF) for each independent variable. A VIF value exceeding 10 was considered indicative of significant multicollinearity, while values above 5 were regarded as moderate concern. To evaluate the association between parental discipline and the mental health issues of children, multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed, with results articulated as odds ratios (ORs) accompanied by 95% confidence intervals (CIs). ORs were interpreted consistently as the odds of meeting the outcome cut-off definitions (Total Difficulties Score > 14; adequate Prosocial Behavior Score ≥ 6), rather than as changes in the underlying constructs or scores. Non-adjusted model was the crude model without covariate adjustments, while Adjust model adjusted for parental gender, parental age, child age, child gender, education level, employment status, annual family income, smoking status, alcohol intake status, marital status. Subgroup analyses, stratified by above covariates were performed using multivariable logistic regression. To control for type I error due to multiple interaction testing, we applied the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Only interactions with FDR q < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Prior to multiple imputation, we conducted missing data pattern analysis by comparing characteristics between participants with complete Age and Child age data versus those with missing data ( Supplementary Table S1 ). The results showed significant differences between groups on several observed variables (parental gender, education level, annual family income, and marital status), supporting the missing at random (MAR) assumption. Multiple imputation was performed using chained equations with 5 imputed datasets and 20 iterations each, under the MAR assumption. All statistical analyses were performed using R ( http://www.r-project.org , The R Foundation) and EmpowerStats ( http://www.empowwerstats.com , X&Y Solutions, Inc., Boston, MA) software. A two-tailed p -value of less than 0.05 was deemed statistically significant. 3 Results 3.1 Demographic information Basic information was divided into two groups based on total difficulties score: ≤14

title: Sustained antidepressant-like effects of psychedelics through 5-HT(2A)R-β-arrestin signaling
abstract: Psychedelics produce long-lasting antidepressant effects, but their hallucinogenic properties limit clinical use. Using structure-guided design of 5-HT 2A R-β-arrestin-biased agonists, we identified β-arrestin signaling as a critical driver of prolonged antidepressant-like effects in mice. Here we show that the slow-dissociation kinetics of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) enable progressive accumulation of 5-HT 2A R engagement during repeated low-dose administration, approaching the receptor occupancy achieved by an acute high dose while avoiding its high peak concentration. This kinetic separation sustains β-arrestin signaling while limiting robust Gα q -mediated Ca 2+  responses. Consistent with this framework, repeated low-dose LSD and repeated low-dose psilocybin pretreatment followed by a high-dose psychedelic challenge produced sustained antidepressant-like behavioral effects in mice. In parallel, these regimens produced no detectable psychedelic-associated behavioral disruption in mice and cynomolgus macaques. Together, these findings uncover the signaling basis of sustained psychedelic efficacy and provide a rational framework for developing nonhallucinogenic psychedelic therapies for psychiatric disorders.

title: Behavioral genomics identifies Creld1 as a cross-modal regulator of somatosensation
abstract: Somatosensation is mediated by dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, which convert physical and chemical stimuli into electrical signals. However, the full repertoire of molecular components underlying somatosensation remains incompletely identified. Here we developed an efficient postnatal CRISPR-Cas9 knockout platform for interrogating DRG-expressed genes (such as Piezo2, Trpv1 and Scn9a) in mice using AAV9-mediated single-guide RNA delivery. Combining this approach with somatosensory behavioral assays, we performed a targeted screen of 20 genes and identified Creld1 as a cross-model regulator of somatosensation. Either single-guide RNA-mediated postnatal knockout or tamoxifen-induced Cre-mediated deletion of Creld1 in DRG neurons resulted in profound behavioral deficits in touch, temperature, pain and itch, whereas its overexpression enhanced touch and thermal responses. Mechanistically, CRELD1 functions as an auxiliary regulator of voltage-gated sodium channels (Na v ) for controlling DRG neuron excitability. Together, this work establishes a robust postnatal screening platform for behavioral genomics and identifies Creld1 as a master regulator of somatosensory function.

title: A vagal gut-brain axis for feeding-induced gastric secretion in mice
abstract: Feeding begins with food-seeking and ends with nutrient absorption and waste elimination. Although meal-related sensory cues shape feeding behavior, how they engage neural circuits to control digestion remains unclear. We dissected vagal gut-brain-gut pathways mediating meal-induced gastric secretion. Stomach-innervating vagal afferents were necessary and sufficient for secretion. Among them, Glp1r +  and Sst +  neurons drove acid, pepsin, and gastrin secretion, whereas Oxtr +  and Vip +  neurons had little effect. Piezo2 was expressed in Glp1r +  mechanosensory afferents, and conditional deletion of Piezo2 attenuated distension-evoked secretion. On the efferent limb, genetically defined vagal motor-neuron subsets showed distinct secretory effects: Cck +  neurons broadly increased acid, pepsin, and gastrin, whereas Grp +  neurons preferentially affected acid secretion. Finally, enteric circuit dissection revealed modular output control, with Calb2 +  neurons driving secretion with minimal motility effects. Together, these results define a cell-type-resolved vagal-enteric architecture for gastric control.

title: A GABAergic preoptic-raphe circuit mediates paradoxical coupling of anxiety and social preference after comparative social deficit
abstract: Social disconnection is a major risk factor for anxiety disorders, the most prevalent mental illnesses worldwide, yet its neural substrates remain unclear. Here, we establish a comparative social deficit (CSD) model in adult male mice that induces a paradoxical phenotype of increased anxiety-like behavior together with heightened social preference, a pattern conceptually similar to human loneliness. Mechanistically, CSD increases the excitability of medial preoptic GABAergic (mPOA Gad2 ) neurons, which bidirectionally regulate CSD-induced behavioral changes. Transcriptomic and electrophysiological analyses identify downregulation of the Kv4.3 potassium channel (Kcnd3) as a molecular driver of mPOA Gad2  hyperexcitability. Furthermore, mPOA Gad2  neurons exert monosynaptic inhibition onto dorsal raphe serotonergic (DRN 5-HT ) neurons. This inhibitory projection, strengthened by CSD, mediates CSD-induced behavioral effects. These findings define a molecular and circuit mechanism by which social disconnection remodels mPOA-DRN interactions to drive the paradoxical coupling of anxiety and elevated social preference, providing a translational framework for understanding loneliness-related psychiatric vulnerability.

title: Clinically unresponsive patients with acute brain injury activate a brain-computer interface
abstract: Brain activation to verbal commands can be detected by EEG in clinically unresponsive patients. These patients with cognitive motor dissociation (CMD) are unable to communicate with the environment despite preserved consciousness. Advanced brain-computer interfaces (BCI) are promising to support motor function in patients with motor neuron disease or spinal cord injury. Our primary objective was to determine if clinically unresponsive patients can control a self-paced, one-way BCI early after acute brain injury. Secondarily, we assessed the association of BCI control with short- and long-term outcomes. We conducted a prospective single-centre cohort study in 41 clinically unresponsive, critically ill and acutely brain injured patients, as well as in a convenience sample of 8 healthy volunteers and 22 conscious critically ill patients. The self-paced BCI analysed EEG in real time and modulated frequency and pitch of a tone that patients controlled by attempting a motor task: patients were provided with instructions 'to make the beep sound faster, keep opening and closing your right hand' alternating with 'to make the beep sound slower, stop opening and closing your right hand'. CMD was detected by applying machine learning to EEG recorded while patients listened to motor commands. Clinical outcomes were recovery of consciousness by hospital discharge, assessed with the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised, and recovery of functional independence at 12 months, defined as a Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended score of 4 or higher (denoting the ability to function independently for 8 h or more). Additionally, we invited conscious patients as well as family members of conscious and clinically unresponsive patients to complete a survey on perceived utility and challenges associated with the BCI. In this study, 13 clinically unresponsive patients (32%) achieved BCI control and 8 of 41 (20%) were CMD-positive. All healthy volunteers and nine conscious patients (41%) were able to control the BCI. Median signal delay for BCI control was 49.8 [interquartile range (IQR) 39.9-75.6] seconds for clinically unresponsive patients, 17.1 (IQR 7.8-19.9) for conscious patients and 15.5 (IQR 12.9-21.2) for healthy volunteers. In the group of 41 clinically unresponsive patients, 4 of 13 patients with (31%) and 1 of 28 without BCI control (4%) recovered clinical consciousness at hospital discharge [odds ratio (OR) 21.2; 95% confidence interval (CI) 2.3-930.7]. At 12 months, 6 of 13 patients with (46%) and 2 of 28 without BCI control (7%) recovered functional independence (OR 9.9; 95% CI 1.8-81.6). None of the patients that were unable to control the BCI and were CMD-negative recovered. Patients with BCI control had shorter times to recovery of functional independence by 12 months than those who did not (hazards ratio 6.0; 95% CI 1.2-30.6). All respondents of the BCI survey (n = 37) expressed strong support for the potential future use of BCI devices. These results suggest that BCI control is a strong predictor of outcomes following acute brain injury and provide initial evidence that a bedside, EEG-based BCI system might permit bidirectional communication in critically ill unresponsive patients.

title: Progenitor transcriptional alterations link fetal and adult pathology in Huntington's disease
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene. Although the mutant huntingtin protein is expressed from conception, clinical symptoms typically emerge in mid-adulthood. Imaging and molecular studies have raised the possibility that HD may involve neurodevelopmental abnormalities, but direct evidence at the single-cell level in the human fetal brain has been lacking. Here we investigated whether early, cell type-specific transcriptional vulnerabilities arise during neurodevelopment, persist into adult pathology, and might be rescued. To address this, we performed single-cell transcriptomic profiling of the lateral ganglionic eminence (LGE) and cortex from a rare, anatomically intact human HD fetal brain, alongside matched controls. These data were complemented by an allelic series of HD mouse embryos and cross-compared with already published human post-mortem brains and brain organoid models' datasets. Neural progenitors displayed the highest number of differentially expressed genes in the human fetal brain, and were also impacted in the HD mouse model, where additional cell types displayed transcriptional alterations. Notably, human HD progenitor transcriptional signatures were moderately enriched in the developing mouse LGE. These progenitors exhibited increased expression of synaptic pathways coupled with reduced expression of cell maintenance genes. Cross-comparison with publicly available post-mortem HD datasets revealed that components of this transcriptional signature persist into adulthood. Furthermore, cellular interactions were found to mitigate these alterations, highlighting a potentially rescuable fetal-to-adult transcriptional signature with important implications for HD pathogenesis and therapeutic strategies. Together, these findings reinforce the view of HD as a disorder with developmental origins, in which early transcriptional changes may shape neuronal function while increasing susceptibility to later neurodegeneration.

title: Early lineage divergence segregates sensory and motor-associative identities in the thalamus
abstract: The thalamus integrates sensory, motor and associative functions through distinct nuclei, yet the developmental principles driving their specification remain unclear. Here we generate a spatiotemporal single-cell multiomic and spatial transcriptomic atlas of the embryonic mouse thalamus, combined with barcoding-based lineage tracing. We identify two major glutamatergic lineages, sensory-related and motor-associative, each governed by different gene regulatory programs and temporal dynamics. These lineages arise from spatially and molecularly distinct progenitor domains, revealing an early segregation of functional identities. Within the sensory lineage, we resolve branching sensory trajectories leading to first-order visual and somatosensory neurons, both emerging from a shared higher-order-like state. Using in silico predictions and in vivo perturbation, we identify Sp9 as a key regulator of visual thalamic fate. Together, our findings define the molecular architecture and developmental trajectories that underpin thalamic modality specification, providing a framework to understand how functional circuits emerge in the mammalian brain.

title: SIK3 controls synaptic localization of NMDA receptors by phosphorylating GluN1
abstract: Synaptic NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs) are central components of all neural computations. NMDAR levels critically vary between synapses but how the synaptic localization of NMDARs is controlled remains unclear. Here we show that SIK3, a serine-threonine protein kinase, localizes to synapses where it phosphorylates the obligatory NMDAR subunit GluN1 at a single site. This single phosphorylation event controls NMDAR recruitment to synapses. Genetic deletion of SIK3 severely and selectively decreases synaptic GluN1 levels by ~60% without altering AMPA-type glutamate receptor levels or inducing major transcriptional changes. Pharmacological inhibition of SIK3 impairs synaptic NMDAR responses within 45 minutes. Mutating the SIK3-phosphorylation site inhibits GluN1 synaptic recruitment. 'Sleepy', a gain-of-function mutation in SIK3 that increases sleep, selectively enhances synaptic NMDAR levels by increasing GluN1 phosphorylation. Thus, SIK3 phosphorylation of GluN1 provides a key signal for recruiting NMDARs to synapses.

title: An acetylcholine-inhibited sleep-active hippocampal interneuron orchestrates memory consolidation
abstract: Memory reactivation during hippocampal ripples is critical for sleep-dependent memory consolidation. However, the molecular-to-circuit mechanism enabling sleep-predominant ripple generation remains unresolved. Here, we discovered that a sparse population of GABAergic interneurons in the mouse hippocampus specializes in gating ripple generation and memory consolidation. While all known genetically labeled hippocampal interneurons were highly active during wakefulness and rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep, genetic targeting of M2 acetylcholine receptor (Chrm2)-expressing neurons isolated a specific population preferentially active during non-REM (NREM) sleep and quiet wakefulness. These acetylcholine-inhibited interneurons inhibited the entire hippocampus in an infra-slow rhythm (∼0.015 Hz). Suppressing their activity in dorsal CA3 or ventral hippocampus impaired spatial and social memory, respectively. Furthermore, Chrm2+ neurons were closely associated with ripples; their activity bidirectionally modulated ripple occurrence via widespread inhibition. Thus, Chrm2+ interneurons are critical in linking neuromodulatory state to memory consolidation, offering genetically targeted access to sleep-active memory circuits implicated in cognitive disorders.

title: Prematurity insults remodel cerebellar development and behaviour
abstract: Preterm survivors often develop motor and socio-cognitive impairments that implicate altered cerebellar development, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. A key challenge is that prematurity involves overlapping perinatal insults that converge on the developing brain, making their individual effects difficult to disentangle. Here, we model two major prematurity-associated insults, maternal immune activation (MIA) and neonatal hypoxia (Hx), in mice. By controlling timing and sequence, we define how these insults shape cerebellar assembly during rapid maturation. Comparative analysis with human tissue confirmed that these insults recapitulate key features of the human preterm cerebellum, establishing the translational validity of this model for dissecting insult-specific outcomes. Behavioral and kinematic profiling revealed divergent motor and social phenotypes, which we traced to insult-specific cerebellar remodelling. Hypoxia compromised both granule cell maturation in the internal granule layer and the principal excitatory afferents to Purkinje cells, a circuit state that manifested as impaired motor execution and stereotyped, sensory-disengaged social investigation. Maternal immune activation, by contrast, expanded the granule cell progenitor layer and reduced Purkinje cell dendritic complexity, a phenotype that preserved social preference but reorganized the kinematic structure of social investigation. When hypoxia followed maternal immune activation, it acted on this primed substrate to produce a distinct state in which the features established by prior inflammation were compounded by granule cell proliferative arrest, progressive mitochondrial dysfunction, and aberrant, hyper-interactive social investigation. Together, these findings reframe prematurity-associated insults as cerebellar reprogramming events shaped by both the identity and sequence of insults, linking distinct mechanistic substrates to divergent neurodevelopmental outcomes.

title: The Roles and Uses of Extracellular Vesicles in Neuroimmunologic Diseases
abstract: Neuroimmunology is a field of neurology focused on the diagnosis and treatment of diseases where the immune system causes inflammation or injury to the nervous system. This includes diseases such as multiple sclerosis, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, autoimmune encephalitis, autoimmune ataxia, stiff person syndrome spectrum disorder, and neuro-rheumatologic diseases such as neuropsychiatric lupus. Over the past couple decades, there have been significant advancements in the diagnostic methods for several neuroimmunologic diseases. Despite these achievements, major needs remain for additional methods to facilitate earlier diagnosis, monitor disease activity and treatment, and elucidate disease mechanisms to aid in the development of novel or tailored treatment strategies. Currently, there is often a trade-off between the invasiveness of neurodiagnostic testing and the level of detail that can be obtained from the test without causing an iatrogenic injury. Here, we discuss the potential of extracellular vesicles (EVs), especially CNS-derived EVs obtained from peripheral blood, as a promising avenue for advancing research and clinical care in neuroimmunology. This article provides a review of the key clinical features and approaches to care for the most common neuroimmunologic diseases. We identify gaps that remain in our current understanding of these conditions. We then highlight how ongoing research in the EV field may address these existing gaps. Finally, we examine the challenges that must be overcome before EV analysis can be more widely adopted in both research and clinical care in this field.

title: Identification of candidate markers for the isolation of neuron-specific extracellular vesicles
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are present in biofluids and may be useful biomarkers to non-invasively monitor brain cells, but isolating cell type-specific EVs remains challenging. Here we introduce an approach to immuno-isolate EVs from neurons and glia based on protein surface markers. We first selected transmembrane proteins suitable as cell type-specific EV markers based on gene expression and EV proteomic data. We developed a high-purity EV isolation method and cataloged the proteins present on EVs in human cerebrospinal fluid and plasma. We then computationally identified cell type-specific candidate markers for isolating EVs from neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and microglia. Using ultrasensitive immunoassays against several predicted neuron-specific proteins, we confirmed one marker, NRXN3, as present on EVs in cerebrospinal fluid and plasma. Finally, we developed efficient EV immuno-isolation methods and applied them to isolate NRXN3 +  EVs. Our work provides a general methodology for the isolation of cell type-specific EVs, advancing the goal of using EVs to study brain diseases.

title: Spatiotemporal remodeling in habenula marks the onset of depression-related phenotypes
abstract: Chronic stress has lasting adverse consequences that can lead, over time, to depression, yet the optimal timeframe for effective therapies remains unclear. The lateral habenula (LHb) has been implicated in stress-related behavioral repercussions, but the precise timing of its contribution is not understood. Here, using spatial transcriptomics, we generated a spatially resolved molecular atlas of the LHb of male mice, revealing a topographically organized and temporally defined remodeling of gene expression after chronic stress. Longitudinal in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of individual LHb neurons revealed progressively heightened excitatory responses to aversive stimuli. These neuronal adaptations mirrored both the progression of transcriptional changes and the emergence of depression-related behavioral phenotypes and were reversed by the antidepressant ketamine. Moreover, chemogenetically limiting LHb neuronal activity or administering ketamine at the onset of these changes exerted antidepressant effects. These findings link spatiotemporal signatures of LHb neuronal ensembles and genetic landscape with the onset of stress-induced depression-related states.

title: Distinct patterns of whole-body coding in human motor cortex and posterior parietal cortex
abstract: Traditional views of cortical motor areas hold that movements of different parts of the body, or effectors, are represented in distinct anatomical locations. The extent of overlap in effector representations has been a topic of debate for decades. We recorded from single neurons in hand areas of the motor cortex (MC) and posterior parietal cortex (PPC) of tetraplegic humans while they attempted movements across the body. We found a population response to every movement tested in both areas; however, the hand knob of MC more selectively responded to hand movements, whereas PPC represented all effectors strongly. Single neurons in MC responded selectively to a single effector or to two effectors that were part of the same limb. In PPC, neurons exhibited mixed selectivity, responding to combinations of effectors. These findings suggest a transition from a highly effector-general representation in PPC to regional effector specificity in MC.

title: Serum β-synuclein predicts dementia conversion and mortality beyond amyloid-β and phospho-tau
abstract: Synaptic dysfunction is among the earliest pathological events in Alzheimer's disease and among the strongest neuropathological correlates of cognitive impairment, yet blood-based synaptic biomarkers are lacking. Whether serum β-synuclein provides prognostic information independent of established amyloid-β (A; CSF Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio) and tau (T1; CSF pTau181) biomarkers has not been determined. We studied 259 non-demented individuals with subjective or mild cognitive impairment from a single-centre memory clinic, classified by CSF biomarkers using externally validated cut-offs into A-T1- controls (n = 97), A-T1+ PASSED ('pTau and Aβ surge with subtle deterioration', n = 65), and A + T1+ Alzheimer's disease (n = 97), with parallel analyses using Aβ40-normalised pTau181. Endpoints comprised dementia conversion (n = 185, median follow-up 4.1 years), all-cause mortality (n = 258, median 7.0 years), longitudinal MMSE trajectories (n = 185), and regional brain volumes (n = 137). Independence from CSF biomarkers was quantified through systematic effect attenuation analysis. Serum β-synuclein was selectively elevated in the Alzheimer's disease group (Cohen's d = 0.69 vs controls, P < 0.001) but not in PASSED individuals (P = 0.40), and was more strongly associated with CSF pTau181 (r = 0.36) than with the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio (r = -0.20) across the cohort. Each standard deviation increase was associated with higher risk of dementia conversion (hazard ratio (HR) = 1.40; 95% CI: 1.11, 1.77; P = 0.005), faster cognitive decline (-0.11 SD/year, 95% CI: -0.18, -0.04, P = 0.002, corresponding to -0.20 MMSE points/year), and higher mortality (HR = 1.33; 95% CI: 1.07, 1.65; P = 0.010). For dementia conversion and mortality, adjustment for continuous CSF pTau181 and Aβ42/Aβ40 produced minimal attenuation (≤13%). Both associations were preserved under Aβ40-normalised T1 staging but not against continuous pTau181 normalised to CSF Aβ40. For cognitive decline, β-synuclein's effect remained significant after Aβ42/Aβ40 adjustment (25% attenuation; P = 0.007) but was substantially attenuated by pTau181 (58.5%; P = 0.186). Serum β-synuclein was associated with lower bilateral temporal lobe volume-the only lobar regions to survive hierarchical testing-with sub-regional involvement spanning the hippocampi, entorhinal cortex and parahippocampal gyrus, and explained 5.0-8.9% of unique variance beyond CSF biomarkers. Plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) showed a strong association with β-synuclein, estimated in the PASSED subgroup (β=0.34 per SD, P < 0.001). Serum β-synuclein provided prognostic information largely independent of CSF Aβ42/Aβ40 across all endpoints and of pTau181 for survival outcomes, while sharing substantial prognostic variance with pTau181 for cognitive trajectory, supporting its candidacy as a blood-based synaptic complement to core Alzheimer's disease biomarkers.

title: TMEM106B risk converges on C-terminal fragment homeostasis: genetics, mechanisms and therapy
abstract: TMEM106B is a genetic modifier influencing susceptibility to multiple neurodegenerative disorders, including frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP-43 pathology (FTLD-TDP), Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy, as well as contributing to healthy brain aging and neuronal reserve. The gene harbours single nucleotide polymorphisms and structural variants that define risk and protective haplotypes, and despite extensive efforts to identify the functional variant within these haplotypes, consensus remains elusive. In this review, we synthesize current knowledge of TMEM106B genetics from human cohorts and mechanistic studies, highlighting how variants may influence its regulatory network and protein levels, with an emphasis on its aggregation-prone C-terminal domain. We further integrate evidence on the roles of TMEM106B within the endo-lysosomal system and beyond, including insights into protein structure, posttranslational modifications, interactors, proteolytic processing, and fibril formation. These findings are contextualized using data from mouse and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models, highlighting current gaps in the available models and the advances required to study its functions and cleavage. Finally, we explore therapeutic strategies targeting TMEM106B, focusing on modulation of expression, specific functional pathways, and fibril formation.

title: Prefrontal ensembles represent freezing of conspecifics
abstract: Social buffering is a process in which the presence of other members of the same species (conspecifics) decreases stress reactions during threat exposure. In parallel, prior reports showed that groups of individuals display synchronous actions in non-threatening situations. However, it is unknown if individuals also synchronize actions when facing threats. Prior studies showed social buffering of freezing in pairs of subjects. We now expand these findings and show social buffering of freezing during exposure to a predator and a shock grid in mice of both sexes in a larger group of four conspecifics. Furthermore, mice also displayed synchronized freezing. The presence of freezing synchrony suggests the existence of a neural representation of conspecific freezing. We reasoned that this encoding might be in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), as this region has been implicated in social behaviors and freezing. Strikingly, mPFC neural activity represented the average level of freezing across conspecifics. MPFC ensembles displayed differential encoding of self and conspecific freezing, and during predator exposure the mPFC encoded the number of conspecifics freezing and conspecific freezing bout duration. These data show, for the first time, neural representation of conspecific freezing, and suggest that the mPFC may coordinate behavioral responses to threat across conspecifics. Significance Statement  Social animals display attenuated threat-elicited responses when encountering threats as a group. However, it is unknown how freezing signals from conspecifics are encoded by the brain when facing threats, as prior work has been limited to studies of pairs, or assays without social interactions. We identify a neural population in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) that represents conspecific freezing during grouped threat exposure, and these cells dynamically represent the duration of other animals' freezing bouts. Strikingly, the activity of these ensembles also represents the number of conspecifics freezing. These findings uncover a previously unknown function of the mPFC to encode conspecific freezing.

title: Emotion-Focused Behavioral Weight Loss Treatment for Adolescents: A Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Family-based behavioral treatment (FBT) efficacy decreases in adolescence, a developmental period of gradual maturation and increasing autonomy during which emotion regulation skills develop.

OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the feasibility and efficacy of FBT alone compared with FBT plus emotion regulation across 6 months of treatment and 12 months of follow-up on adolescent weight change, emotion regulation, emotional eating, and parent weight change.

DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This parallel-group randomized clinical trial of adolescents 13 to 16 years of age with body mass index (BMI) in the 85th percentile or higher but less than the 99.9th percentile was conducted from August 29, 2019, to January 4, 2024, at 2 university clinics. Central randomization was completed by a statistician, and outcome assessors were blinded to treatment condition. The majority of treatments and assessments were delivered remotely via video conference due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

INTERVENTIONS: FBT plus emotion regulation vs traditional FBT skills alone for weight loss. FBT included nutrition and physical activity education, behavior change strategies, and parenting skills. Both treatments had 6 months of adolescent and parent groups and behavior coaching sessions. The combined group included FBT skills and added dialectical behavior therapy and emotion-focused therapy.

MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The main outcomes were adolescent weight (body mass index [BMI] z score (BMIz) and BMI as a percentage of the 95th BMI percentile [%BMIp95]), emotion regulation skills (measured by Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale [DERS] scores), emotional eating behaviors (measured by Emotional Eating Scale [EES] scores), parent weight, and feasibility and acceptability of treatment. Primary outcome analyses used an intention-to-treat approach.

RESULTS: A total of 166 (FBT plus emotion regulation = 84; FBT = 82) dyads (adolescents: mean [SD] age, 14.3 [1.2] years; 95 [57%] female; mean [SD] BMIz, 2.2 [0.6]; mean [SD] %BMIp95, 120.4 [21.4]; parents: mean [SD] age, 45.3 [6.5] years; 141 [85%] female; mean [SD] BMI, 32.6 [7.0]) were assessed at baseline, midtreatment, posttreatment, and 6- and 12-month follow-up visits. There were no statistically significant differences in posttreatment weight loss among adolescents receiving FBT plus emotion regulation compared with FBT (difference in BMIz, 0.03 [95% CI, -0.05 to 0.10]). However, adolescents in FBT plus emotion regulation did not regain as much weight at the 12-month follow-up (difference in BMIz, -0.09 [95% CI, -0.17 to -0.02]). At the 12-month follow-up, 4% (95% CI, 1%-12%) of adolescents in FBT and 22% (95% CI, 8%-48%) of adolescents in FBT plus emotion regulation lost a clinically significant amount of weight (≥0.20 BMIz). At 12 months' follow-up, parent weight (difference in BMI, 0.51 [95% CI, -0.03 to 1.05]) and adolescent emotion regulation (difference in DERS scores, -0.06 [95% CI, -0.25 to 0.50]) did not differ by treatment. By contrast, the FBT plus emotion regulation group had lower scores than the FBT group on emotional eating (difference in EES scores, -0.39 [95% CI, -0.63 to -0.15]).

CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this randomized clinical trial of 166 parent-adolescent dyads, adding emotion regulation skills to FBT did not improve weight loss during treatment but was associated with less weight regain and lower emotional eating through the 12-month follow-up. These findings suggest that adding emotion regulation skills to an FBT program may attenuate weight regain and decrease emotional eating among adolescents.
