title: The impact of state- and county-level anti-sexual and gender minority structural stigma on psychotherapy outcomes among a national sample of college students
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: While structural stigma against sexual and gender minorities (SGMs) has been well-established to negatively impact SGM mental health, its influence on therapy outcomes for SGM living in more stigmatizing environments remains unclear.

METHOD: Using the Center for Collegiate Mental Health Standardized Data Set (student n = 416,339; institution n = 216), we examined the impact of stigma on baseline symptoms, treatment attendance, and psychotherapy outcomes among SGM compared with non-SGM students. The self-report Counseling Center Assessment of Psychological Symptoms Distress Index, a measure of general psychiatric symptoms, was our primary outcome. We examined outcomes and attendance across eight sessions of psychotherapy, using multilevel modeling. Time-varying (years 2012-2022) sexual and gender-based structural stigma composites for the institutions' states and counties were calculated using data on both public opinion and laws and policies impacting SGM individuals.

RESULTS: SGM students entered treatment with more severe Counseling Center Assessment of Psychological Symptoms Distress Index symptoms compared to non-SGM students (ds = 0.36-0.41). Higher county-level gender-related stigma predicted more severe symptoms among gender-diverse students (ps = .025-.010). SGM students attended relatively more psychotherapy sessions in counties with greater sexual structural stigma (p < .001). However, SGM students did not demonstrate meaningfully different symptom change trajectories relative to non-SGM compared to non-SGM students, and structural stigma was not associated with changes in Counseling Center Assessment of Psychological Symptoms Distress Index scores when accounting for SGM identity (all ps > .250).

CONCLUSION: Structural stigma was not associated with poorer treatment outcomes for SGM students receiving naturalistic psychotherapy at collegiate counseling centers. Rather, these results highlight the potential resilience-building effects of psychotherapy, even within stigmatizing contexts. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

title: Effects of an internet-delivered behavioral self-monitoring intervention on depressive symptoms in older widowed adults: A randomized controlled trial
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Late-life bereavement triggers substantial change to surviving spouses' routine health behaviors. Behavioral self-monitoring interventions are promising tools for promoting change across multiple behavioral domains, yet little is known about their efficacy in the spousal bereavement period. This trial evaluated the efficacy of an internet-delivered behavioral self-monitoring intervention for reducing depressive symptoms in older widowed adults.

METHOD: We conducted an assessor-blind randomized controlled trial at a single site in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, from January 2020 to August 2025. We randomly assigned adults aged 60+ years who experienced the recent death of a spouse or life partner and had subsyndromal depressive symptoms (defined as a Hamilton Depression Rating Scale score of ≥9) to either behavioral self-monitoring or enhanced usual care. We measured change in Hamilton Depression Rating Scale at 3 months as our primary outcomes using intent-to-treat analyses. Secondary outcomes included changes in anxiety, complicated grief, and posttraumatic stress at 3 months.

RESULTS: We randomized 151 protocol-eligible patients to either our intervention or control arms. Their M (SD) age was 70.3 (6.9) years, 121 (81%) were female, and 124 (82%) completed their 3-month follow-up assessment. The intervention produced significant effect size improvements in depression, Cohen's d = 0.48; 95% confidence interval (CI) [0.1, 0.8]; p < .001, anxiety (0.57; 95% CI [0.2, 0.9]; p < .001), but not in complicated (prolonged) grief or posttraumatic stress.

CONCLUSIONS: Internet-delivered behavioral self-monitoring for older widowed adults is more effective than enhanced usual care at reducing depression and anxiety symptoms during the spousal bereavement period. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

title: Basic-level category processing advantage in fear generalization and its modulation by threat-conditioned stimulus diversity: Behavioral and event-related potential evidence
abstract: Category-based fear generalization refers to the extension of acquired fear responses to novel stimuli sharing categorical cues with a threat stimulus. Categories are organized into superordinate, basic-level, and subordinate levels, which differ in cognitive processing advantages; however, whether this categorical advantage influences fear generalization remains unclear. Experiment 1 used a discriminative fear conditioning paradigm, employing subordinate exemplars of birds and measuring tools as the threat-conditioned stimulus (CS+) and the safety-conditioned stimulus (CS-), respectively. During the generalization test, we included generalization stimuli sharing either the same basic-level category (GS Basic ) or the same superordinate category (but different basic-level category) as the CS+. Fear generalization was assessed via shock expectancy ratings and skin conductance responses. Experiment 2 manipulated CS+ diversity (high vs. low) in the same task while recording electroencephalography to examine its moderating role. Behaviorally, acquired fear generalized more robustly to GS Basic  than to GS sharing the same superordinate category (GS Superordinate ). Participants in the high-diversity group showed higher shock expectancy ratings for both the CS+ and GS Basic  than those in the low-diversity group. Event-related potential results revealed that GS Basic  elicited P2 and N400 amplitudes comparable to those of the CS+, and exhibited more positive P2 and less negative N400 amplitudes than GS Superordinate  and CS-. Moreover, only the CS+ and GS Basic  elicited more positive LPP amplitudes than CS-. These findings suggest that early attentional allocation, late semantic processing, and motivational attention collectively constitute the electrophysiological basis of the basic-level category processing advantage in fear generalization, offering implications for the intervention of anxiety disorders.

title: Incorporating Data From Text Messages and Email Into Psychotherapy: Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract:
Abstract Background As digital communication becomes central to daily life, psychotherapy increasingly has access to patients’ electronic media data. Although digital phenotyping has been widely studied, less is known about whether incorporating personal communication data, such as text messages, improves clinical outcomes in psychotherapy. Objective This study aimed to determine whether integrating personalized text message data into psychotherapy improves depression, anxiety, health-related quality of life, and therapeutic alliance and to examine whether increased access to collateral information influences clinical decision-making. Methods The Electronic Media and its Impact on Psychotherapy (EMAP) study was a randomized controlled trial conducted in adult and geriatric outpatient and partial hospitalization settings at an academic psychiatric hospital. Participants receiving psychotherapy for primary depression or anxiety (n=101) were randomized to electronic media–enhanced therapy (EME; n=52) or treatment as usual (TAU; n=49). In EME, research staff reviewed participants’ text messages prior to sessions using personalized mood-related key terms and presented aggregated findings on a Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA)–compliant clinician dashboard. TAU participants received standard care without message review. Outcomes included change scores for the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7), the 36-item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36), and the Working Alliance Inventory–Short Revised (WAI-SR). Linear regression and nonparametric tests compared groups. Moderation analyses assessed whether the frequency of information access influenced treatment changes. Results No statistically significant between-group differences were observed in anxiety or working alliance. Among participants with SF-36 follow-up data (n=65), EME participants demonstrated greater improvement in the pain subscale. Greater frequency of information access was associated with increased treatment-related changes in the EME group. Access to additional collateral information was associated with more clinical actions but not with improved distal outcomes. Conclusions Integrating personalized text message data into short-term psychotherapy did not significantly improve depression or anxiety, and it neither improved nor worsened therapeutic alliance. However, access to greater amounts of collateral information, including electronic media, influenced clinical decision-making, suggesting nuanced and context-dependent effects.

Introduction Over the past decade, the digitization of everyday life has meant that devices such as smartphones serve as conduits for everyday function and communication [ 1 ]. Interpersonal communication now includes digital media such as text messages, blogs, emails, and social media; much of this communication is chronicled and preserved in ways that did not exist until the advent of these technologies. Increasingly, psychiatry, and particularly the realm of psychotherapy, has begun to recognize the ways in which digital data can be incorporated into care. A vast literature exists in the domain of digital biomarkers and digital phenotyping [ 2 - 5 ], where sensors and devices track behavior and, in turn, generate objective measures of activity, sleep, mood, and parameters such as medication responses and side effects. However, a simpler and more intuitive use of this digital collateral information available through digital media and communication—such as text messages—has been relatively understudied. Psychotherapy relies on patient recall of key information, events, and interactions. There is evidence to indicate that clinicians sporadically incorporate information from digital communications into therapy sessions and that including this information may have a positive impact on the psychotherapeutic process [ 6 - 8 ]. However, emerging evidence also indicates that the effectiveness of these approaches may be situational and that outcomes may vary depending on how data are presented and accessed. For instance, one study [ 9 ] found that the use of a dashboard that presented clinicians with broad metrics, such as time spent on a smartphone during the night, miles walked per week, and top searches on social media, led to no statistically significant changes in patients’ well-being scores. A follow-up study [ 10 ] also found that clinician use of such a digital dashboard did not improve well-being. Notably, both studies found that patients and clinicians alike appreciated the awareness the dashboard brought to patients’ digital use. Patients also reported feeling comfortable and positive about the dashboard experience [ 10 ]. This suggests that the impact of this approach may be subtle and nuanced, a notion that is being increasingly replicated in other studies [ 11 ]. However, neither study investigated whether there was a differential impact from evaluating more personal communication, such as email or text messages. Investigating this is relevant because Liu et al [ 12 ] demonstrated that the language in text messages strongly correlates with the severity of self-reported depressive symptoms. This finding was based on sentiment analysis of existing text messages; however, how it may translate into real-time inclusion of text messaging content into psychotherapy is unknown. There are important implications for gaining a more sophisticated understanding of how access to broader information from digital communication and media impacts outcomes in psychotherapy. Spending time in a session reviewing digital content can take away from time spent engaged directly with patients [ 13 ], and it is not clear how this may impact rapport. It is also not clear whether any benefits are empirical or situational. Finally, because there is great interindividual variance in how individuals across the age span express emotion in electronic communication [ 14 ], there is a need for guidelines around how to optimize the use of electronic media. To address these knowledge gaps, we conducted a randomized controlled trial of an intervention in which research staff performed a personalized review of patients’ text message communication prior to a psychotherapy session. This information was aggregated into an interactive dashboard for clinicians to access during their sessions with patients. We sought to assess whether (1) access to collateral information about text communication impacted depression and anxiety, (2) using a dashboard to review this information during therapy sessions impacted the therapeutic alliance, and (3) accessing more collateral information, including digital communication, during therapy sessions impacted the way therapists planned treatment for each session. We hypothesized that patients receiving care incorporating electronic media would experience greater reductions in depression and anxiety, improved health-related quality of life scores, and a stronger working alliance compared with those receiving treatment as usual (TAU). Additionally, we explored how clinicians used data during sessions and whether increased data access influenced their approach to care. Methods Participants This study was conducted in the adult and geriatric outpatient and partial hospitalization programs at McLean Hospital, an academic psychiatric hospital affiliated with Mass General Brigham Health and Harvard Medical School. Recruitment occurred from July 2020 to July 2023. We initially contacted clinicians providing outpatient psychotherapy, including psychiatrists, psychologists, and social workers. Clinicians were eligible if they offered psychotherapy, regardless of whether they also prescribed medications concomitantly. On the basis of referrals from clinicians, we recruited individuals engaged in individual psychotherapy for primary diagnoses of anxiety or depression. Individuals with cognitive impairment, active psychosis, or active substance use disorders were excluded, since this study focused primarily on psychotherapy outcomes for depression and anxiety. Of note, the study protocol was originally designed prior to the COVID-19 pandemic but was adapted since the pandemic-related lockdown was imposed shortly after the study was approved by the institutional review board (IRB). Protocols were adjusted to allow for recruitment and administration of the study procedures virtually, whereas the original protocol was designed for in-person visits. Study visits occurred between August 2020 and July 2023. Intervention Participants in this study were randomized into 2 groups using randomized number sequencing: the electronic media–enhanced therapy (EME) group and the TAU group. Participants were assigned in a 1:1 ratio between groups using a pregenerated random allocation sequence. Participants were assigned sequentially according to this randomization list as they were enrolled. The study was not blinded, and allocation was not concealed. The EME group received therapy augmented by the collection and analysis of electronic media data, while the TAU group received standard clinical treatment without the incorporation of electronic media data. Both groups were administered standardized scales. For both the EME and TAU groups, research assistants met with participants prior to each scheduled clinical session. During these meetings, which lasted approximately 30 minutes, study staff administered questionnaires assessing participants’ use of messaging apps (eg, text messages, Facebook Messenger, and WhatsApp). The questionnaires included both objective measures (eg, frequency and number of active conversations) and subjective items assessing participants’ comfort with the research process. In the EME group, research assistants also reviewed participants’ messaging content using Zoom’s screen-sharing feature. Participants were instructed on how to share their screens and were asked to search their messages for 12 preselected key terms that reflected emotional valence for mood states such as depression and anxiety. These terms were chosen based on consensus of the research team, informed by both clinical experience and prior research. In consultation with the participant’s clinician, each participant was provided with a personalized list of 12 key terms, which were updated as necessary. For participants in partial hospitalization programs, key terms were identified within the previous day’s messaging to account for the shorter duration between clinical visits. The standardized scales administered to both groups were as follows: (1) the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) [ 15 ], (2) the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) [ 16 ], (3) the Working Alliance Inventory–Short Revised (WAI-SR) [ 17 ], (4) the RAND Medical Outcomes Study 36-item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36) [ 18 ], and (5) the McLean Collateral Information and Clinical Actionability Scale (M-CICAS) [ 7 ]. Collected data were entered into a Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA)–compliant platform developed by Mirah, a Boston-based company. Mirah is an established digital behavioral health platform that provides software for the secure delivery of measurement-based care tools and patient-reported outcomes. For this study, Mirah custom-designed a portal that enabled data collection, data storage, and a clinician-facing dashboard that presented aggregated data from messages as well as the standardized scales. Clinicians reviewed the data before or during psychotherapy sessions. Any content that raised clinical concerns during presession data collection was forwarded to the principal investigator (PI) and the participant’s therapist for further evaluation and action. Since all psychotherapy sessions were conducted in person or virtually at McLean Hospital, a well-established infrastructure and protocols were in place to manage any decompensation or severe symptoms and would be activated at the clinicians’ discretion. In the TAU group, no review of messaging content occurred. Instead, research assistants focused on collecting self-reported data on mood and health functioning, which were also tracked using the same Mirah platform. Research Assistant Training Before engaging in data collection, all research assistants underwent training to ensure interrater reliability. The training, conducted by the PI or a clinical coinvestigator, involved a certification process requiring research assistants to identify 10 emotionally charged sentences out of 20 conversational samples with at least 90% accuracy. Research assistants were also trained to detect content that might raise safety concerns and to follow appropriate procedures for managing these concerns. Once certified, research assistants were authorized to record relevant data, including the frequency of key terms used in participants’ messaging, the emotional tone of these messages, and the identities of the individuals involved in the conversations. Assessments During therapy sessions, clinicians in both groups reviewed the mood scales, health data, and collected collateral information, including messaging behavior for participants in the EME group. Clinicians were encouraged to incorporate this information into their clinical decision-making but retained discretion over how to use the data. In the EME group, clinicians could choose to view specific messaging content, especially if there were concerns about suicidality, mood changes, or disorganized thoughts. Any emergent concerns related to safety or mental health were immediately triaged by the therapist or a licensed clinician on the study team, with the PI available for further consultation if necessary. After each clinical session, both patients and clinicians completed assessments. The WAI-SR was administered to clinicians and patients at baseline and final visits to assess the therapeutic alliance. For participants in partial hospitalization programs, the assessment schedule was adjusted to account for their shorter treatment duration. In these cases, mood and health questionnaires were administered between daily clinical sessions. title: Efficacy of progressive muscle relaxation training in post-traumatic stress disorder after the Kahramanmaraş earthquake: a randomized controlled trial
abstract:
Background The February 6, 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquake was one of Turkey’s most devastating natural disasters, causing serious psychological issues, especially Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). Although various treatments exist for PTSD, they can be costly and sometimes ineffective. Progressive Muscle Relaxation Training (PMRT) is a low‑cost, self‑administered technique with no side effects, but randomized controlled trials on its effectiveness for post‑earthquake PTSD remain very limited. This randomized trial examined whether PMRT effectively treats PTSD in individuals after the Kahramanmaraş earthquake. Methods The study included 44 earthquake-affected individuals aged 18–65 who met at least one of the following criteria: formal DSM-5 PTSD diagnosis by a psychiatrist, or a PCL-5 score of 47 or higher (indicating clinically significant PTSD symptoms). Based on power analysis, 22 participants were assigned to each group via block randomization: PMRT and control. All received PTSD and healthy lifestyle information; those on ongoing treatment continued. The PMRT group additionally received 6 weeks (twice/week, 20–30 min/session) of telerehabilitation-based PMRT. Assessments (PCL-5, DASS-21, PSQI, FSS, SF-36) were conducted pre- and post-intervention. Time-group interactions were analyzed with two-way mixed ANOVA ( p < 0.05). Results In the PMRT group, PTSD symptom severity significantly decreased after the intervention ( p < 0.001; η² p = 0.735). Significant improvements were also observed in depression (η² p = 0.435), anxiety (η² p = 0.521), stress (η² p = 0.504), sleep quality (η² p = 0.632), fatigue (η² p = 0.477), and both physical (η² p = 0.727) and mental (η² p = 0.630) components of quality of life compared to the control group ( p < 0.001). In the control group, no significant changes were observed in these parameters, while sleep quality and physical health deteriorated in the control group. Conclusion PMRT was associated with greater improvements in PTSD symptoms, psychological well-being, sleep quality, fatigue, and quality of life compared to an education-only control group. Telerehabilitation may offer a practical advantage when face-to-face care is limited, although this remains speculative. Clinical trial registration number NCT07164261 -02.09.2025.

Background Earthquakes are among the most destructive natural disasters, negatively affecting survivors both physically and psychologically [ 1 ]. Major earthquakes can lead to long-lasting psychological problems in exposed individuals, and one of the most common psychiatric conditions resulting from this traumatic process is Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) [ 2 ]. The most recent and striking illustration of this phenomenon is the twin earthquakes that struck near Kahramanmaraş on February 6, 2023, registering magnitudes of 7.7 and 7.6. These seismic events, separated by a nine-hour interval, had a direct impact on 11 provinces. Over 14 million individuals personally experienced the disaster, and more than 50,000 fatalities were reported [ 1 , 3 ]. Beyond the extensive destruction of life and property, the earthquakes also triggered severe psychiatric conditions among survivors, including PTSD, anxiety, and depression [ 2 – 4 ]. In a meta-analysis conducted by Çınaroğlu and colleagues, the prevalence of probable PTSD among adults after the Kahramanmaraş earthquake was reported to be 41% [ 3 ]. The long-term psychological impact of earthquakes has been well documented. Following the 1999 Marmara earthquake, the 36-month prevalence of PTSD was 19.2% [ 5 ], and a systematic review of studies conducted over 10 years after the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake confirmed that PTSD represents a substantial long-term burden among survivors [ 6 ]. The fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders-5 (DSM-5) defines PTSD as a psychiatric condition arising from direct traumatic exposure, witnessing a traumatic incident, or repeatedly learning about traumatic details. This disorder encompasses four distinct symptom domains: (i) intrusive re-experiencing (such as distressing memories, flashbacks, or nightmares), (ii) persistent avoidance of trauma-related stimuli, (iii) negative alterations in thoughts and emotions (including self-blame or ongoing negative affect), and (iv) heightened arousal and reactivity (manifesting as hypervigilance or exaggerated startle responses) [ 1 , 7 ]. Current clinical guidelines prioritize trauma-focused psychotherapy for PTSD, with pharmacotherapy (primarily selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) serving as a secondary option. However, these treatments can be costly, do not always provide satisfactory results, and symptoms often follow a persistent course [ 8 ]. Nevertheless, various physiotherapy approaches such as aerobic, breathing, relaxation, stretching, and strengthening exercises can also be used in the management of PTSD [ 4 , 9 , 10 ]. Progressive Muscle Relaxation Training (PMRT) is an active relaxation technique developed by Edmund Jacobson in 1938. This technique is based on the sequential contraction and relaxation of different muscle groups [ 11 , 12 ]. PMRT is a self-administered method with no adverse effects, easy, accessible, and economical [ 13 ]. This technique increases parasympathetic nervous system activity; thus, anxiety and stress levels decrease, sleep quality improves, and physical and mental relaxation is achieved [ 11 ]. In studies conducted with different groups in the literature, PMRT has been reported to be effective in reducing depression, anxiety, and stress, as well as improving sleep and quality of life [ 11 , 13 , 14 ]. However, randomized controlled trials investigating the efficacy of PMRT in individuals who develop PTSD after disasters are quite limited [ 4 , 15 ]. Furthermore, different results have been reported regarding the effect of PMRT on PTSD symptoms in existing studies [ 4 , 15 ]. This situation necessitates further research on this topic. Therefore, this randomized controlled trial aims to investigate the efficacy of Progressive Muscle Relaxation Training (PMRT) delivered via telerehabilitation on PTSD symptom severity, depression, anxiety, stress, sleep quality, fatigue, and quality of life in individuals who developed PTSD after the February 6 Kahramanmaraş earthquake. Methods Study design This study was a randomized controlled, parallel-group, pretest-posttest interventional study conducted to evaluate the efficacy of PMRT in individuals who developed PTSD after the February 6, 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquake. This trial complied with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines and was prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov on September 2, 2025 ( NCT07164261 ). The recruitment period was between September 2, 2025 and March 20, 2026, with the first enrollment and first randomization on September 2, 2025. Participants Eligible participants were individuals directly affected by the February 6, 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquake, aged between 18 and 65 years. Participants were included if they met at least one of the following two criteria: (i) they had been formally diagnosed with PTSD by a psychiatrist based on DSM-5 criteria, or (ii) they obtained a score of 47 or higher on the Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Checklist-5 (PCL-5), indicating clinically significant PTSD symptoms. Participants were recruited from two different sources. Those with a formal DSM-5 PTSD diagnosis were identified among patients presenting to the psychiatry outpatient clinic of Tatvan State Hospital. The diagnostic process was conducted during routine outpatient care and included evaluation of trauma exposure (Criterion A), intrusion symptoms (Criterion B), avoidance symptoms (Criterion C), negative alterations in cognition and mood (Criterion D), alterations in arousal and reactivity (Criterion E), duration exceeding one month (Criterion F), clinically significant distress or functional impairment (Criterion G), and exclusion of other conditions (Criterion H). No structured clinical interview (e.g., CAPS-5 or SCID-5) was administered specifically for research purposes. Those who met the PCL-5 cutoff score of ≥ 47 without a prior formal diagnosis were recruited through social media announcements (WhatsApp, Instagram). For these participants, the terms “probable PTSD” or “clinically significant PTSD symptoms” are used throughout the manuscript. Exclusion criteria were as follows: exposure to a disaster other than the Kahramanmaraş earthquake (e.g., war, flood, landslide); presence of uncontrolled chronic comorbidities (including diabetes or hypertension); diagnosis of severe psychiatric disorders (such as dementia, psychosis, or manic episodes); musculoskeletal conditions interfering with exercise participation; completion of Progressive Muscle Relaxation Training within the preceding year; communication difficulties; and inability to utilize necessary technology for telerehabilitation. Regarding safety procedures, all participants with a formal psychiatric diagnosis remained under the regular follow-up of a psychiatrist at the same state hospital throughout the study period, while those identified via the PCL-5 alone were provided with contact information for psychiatric support services. Participants who exhibited worsening of depressive symptoms or endorsed suicidal ideation during the pre- or post-assessment were planned to be referred for immediate psychiatric evaluation. No such adverse events occurred during the study (Fig. 1 ) [ 4 , 14 ]. After completion of the 6-week intervention period, all participants in both groups were offered the PMRT protocol. Participants with persistent or worsening symptoms, including those in the control group, were referred to the psychiatry outpatient clinic of Tatvan State Hospital for further psychiatric evaluation and appropriate treatment. Sample size Sample size was calculated using GPower software (version 3.1). Based on the PCL scores of the applied muscle relaxation group (pretest: 71.1 ± 7.9; posttest: 61.6 ± 13.2) from the study by Hinton and colleagues (2011), the within-group effect size (Cohen’s d) was calculated as 0.82 using a paired-samples t-test. It was determined that a total of 44 participants, 22 in each group, were needed to achieve 95% power with an effect size of 0.82 and α = 0.05 [ 16 ]. Randomization and blinding Participants were divided into two groups using block randomization with computer-based randomization software. The block size was determined as 4. Twenty-two participants were assigned to the PMRT group and 22 to the control group. Due to the nature of the study (active intervention group and control group), it was not possible to blind the participants and the physiotherapist administering the intervention to group assignment; therefore, the study was conducted as open-label. However, the assessors (researchers conducting the pretest and posttest measurements) were blinded to group assignment, and the statistician performing the data analysis also worked blinded to group assignments. Interventions Progressive Muscle Relaxation Training (PMRT): Participants in the PMRT group received PMRT for 6 weeks, twice a week, 20–30 min per session, individually (one-on-one) via telerehabilitation, in addition to their standard treatment. Due to limited access to face-to-face healthcare services after the disaster, the training was delivered via telerehabilitation using an online video conferencing platform. The PMRT protocol was based on Jacobson’s original method and involved the sequential contraction and relaxation of 16 different muscle groups. Before starting the application, individuals were taught how to contract and relax their muscles in a comfortable supine position. Then, together with deep breathing, they were asked to perform 3 repetitions of sequential contraction (10–15 s) and relaxation (15–20 s) of different muscle groups (upper extremity, head, neck, trunk, and lower extremity) (Fig. 2 ). To ensure standardization of the program, an audio recording using Jacobson’s PMRT protocol was used [ 4 , 17 ]. Standard Treatment: All participants in both the PMRT and control groups received information about PTSD (definition, etiology, treatment) and healthy lifestyle (physical activity, nutrition, stress management, sleep hygiene) [ 9 ]. Regarding concomitant treatments, at baseline, two participants in the control group were on pharmacological treatment for PTSD (one on paroxetine 20 mg/day, one on sertraline 50 mg/day). However, both participants discontinued their medication under the supervision of their prescribing psychiatrist during the study period. No participants in the PMRT group were receiving pharmacological treatment for PTSD at any point during the study. Regarding psychological treatments, although four participants (two in each group) had a history of psychotherapy before the study, none of the participants in either group received any form of psychological treatment during the 6-week intervention period. Therefore, no concurrent psychological treatment that could potentially influence the study outcomes was administered during the intervention (Table 1 ). Data collection tools Assessments were conducted at two time points: before the intervention and after the 6-week intervention. Sociodemographic data, including age, gender, marital status, body mass index (BMI), and habits related to smoking and medication use, were collected using a standardized form. Physical activity levels were evaluated with the International Physical Activity Questionnaire-7 (IPAQ-7). This instrument contains seven items. The total score is derived from the duration (in minutes) and frequency (days per week) of walking, as well as moderate and vigorous physical activities, each performed for a minimum of ten minutes. Based on the total score obtained, participants were categorized into three physical activity levels: inactive (less than 600 MET-min/week), minimally active (600 to 3000 MET-min/week), and very active (more than 3000 MET-min/week) [ 18 ]. These assessments were performed only before the intervention. The Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Checklist (PCL-5) is a 20-item self-report scale that assesses PTSD symptom severity based on DSM-5 criteria. Respondents rate each item on a 0–4 scale, yielding total possible scores from 0 to 80, with elevated scores reflecting greater symptom severity. The Turkish version has been validated and reliability has been established, and a cutoff score of 47 or above, recommended for clinical diagnosis, was used in this study [ 19 ]. The Depression Anxiety Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21) is a 21-item self-report instrument that evaluates three distinct psychological domains: depression, anxiety, and stress. title: Characterizing Behavioral Engagement in Smartphone Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Obsessive Compulsive Disorder: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract:
Abstract Background Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) are increasingly popular for their ability to disseminate evidence-based treatments in a scalable, accessible way. Engagement with digital treatments is critical for effectiveness but remains poorly defined and measured. Most studies rely on subjective self-reports or 1 or 2 objective metrics, overlooking the multidimensional nature of how users interact with DMHIs. Objective This exploratory secondary analysis applied a road map for comprehensive behavioral engagement measurement, developed for a prior smartphone cognitive behavioral therapy program for body dysmorphic disorder, to a 12-week randomized controlled trial of smartphone cognitive behavioral therapy for obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD; N=60). Aims were to (1) comprehensively characterize behavioral engagement using 21 objective app analytics-based variables, (2) identify distinct behavioral engagement profiles via cluster analysis, (3) assess whether profiles were differentially associated with OCD symptom change, and (4) evaluate associations between profiles and pretreatment credibility, expectancy, posttreatment satisfaction, and perceived app quality. Methods Behavioral engagement was measured via 21 objective variables derived from app analytics, spanning use volume, frequency, feature usage, session duration, and temporal patterns. Hierarchical agglomerative cluster analysis identified engagement profiles. Associations between cluster membership and OCD severity change (Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale) were examined using hierarchical generalized linear mixed models. Objective measures were complemented with subjective self-reports: namely, cluster differences in treatment credibility, expectancy, satisfaction, and perceived app quality were examined using ANOVAs and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. Results Cluster analysis indicated a 3-cluster solution representing high (cluster 1: 21/60, 35%), moderate (cluster 2: 31/60, 52%), and low (cluster 3: 8/60, 13%) app users. All 3 clusters experienced significant reductions in OCD severity, with no significant differences in pre- to posttreatment Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale change across clusters. Descriptively, cluster 1 had a higher rate of treatment responders than cluster 3. While clusters 1 and 2 had similar perceptions of treatment credibility and expectancy at baseline and satisfaction at posttreatment, cluster 3 perceived the intervention as significantly less credible, had lower expectations, and reported significantly lower satisfaction than cluster 2. All clusters rated app quality as similarly high. Conclusions Comprehensive behavioral engagement measurement is feasible and informative across different DMHIs and clinical populations. The finding that all engagement profiles showed comparable symptom improvement challenges simple dose-response assumptions and may suggest that multiple paths of engagement can be therapeutically beneficial; nonsignificant differences in improvement across clusters may also reflect limited power to detect differences. Pretreatment credibility and expectancy are associated with engagement patterns, identifying a potential modifiable intervention target.

Introduction Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) have the potential to expand access to care, offering scalable and flexible treatment options. However, their effectiveness depends on user engagement, a critical yet commonly overlooked factor in digital tools [ 1 - 3 ]. Engagement is a multidimensional construct that encompasses behavioral indicators of intervention use (eg, frequency, duration, breadth, and depth) and subjective experience (eg, affective response, interest, and attentional focus) during interactions with the intervention [ 3 , 4 ]. Despite its importance, engagement measurement has historically been oversimplified: most studies use self-report measures of satisfaction or acceptability that are vulnerable to demand characteristics [ 5 , 6 ]; those that incorporate objective data typically include only 1 or 2 such variables, such as login counts or total time on the app [ 6 - 8 ]. Considering only 1 or 2 objective measures of engagement overlooks nuances of how users interact with DMHIs. For example, 2 users may log into an app the same number of times, but one may do so consistently over 8 weeks, whereas the other logs in intensively at first and then disengages. Certain intervention content, such as exposure with response prevention (ERP) for obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), may be most effective when practiced consistently over time. Thus, these 2 usage patterns reflect meaningful differences in treatment exposure, yet they appear identical when measured by login counts alone. Similarly, measuring total time on an app does not capture how time is distributed across content areas. Time spent on ERP modules may be more strongly associated with OCD symptom improvement than time spent on less therapeutically active modules. Altogether, there is value in measuring engagement comprehensively to capture quantity, quality, and context of use. We previously developed a road map for comprehensive behavioral engagement measurement in a trial of smartphone-delivered cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) [ 9 ]. Using 19 app analytics-derived variables ranging from use volume, frequency, feature usage, session duration, and temporal regularity, cluster analysis identified three engagement profiles: (1) “deep” users, who engaged selectively with content but for extended durations; (2) “samplers,” who interacted briefly with most content; and (3) “light” users, with minimal and sporadic use. Engagement profiles were not significantly associated with differential treatment outcomes, although trends suggested that deep engagement may be linked to greater improvement compared with light use. This work demonstrated a novel approach to comprehensive behavioral engagement measurement. Our initial study in smartphone CBT for BDD was limited to a single clinical condition and intervention. However, each DMHI has unique features, content, and capabilities that will drive different use patterns, and each clinical target may require different patterns of use to achieve adequate treatment response. Thus, a next step is to test whether this measurement approach adapts and generalizes to new populations and interventions. Digital CBT for OCD offers a relevant second test of this measurement approach for a couple of reasons. First, access to evidence-based treatment for OCD is limited by a shortage of providers [ 10 ]. Many who do initiate OCD treatment do not receive guideline-concordant ERP [ 11 , 12 ]. DMHIs may help address these barriers, but their success hinges on user engagement. Second, CBT for OCD presents unique engagement challenges that give an opportunity to test whether our approach can be tailored to the distinctive considerations of a specific condition and intervention. Namely, ERP is aversive and may elicit disengagement [ 13 ], particularly in self-directed DMHIs, where no therapist is present to provide support and accountability. Altogether, digital CBT for OCD offers a relevant test case to evaluate whether our behavioral engagement measurement approach can capture clinically meaningful patterns of use in a distinct condition and intervention. Our prior work measuring engagement in smartphone CBT for BDD was also limited by an exclusive focus on capturing engagement through app analytics; we did not consider subjective engagement dimensions in tandem. For the most comprehensive view into user engagement patterns, objective behavioral metrics can be complemented and supplemented by participant-rated indices of engagement, such as treatment credibility, expectancy, and satisfaction, which reflect user attitudes about the intervention. For instance, a treatment’s early credibility, and participants’ initial expectancies about treatment, may shape behavioral engagement. Prior research suggests that treatment credibility and expectancy predict outcomes in exposure-based treatment for OCD [ 14 , 15 ]. However, to our knowledge, whether self-reported credibility and expectancy predict patterns of objective behavioral engagement with a DMHI has not been examined. Establishing such connections would provide actionable targets for improving intervention uptake and sustained use. In this study, we applied and extended our prior behavioral engagement measurement road map [ 9 ] to examine objective (app analytics) and subjective (self-report) measures of engagement with smartphone-delivered CBT for OCD (“ Perspectives OCD ,” N=60) [ 16 ]. This study extends our prior work in 3 ways: by testing the comprehensive behavioral engagement measurement approach in a new clinical population and intervention, by integrating objective and subjective engagement indicators to address a limitation of the prior study, and by examining whether pretreatment credibility and expectancy predict objective engagement profiles—a novel question in the DMHI literature. Aims were to (1) comprehensively characterize behavioral engagement; (2) identify distinct behavioral engagement profiles among users, via cluster analysis of 21 variables derived from app analytics; (3) assess whether engagement profiles were associated with symptom change over time; and (4) evaluate associations between engagement profiles and subjective indicators of treatment credibility, expectancy, satisfaction, and perceived app quality. Based on our prior findings in BDD [ 9 ] and broader DMHI research [ 17 , 18 ], we expected to identify distinct behavioral engagement profiles across multiple dimensions. While we hypothesized that profiles characterized by greater engagement, particularly involving more interaction with ERP content, would be associated with greater clinical improvement and more favorable ratings on measures of treatment credibility, expectancy, satisfaction, and quality, we expected these associations to be modest based on mixed findings in extant literature. Methods Overview and Study Design This is a secondary analysis of a 12-week randomized controlled trial comparing Perspectives OCD to HealthWatch, an online general health psychoeducation program validated as an attentional control for DMHIs [ 19 ]. In this study, only data from the Perspectives OCD condition were used (N=60). Full descriptions of study design, intervention, eligibility criteria, and procedures are reported in the primary manuscript [ 16 ] and clinicaltrials.gov record ( NCT04136626 ). A STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) checklist is provided in Multimedia Appendix 1 [ 20 ]. Smartphone CBT for OCD Perspectives OCD is a self-paced Android and iOS-compatible app with seven core modules that cover (1) psychoeducation, which oriented users to the CBT model of OCD and guided personalized goal setting; (2) cognitive restructuring to identify and reappraise OCD-related cognitive distortions; (3) ERP, which guided users through graded exposure to OCD triggers while refraining from compulsions; (4) mindfulness and mindful grounding (2 modules), which included audio exercises teaching mindfulness and attentional retraining skills; (5) values-based living and self-esteem, which helped users set activity goals aligned with their values and identify and modify negative core beliefs; and (6) relapse prevention. During goal setting, participants selected 1-4 OCD symptom domains (ie, contamination, over responsibility, perfectionism, aggressive, sexual, and scrupulosity obsessions). Within the ERP modules, the app then presented symptom-specific graded exposure hierarchies for each selected domain, which participants could complete in any order, skip if irrelevant, and supplement with user-created custom exposures. All app modules unlocked sequentially and contained psychoeducational reading complemented by short interactive exercises that could be repeated as often as desired. Useful exercises could be added to “favorites” for easy repetition. Perspectives OCD was delivered with light-touch coach support. Each participant was assigned a trained, bachelor’s-level coach who provided 2 brief phone calls at onboarding and midtreatment, respectively, as well as asynchronous in-app messaging. Coach support was focused on encouraging regular use, clarifying CBT content, and troubleshooting practical barriers, without delivering psychotherapy outside the app. Participants were encouraged to use the app daily and progress at their own pace over 12 weeks. See Wilhelm et al [ 16 ] for a full description of the intervention and participant journey. Participants Eligible participants included adults aged 18 years and older in the United States with a primary diagnosis of OCD, confirmed via the Mini International Neuropsychiatric Interview (MINI; [ 21 ]), who owned a smartphone with a data plan. Individuals were excluded if they were in concurrent psychotherapy or used another OCD-related app, had received 4 or more prior sessions of CBT for OCD, or had initiated or changed psychotropic medication in the past 2 months; stable medication was permitted. Additional exclusion criteria included current severe substance use disorder, current severe major depressive disorder, current posttraumatic stress disorder, lifetime bipolar disorder or psychosis, and acute suicidal ideation. Participants were recruited nationally from the Massachusetts General Hospital Center for OCD and Related Disorders via social media advertisements, professional organizations, and colleague referrals, between July 2021 and July 2023. Procedures Ethical Considerations Procedures were approved by the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board (protocol number 2018P001669) and monitored by a Data Safety and Monitoring Board. The primary study’s informed consent form covered use of deidentified data for secondary research analyses. After providing written informed consent, participants were randomized 1:1 to Perspectives OCD or HealthWatch, using computer-generated block randomization (block size 4), stratified by stable psychotropic medication status. The randomized assignment was concealed from participants until baseline clinician-rated assessments were completed and eligibility was confirmed; all participants were provided onboarding instructions to their assigned treatment the same day. As noted previously, only those participants assigned to the Perspectives OCD condition were included in current analyses. Data were stored deidentified on the secure REDCap (Vanderbilt University) [ 22 , 23 ] and Dropbox for Business platforms to protect participant privacy. Participants were compensated US $25 for midtreatment and posttreatment assessments. title: Concentrated Exposure Therapy vs Internet-Based Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract:
Key Points Question Is the Bergen 4-day treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder superior to internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy in reducing obsessive-compulsive symptoms? Findings In this randomized clinical trial of 119 adults with obsessive-compulsive disorder, the Bergen 4-day treatment group was found to be superior to internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy in reducing obsessive-compulsive symptoms, with large effects at 3-month follow-up. Meaning These findings suggest the Bergen 4-day treatment is effective for patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder.

This randomized clinical trial evaluates the efficacy of the Bergen 4-day treatment compared with internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy in reducing obsessive-compulsive disorder symptom severity.

Importance Given the high prevalence, chronicity, and associated disability of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), optimizing treatment is a global priority. The Bergen 4-day treatment (B4DT), a concentrated exposure-based intervention, may reduce treatment burden and improve access to evidence-based care. Objective To evaluate the efficacy of B4DT compared with internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy (iCBT) in reducing OCD symptom severity. Design, Setting, and Participants Single-center randomized controlled trial (1:1 allocation). Between May 8, 2024, and August 8, 2025, adults (aged 18 to 72 years) with OCD were enrolled and were followed up for 3 months. Key exclusion criteria included schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, acute suicidality, substance dependence, and recent psychopharmacological changes. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, 6 weeks, 8 weeks (posttreatment), and 3 months (follow-up) by masked evaluators. Interventions Patients were randomized to B4DT (including preparatory sessions) or an 8-week unguided iCBT program. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was the change in OCD symptom severity, measured by the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS). Secondary outcomes included self-reported OCD (OCI-R), dysfunctional cognitions, quality of life, depressive symptoms, experiential avoidance, global functioning, self-esteem, and treatment satisfaction. Results A total of 253 individuals were screened, and 119 were enrolled after 53 were found to be ineligible and 81 declined to participate. Sixty of the 119 randomized participants (mean [SD] age, 33.5 [10.1] years; 79 [66.4%] women) were assigned to B4DT and 59 to iCBT. The primary analysis included all randomized participants (intention-to-treat). B4DT was associated with significantly greater reductions in OCD symptoms (Y-BOCS) than iCBT, with large effects at posttreatment (mean [SE] difference, −7.9 [0.9]; 95% CI, −9.7 to −6.0; Hedges g , −1.6) and sustained effects at 3-month follow-up (mean [SE] difference, −5.6 [1.1]; 95% CI, −7.8 to −3.4; Hedges g , −1.0). Secondary outcomes consistently favored B4DT. Response and remission rates at 3-month follow-up were higher with B4DT (35 of 57 [61.4%] vs 11 of 44 [25.0%] and 24 of 57 [42.1%] vs 6 of 44 [13.6%], respectively). Conclusions and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial of 119 adults with OCD, B4DT was superior to iCBT in reducing OCD symptom severity, with sustained benefits. Its brief, concentrated format may represent a scalable strategy to improve access to effective OCD treatment globally. Trial Registration German Clinical Trials Register: DRKS00034236

Introduction Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) affects 1% to 3% of the population and is associated with substantial functional impairment, reduced quality of life, and societal burden worldwide. 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 Exposure and response prevention (ERP) is the recommended first-line psychological treatment 5 , 6 and has demonstrated robust efficacy across meta-analyses. 7 , 8 However, access to and usage of ERP remain limited due to shortages of trained therapists, long waiting times, 9 and treatment refusal and dropout, 10 further limiting its scalability in routine care. These challenges have recently been highlighted in a report by the International OCD Foundation that points out persistent barriers to access to evidence-based OCD care. 11 As mental health systems increasingly emphasize efficiency and accessibility, optimizing delivery formats while preserving clinical benefits is a priority. 12 The Bergen 4-day treatment (B4DT) was developed as a concentrated ERP intervention (cERP) with an intention-focused approach that is delivered over 4 consecutive days following a brief preparatory phase. 13 By compressing treatment traditionally delivered over several months into 4 days, B4DT aims to enhance efficiency and accessibility while maintaining therapeutic intensity. A key innovation is the Leaning into Anxiety (LET) protocol, 13 in which patients are guided to intentionally engage with feared stimuli. This approach emphasizes willingness and approach behavior, potentially altering how patients relate to anxiety during and beyond exposure. Studies conducted primarily in Scandinavia report high response and remission rates. 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 However, the existing evidence is dominated by uncontrolled designs. Only 1 randomized clinical trial (RCT) has evaluated B4DT, comparing it with waiting list and structured self-help conditions. 19 Although that study provided important proof-of-concept evidence, it did not address whether B4DT confers incremental benefit over scalable digital cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) interventions that are increasingly being implemented within stepped-care systems. Moreover, waiting list comparisons may inflate estimated treatment effects relative to more stringent controls, 20 and psychotherapy trials more broadly can be susceptible to researcher allegiance effects associated with observed outcomes. 21 , 22 Determining whether a concentrated, specialist-delivered intervention, such as B4DT, confers meaningful advantages over scalable alternatives is central to contemporary stepped-care models. Internet-based CBT (iCBT) is an evidence-based and cost-effective approach that is increasingly being used, even with minimal guidance. 23 , 24 As digital-first pathways expand, comparative effectiveness data are needed to guide resource allocation, particularly given that digital interventions often yield smaller effects and have higher dropout rates than therapist-guided approaches. 25 Methodological considerations further complicate the interpretation of findings in prior B4DT studies. In several studies, baseline was assessed immediately before the core exposure phase, following a preparatory period. Because B4DT includes structured preparation, defining baseline at that point may obscure treatment-related change and limit comparability with standard ERP trials, which define baseline before initiation of therapeutic procedures. In addition, this approach may introduce sampling bias as individuals who discontinue during the preparatory phase may not be represented. This RCT addressed these gaps by comparing B4DT with an active, evidence-based iCBT intervention. 26 Baseline assessment was conducted prior to the preparatory phase to capture the full intervention trajectory and align with established ERP methodology. This study provided the first evaluation of B4DT against an active, evidence-based treatment and generated clinically actionable evidence to inform treatment selection, implementation strategies, and health system resource allocation in OCD care. The primary hypothesis was that participants receiving B4DT would demonstrate greater reductions in OCD symptom severity from baseline to 3-month follow-up compared with those receiving the active control condition (iCBT) as measured by the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS). Secondary hypotheses concerned the superiority of B4DT compared with iCBT in all secondary outcomes, including quality of life, depressive symptoms, global functioning, response and remission rates, and treatment acceptability. Methods Study Design This single-center RCT was conducted at the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf, Germany. Between May 8, 2024, and August 8, 2025, participants were enrolled. The study compared B4DT (adapted for use in Germany) with an active control condition consisting of an iCBT program for OCD. 26 The protocol was prospectively registered and approved by the local ethics committee (No. LPEK-0747). All participants provided written informed consent. The trial was conducted and reported in accordance with the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials ( CONSORT ) reporting guidelines. The study protocol was compiled based on preregistered materials and is available in Supplement 1 . Patients were not involved in the design, conduct, or reporting of the study. Patient organizations (eg, German Society for OCD, OCD Land) assisted with the recruitment. Assessments were conducted at baseline (t0), 6 weeks later (t1), posttreatment (t2; approximately 8 weeks after baseline), and 3-month follow-up (t3). A 12-month follow-up assessment (t4) was added during the course of the study to assess longer-term outcomes and will be analyzed separately from the primary end point analyses. Participants Eligible participants were adults aged 18 to 75 years with a primary diagnosis of OCD (according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders [Fifth Edition]), verified using the Diagnostic Interview for Anxiety, Mood, and OCD and Related Neuropsychiatric Disorders (DIAMOND). 27 The DIAMOND interview was administered to assess eligibility and identify any exclusion criteria. Diagnostic modules not relevant to the study objectives or the eligibility assessment (eg, neurodevelopmental disorders, somatic symptom and related disorders, and selected other disorders) were omitted. Participants were not required to be treatment naive, reflecting routine clinical practice. Previous ERP experience was recorded at baseline. If patients were taking medication, stable psychopharmacological treatment was required for at least 6 weeks prior to study entry. Exclusion criteria were acute suicidality, impaired intellectual functioning, current psychotic disorder (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder), autism spectrum disorder, substance dependence, insufficient German language proficiency, contraindication for in vivo exposure (eg, severe cardiovascular disease), and neurological disorder associated with secondary OCD. Randomization The random allocation sequence was generated using computer-generated block randomization (block size = 8). No matching, stratification, or minimization procedures were applied. After baseline assessment (t0), participants were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to B4DT or iCBT according to the predefined allocation sequence via email. The person responsible for allocation was not involved in baseline assessments. Outcome assessors were blinded to treatment allocation. Interventions cERP Therapy The intervention consisted of 2 preparatory individual 50-minute sessions with each participant followed by 4 consecutive days of B4DT delivered in small groups (typically 4 patients) by trained therapists with a 1:1 patient-to-therapist ratio. During the pilot implementation, 28 , 29 the therapists were trained and certified by the Bergen team. Subsequently, newly appointed therapists were trained and supervised by certified B4DT therapists within the Hamburg team. Throughout the trial, all treatment groups were supervised by 3 B4DT group leaders (L.J., J.S., and A.H.Y.) to ensure treatment fidelity. Day 1 focused on manualized psychoeducation and individualized exposure planning in the group. On days 2 and 3, participants completed concentrated, individually tailored in vivo exposure exercises across multiple OCD-relevant situations, supported by therapists throughout each day, and self-guided ERP exercises in the evening and the following morning. Group meetings were held to review progress and challenges and to share learnings. On the afternoon of day 3, a psychoeducation session for relatives was conducted. Day 4 focused on consolidation of treatment gains, relapse prevention, and planning of self-guided ERP for the upcoming 30 days. An individual booster session was scheduled approximately 3 months after treatment. The intervention was based on the original Bergen B4DT protocol and retained its core therapeutic principles, treatment structure, therapist-to-patient ratio, and exposure-based approach. Minor contextual adaptations, including refinements to preparatory sessions and culturally adapted patient materials, were made to support implementation in the German health care context. iCBT Participants in the control group received access to an unguided, OCD-specific iCBT program consisting of eight modules. 26 , 30 The program was delivered in its fixed, prestructured version, which comprises psychoeducation and CBT-based exercises targeting obsessions and compulsions, including a dedicated ERP module, alongside modules on mindfulness, self-esteem, and social skills. The intervention was entirely self-guided, although participants could contact the study team for technical support if needed. Participants in both groups were allowed to continue treatment as usual, including pharmacological treatment and outpatient psychotherapy. Outcomes The primary outcome was change in obsessive-compulsive symptom severity as measured by the Y-BOCS 31 from t0 to t3. Secondary outcomes were Y-BOCS–defined response and remission rates and changes in self-reported obsessive-compulsive symptoms (Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory–Revised [OCI-R] 32 ), depressive symptoms (Patient Health Questionnaire–9 [PHQ-9] 33 ), quality of life (World Health Organization Quality of Life–BREF, global item [WHOQOL-BREF] 34 ), self-esteem (Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale [RSE] 35 ), experiential avoidance (Brief Experiential Avoidance Questionnaire [BEAQ] 36 ), obsessive beliefs (Obsessive Beliefs Questionnaire–44 [OBQ-44] 37 ), and global functioning (Global Assessment of Functioning [GAF] 38 ). Treatment satisfaction was assessed using the Client Satisfaction Questionnaire–8 (CSQ-8 39 ). Additional prespecified measures, including adverse effects assessed using the Inventory for the Assessment of Negative Effects of Psychotherapy, were not part of the confirmatory testing and are therefore not included in the current efficacy analyses. Outcome Assessors and Interrater Reliability The DIAMOND diagnostic interview and Y-BOCS assessments were conducted by advanced psychology students and graduate psychologists who were blinded to treatment allocation. Follow-up assessments at t3 were conducted in person whenever feasible. However, to maximize retention and accommodate participant preferences, secure video conferencing was used when an in-person assessment was not feasible.
