title: Cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression as processes of change in transdiagnostic guided self-help cognitive behavioral therapy for adults with internalizing distress: Disaggregating within- versus between-person variability
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Processes of change in cognitive behavioral therapies (CBTs) remain frequently debated, perhaps due to methodological difficulties in conducting rigorous process research. We investigated two contrasting emotion regulation strategies, cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression, as processes of change in CBT disaggregating within- from between-person changes.

METHOD: We examined whether week-to-week changes in cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression (Emotion Regulation Questionnaire) predicted subsequent changes in distress (Kessler-6 Psychological Distress Scale) and well-being (World Health Organization-5 Well-Being Index) pooling two trials of a guided self-help CBT based on acceptance and commitment therapy. We used a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model to disaggregate between- versus within-person changes. Participants (N = 274) were 82% female, 80% non-Hispanic White, and mean age 37 years (SD = 13).

RESULTS: At the within-person level, week-to-week changes in reappraisal were consistently associated with subsequent changes in distress but less consistently with well-being. Changes in expressive suppression were less consistently associated with subsequent changes in distress or well-being. The associations between reappraisal and distress were robust to different model specifications, including detrending.

CONCLUSIONS: Cognitive reappraisal may be involved in the process of change in CBTs, including the so-called "third-wave" CBTs, which have traditionally de-emphasized its importance. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

title: In-session cortisol reactivity as a predictor of treatment response in Korean patients with PTSD
abstract: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is associated with hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis dysregulation, and in-session cortisol reactivity during exposure-based therapy may carry prognostic value. This study examined whether within-session salivary cortisol reactivity during Written Exposure Therapy (WET) predicts treatment response in Korean patients with PTSD. In a secondary analysis of a non-randomized waitlist-controlled trial (N = 41), cortisol was collected before and 15 min after the writing task at each of five sessions. Treatment response was defined using the reliable change index and assessed with the CAPS-5 and PCL-5 at the 6-week assessment, 12-week follow-up, and 24-week follow-up. Post-session cortisol suppression was numerically observed across all five sessions but reached significance only at Sessions 2 and 3. No significant group differences in Session 1 cortisol reactivity were found at the 6-week assessment; however, at 12-week follow-up responders showed significantly greater Session 1 cortisol suppression than non-responders on both CAPS-5 and PCL-5 (rs = 0.502 and 0.651, respectively), and this discrimination persisted at 24-week follow-up for PCL-5 (r = 0.563) but not CAPS-5. Subjective distress and cortisol reactivity were largely independent. These findings suggest that efficient HPA axis regulation during the first WET session may serve as an early biological marker of treatment consolidation.

title: Identifying predictors of treatment response in Hoarding Disorder using machine learning
abstract: The current gold standard treatment for Hoarding Disorder (HD) is cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). However, typical symptom reduction is 25% and only about one third of individuals achieve a clinically meaningful response. We used machine learning (ML) to identify predictors of treatment response using data from a non-inferiority trial of clinician vs peer-led group CBT for HD. Assessments were completed for 323 individuals with HD at post-treatment (N = 323) and at one-year follow-up (N = 183). Assessments included neuropsychological testing, symptom severity and psychiatric diagnoses, beliefs about treatment, treatment participation, and adherence measures. Outcomes included changes in HD severity (Saving Inventory-Revised) and functioning (Activities for Daily Living-Hoarding), which were modeled separately. Linear regression and decision tree models were optimized with cross-validation and used to select predictors of response. LASSO was used to distinguish predictors for symptom trajectories (sustained response, regressed response, late response, non-response) determined at one-year follow-up. Optimized models found that reduction in HD severity immediately post-treatment was predicted only by beliefs that treatment was beneficial. Improvement in HD functioning post-treatment was predicted by beneficial beliefs about treatment, memory related saving, and better sustained attention. At follow-up, higher HD severity reduction was predicted by identifying as non-White, more time maintaining progress, and beneficial treatment beliefs. Higher HD functioning reduction at follow-up was predicted by memory related saving, beneficial treatment beliefs and better performance on a sorting task at pre-treatment. Beliefs about treatment, possessions as memory support, sorting, attention, and visual memory may be key factors in treatment response.

title: Neurofeedback for Management of Musculoskeletal Pain: A Randomized Control Trial Using DOMS
abstract:
Introduction Chronic musculoskeletal (MSK) pain is associated with maladaptive neuroplasticity, often reflected in altered alpha activity (8–13 Hz). Neurofeedback may offer a way to modulate this activity, yet most protocols target alpha activity during rest, despite movement being a common pain trigger. This study investigated whether neurofeedback during movement could modulate alpha activity and reduce pain in healthy individuals experiencing induced pain via delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS). Method This experiment was a randomized, two‐armed, parallel‐group trial. Twenty‐nine participants were included (15 females, mean age = 28 years). Exclusions included neurological, psychiatric, MSK conditions. Participants were randomly assigned to an intervention group (aiming to reduce alpha activity) or a control group (aiming to increase it). Alpha activity was assessed as the alpha power during rest and movement. DOMS was induced using eccentric exercise of muscle extensor carpi radialis in Session 1. Neurofeedback was administered in Session 2, where participants underwent three blocks of neurofeedback training, using individualized EEG‐based visual feedback to modulate alpha activity. Session 3 assessed potential lasting neurofeedback effects. Pain was rated across the three sessions, which took place 24–48 h apart. Results DOMS induction was confirmed by increased pain ( p < 0.001, r = 0.82) and reduced alpha activity during movement ( p = 0.017, r = 0.49). Neurofeedback did not significantly alter alpha activity ( p = 0.114, W = 0.05 for the control group, p = 0.338, W = 0.037 for the intervention group). Conclusion A single neurofeedback session was insufficient to modulate brain activity or pain perception. Methodological factors, including limited training duration and participants’ strategies, may have contributed to the lack of an observable effect. Significance Although neurofeedback did not result in significant changes after one session, the observed alpha modulation following DOMS highlights the relevance of targeting neuroplasticity during MSK pain. Future studies should optimize training protocols and consider multisession designs to enhance clinical applicability.

1. Introduction WHO estimates that 20–33% of the world’s population is affected by chronic musculoskeletal (MSK) pain, making it a major cause of disability and reduced quality of life [ 1 ]. MSK pain often originates from repetitive movements or exertion, initially presenting as acute nociceptive pain. If unresolved, it might lead to maladaptive neuroplastic changes, including persistent activation of spinal neurons independent of peripheral stimuli and structural changes in the brain regions involved in pain processing [ 2 , 3 ]. These changes can contribute to the development of pathological chronic pain [ 1 , 4 – 6 ]. Current treatments include pharmacological and nonpharmacological approaches. Pharmacological treatments have side effects and can lead to dependence or addiction [ 7 ]. Nonpharmacological methods include passive modalities, such as heat or cold exposure, exercise, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, together with management of psychological factors [ 1 ]. There is limited and varying evidence on the efficacy of passive interventions [ 1 ]. Exercise therapy is widely recommended as a treatment for chronic MSK pain and is supported by systematic reviews and international clinical guidelines [ 8 , 9 ]. Nevertheless, treatment effects vary considerably between individuals, and long‐term adherence remains a challenge in clinical practice [ 9 , 10 ]. Together, these limitations highlight the need to explore complementary approaches that may further improve treatment outcomes, such as neurofeedback. Neurofeedback may counteract maladaptive plasticity by training individuals to regulate specific neural patterns [ 11 , 12 ]. EEG‐based neurofeedback for management of pain typically targets frequency bands related to pain processing, where alpha activity has received particular attention due to its association with pain perception [ 7 , 11 , 13 – 15 ]. Several studies have reported pain reduction following protocols aimed at increasing alpha power during rest [ 13 , 16 ], although other studies found no significant differences between active and sham groups, despite both showing increased alpha and reduced pain [ 18 , 19 ]. These mixed findings suggest that evidence for a consistent association between alpha activity modulation and pain reduction remains inconclusive. Importantly, MSK pain is often movement‐evoked, yet most neurofeedback protocols are designed for resting conditions. Mrachacz‐Kersting et al. [ 20 ] demonstrated that targeting alpha reduction during movement led to reductions in both alpha activity and pain after three sessions [ 20 ]. Similarly, Gervasio et al. [ 21 ] found that individuals with chronic MSK pain exhibited increased alpha power during movement but not at rest, compared to healthy controls, highlighting the relevance of movement‐specific alpha modulation [ 21 ]. This study aims to provide a proof of concept for the effectiveness on neurofeedback in modulating alpha activity during movement in the context of MSK pain management. Delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS), which induces acute MSK pain 24–48 h after exercise, has been proposed as a suitable experimental model of chronic MSK pain [ 22 ]. Moreover, previous research has shown that a single neurofeedback session can effectively modulate event‐related alpha activity in healthy participants [ 23 ]. Therefore, the current study investigates how DOMS‐induced pain affects alpha activity during movement and whether a single neurofeedback session can modulate these changes in healthy individuals. 2. Method 2.1. Participants This experiment was a randomized, two‐armed, parallel‐group trial designed to investigate the effects of EEG‐based neurofeedback on alpha activity and pain perception in healthy individuals following experimentally induced DOMS. CONSORT guidelines were followed for reporting. Participants were recruited via social media and oral outreach. A total of 30 individuals were enrolled. Inclusion criteria were age between 18 and 65 years and general good health, assessed based on participants’ self‐report [ 24 ]. Exclusion criteria included active drug use, pregnancy, or a previous or current diagnosis of neurological, psychiatric, or MSK disorders, recent surgery or fractures, participation in other clinical trials involving pain, or engaging in muscle training more than twice per week. Additional exclusion criteria were consumption of alcohol, caffeine, nicotine, or painkillers on test days, and inability to cooperate. One participant withdrew after the first session due to illness, resulting in 29 participants completing all three sessions. The final sample consisted of 15 females and 14 males (mean age = 28 years, SD = 9.6). The majority were right‐handed ( n = 27, 93.1%). Prior to participation, all individuals received written and verbal information about the study procedures, potential risks, and their rights as research participants. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The study was approved by the Scientific Ethical Committee of the North Denmark Region (N‐20240018). 2.2. Study Design Participants were randomly assigned to either the intervention or control group in a 1:1 ratio using a computer‐generated randomization plan. Group allocation was blinded to participants. Both groups received active neurofeedback based on their event‐related alpha activity. The intervention group was instructed to decrease alpha activity, while the control group was instructed to increase it. This design was chosen due to conflicting evidence regarding the directionality of alpha modulation in pain perception, allowing for exploratory analysis of its effect. It was hypothesized that both groups would be able to modulate alpha activity, but only the intervention group would experience a reduction in pain. 2.3. EEG and EMG Setup EEG and EMG signals were recorded using the Enobio 8 system (Neuroelectrics, Spain). EEG electrodes were placed according to the international 10–10 System. The selected electrodes were Cz, with either C3 or C4 selected based on handedness, C3 for right‐handed and C4 for left‐handed participants. EMG signals were recorded from m . Extensor carpi radialis. Electrode placement was determined by measuring the forearm length from the lateral epicondyle of the elbow to the radial and ulnar styloid processes at the wrist. The EMG electrode was positioned at 90% of this length, closest to the elbow [ 25 ]. The skin was shaved and disinfected prior to placement. Ambu Neuroline 720 electrodes with press‐stud connector were used. The reference electrode for both EEG and EMG was placed on the earlobe, with electrode gel applied to ensure signal quality. 2.4. Data Acquisition Data were wirelessly transmitted from the Enobio 8 to the NIC2 software with a 500‐Hz sample rate. Custom interfaces developed in MATLAB App Designer (Mathworks Inc, USA) were used to receive and process data. 2.5. Data Processing Signal processing was performed in MATLAB App Designer (Mathworks Inc, USA). EMG signals were filtered using a second‐order Butterworth high‐pass filter and band‐pass filer with cutoff frequencies of 55 Hz, and 2 and 40 Hz, respectively. All data were reference to the earlobe. EEG data were visually inspected for quality during the recording. Recordings with extensive ocular and muscle artifacts were removed from analyzed data. Extensive artifacts were defined through offline visual inspection as artifact contamination that dominated the recording to such a degree that reliable interpretation of the EEG signal was not possible. This assessment was based on visual evaluation of the overall signal quality rather than an automated artifact rejection pipeline or a predefined quantitative criterion, allowing for individualized assessment of data quality on a recording‐by‐recording basis. However, as neurofeedback included real‐time processing of the data, this step was not implemented during the neurofeedback intervention. EEG power was calculated using the fast Fourier transform (FFT), after which the power spectral density (PSD) was computed for the alpha band (8–12 Hz). PSD during movement was extracted using a single epoch from movement onset to one second postonset, with the 200–800‐ms window following movement onset identified as the interval of greatest alpha power increase [ 21 ]. For resting‐state EEG, the same epoch length was used with no overlap to ensure similar processing methods. 2.6. Experimental Protocol The experiment consisted of three sessions. The overall structure of the experiment protocol can be seen in Figure 1 . Session 1 included a baseline measurement of alpha activity and pain perception followed by DOMS induction. Session 2, conducted 24–48 h later, included neurofeedback training across three blocks, with baseline measurements taken before and after training. Session 3, held 24–48 h after Session 2, included a final baseline measurement to assess lasting effects of neurofeedback. All sessions were conducted under controlled environmental conditions: lights were turned off, blinds, though not fully opaque, were lowered and background noise was minimized. 2.6.1. Baseline Participants were seated upright approximately 1 m from a fixed visual point at eye level, with arms resting on armrests. Baseline measurements included EEG recording during rest and movement, pressure pain threshold (PPT), numerical rating scale (NRS), and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) collected in Session 2. Resting EEG was recorded for 2 minutes with eyes open. Participants were instructed to minimize movement and focus on a visual point. Movement‐related EEG was recorded during five concentric movements of m . Extensor carpi radialis, each followed by a 5–10‐s relaxation. Prior to movement‐related EEG recording, a calibration procedure was performed to detect movement onset. A movement was detected when the average signal in a 50‐sample window exceeded a dynamic threshold, calculated from the mean and standard deviation of a previous 5000‐sample window, multiplied with a participant‐specific constant [ 26 ]. A beep signaled movement detection during calibration. If detection failed, the multiplier was adjusted and calibration repeated until consistent detection was achieved. The final multiplier was stored and used for movement detection during the session. PPT was assessed using an Algometer type II (SBMEDIC), applying perpendicular pressure to the m . Extensor capri radialis. The pressure was applied at a point 1 cm distal to the EMG electrode. Participants pressed a handheld button when discomfort was felt. The procedure was repeated three times with 30 s between each procedure, and the mean was used as the final PPT. PPT assessments were performed by the same assessor (K. A. G), who was trained in the use of the algometer. NRS was used to assess pain intensity during movement, where 0 indicated no pain and 10 indicated the worst imaginable pain. 2.6.2. DOMS Protocol DOMS was induced through repeated eccentric work of the m . Extensor carpi radialis, using a load equivalent to 80% of the participant’s one‐repetition maximum (1RM) [ 27 ]. The 1RM was determined by incrementally adjusting a handheld weight, starting at 8 kg, with 1‐kg increases or decreases based on performance. 1RM was defined as the highest weight where a participant would perform a full eccentric movement lasting 5 s. Participants rested for at least 30 s between attempts for 1RM. The current study employed a short rest period between attempts due to the small load increments minimizing cumulative fatigue effects. To induce DOMS, eccentric movements were paced using a metronome set to 24 beats per minute, corresponding to one repetition every 5 seconds. The protocol consisted of three sets of 10 repetitions, with 2‐minute rest intervals. The exercise was repeated 10 times, followed by a 2‐minute rest. If the participant was able to complete the set, the procedure with 10 repetitions and rest was repeated two additional times. If a participant was unable to complete a set, the weight was reduced by 1 kg, and the set was repeated [ 27 ]. 2.6.3. Neurofeedback Neurofeedback training was conducted with participants seated in the same position as during baseline measurements. Participants performed self‐paced concentric contractions of m . Extensor carpi radialis approximately every 10 s. Each session included three blocks of training. The threshold for successful modulation was individualized based on the median event–related alpha power from the preceding EEG recording. title: TIRELESS study protocol: non-inferiority study of nurse-led web-based cognitive behavioral therapy for cancer-related fatigue in patients with incurable cancer
authors: van der Pas HB et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Fatigue is a prevalent and debilitating symptom for patients with incurable cancer. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can significantly reduce cancer-related fatigue in this patient group. However, implementation of CBT into clinical care is difficult as the intervention is time-intensive, costly, and requires face-to-face consultations with a specialized CBT therapist. Since nurses already support patient with symptom management, including fatigue, internet supported CBT delivered by nurses could be a promising alternative for patients with incurable cancer. The primary aim of this study is to determine the non-inferiority of nurse-led web-based CBT in its effect on cancer-related fatigue, compared to CBT provided by CBT therapists.

METHODS: The study is a prospective, non-randomized study using historical cohorts as the benchmark for comparison. Severely fatigued patients with incurable cancer of a solid tumor receive a 12-week nurse-led web-based CBT intervention. Primary and secondary outcome measures are assessed at baseline, post-intervention (14 weeks), and follow-up (26 weeks). The primary outcome measure is fatigue severity assessed with the Checklist Individual Strength (CIS-subscale fatigue severity). Secondary outcomes include functional impairment, quality of life and fatigue assessed with EORTC-QLQ-C30, and health care costs. Primary and secondary outcomes of the TIRELESS study and the benchmark are compared to determine non-inferiority. Non-inferiority of fatigue reduction is concluded if the upper bound of the one-sided 95% CI does not exceed + 5 on the CIS, with higher scores indicating more severe fatigue. In addition, interviews are conducted to gain insight in nurses' and patients' experiences with the intervention. These data are analyzed applying a thematic analysis method. Recruitment has started in June 2024.

DISCUSSION: Especially for this burdened patient group, integration of CBT for fatigue in routine medical care is essential. With the TIRELESS study, we aim to reduce patient burden, foster scalability and accessibility of CBT for fatigue, and increase patients' self-management. If this approach is non-inferior to the original evidence-based (benchmark) intervention, this will enable implementation of cancer-related fatigue interventions for the growing group of patients with incurable cancer.

title: Twelve-month follow-up of parent-based child anxiety treatment
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Supportive Parenting for Anxious Childhood Emotions (SPACE) is an efficacious parent-based treatment for child anxiety disorders. Little is known about the maintenance of treatment gains following SPACE, and no comparative follow-up studies have been conducted. We address both gaps by examining child anxiety severity up to 12 months following SPACE and cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). We also examine whether reductions in family accommodation of child anxiety are maintained through follow-up in both treatments.

METHOD: Participants were 125 mother-child dyads enrolled in a randomized controlled noninferiority trial comparing posttreatment outcomes of SPACE and CBT. Parents and children in both treatments completed measures of child anxiety severity and family accommodation at pre-, mid-, and posttreatment and at 3-, 6-, and 12-month follow-ups. Linear mixed models were used to examine effects of time, treatment, and their interaction across all assessment intervals, with particular interest in maintenance at 12-month follow-up.

RESULTS: SPACE and CBT both produced significant reductions in parent- and child-rated anxiety severity and family accommodation over time, indicating gains were maintained similarly for both treatments through 12-month follow-up. Parent (but not child) ratings of child anxiety severity were lower for SPACE than CBT at posttreatment and 12-month follow-up.

CONCLUSIONS: Results are the first to show maintenance of treatment gains up to 1 year following SPACE, comparable to CBT. These findings may inform clinical decision making and guide the selection of interventions that optimize both short- and longer term outcomes for anxious children and their families. title: What happens after being not-on-track? Patterns of change, profiles and prediction of at-risk patients
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Clinicians often struggle to accurately identify patients at risk of treatment failure. Feedback-informed treatment offers real-time outcome monitoring to help detect and address potential treatment failures early. This study examined patterns of change among not-on-track (NOT) patients during feedback-informed treatment, explored how patients' characteristics related to these patterns, and assessed the feasibility of predicting them.

METHOD: Data from 573 NOT patients in a university outpatient psychotherapy clinic were analyzed. Growth mixture modeling identified distinct change trajectories, omnibus tests compared patients' characteristics across patterns, and multinomial logistic regression evaluated the predictive value of these characteristics.

RESULTS: Three distinct patterns of change emerged, differing in symptom severity at the point of being flagged as NOT and in subsequent treatment response: C1: severe-modest responders, C2: severe-fast improvers, and C3: moderate-improvers. The patterns were differentiated by key intake variables, including symptom severity, personality disorder traits, interpersonal problems, and emotion regulation difficulties. Two of the patterns were predicted with acceptable accuracy.

CONCLUSION: All patient subgroups demonstrated improvement. Nevertheless, they became NOT for different reasons, and their responses were associated with different clinical characteristics. These findings suggest that a NOT alert should not be interpreted as a homogeneous signal, and patients may require different adaptations. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

title: The impact of threat- and safety-enhancing information on the acquisition of fear of interoceptive threat
abstract: Social learning, such as learning through verbal instruction, has been proposed to play a crucial role in the development pathological fear of bodily sensations. Despite the ubiquity of verbal information in daily life, the effects of verbal information on subsequent interoceptive fear learning remain empirically untested. Therefore, we aimed to examine how verbal information about the threatening vs. benign nature of bodily sensations influences subsequent interoceptive fear conditioning. 77 healthy participants were randomly assigned to receive either threat- or safety-enhancing information about bodily sensations before completing an interoceptive fear acquisition and extinction task. Two geometric symbols served as CSs and temporary dyspnea (inspiratory load) as the US. Verbal reports indicated successful differential learning in both groups, with no modulation of information type. However, participants of the threat information group showed no differential response in startle response magnitudes towards CS + relative to CS-, indexing that the activation of brain defensive networks, that did not differ between CS+ and CS-. This pattern might suggest a generalization of, or failure to inhibit defensive activation toward the safety stimulus. In contrast, the safety information group exhibited significantly smaller startle response magnitudes towards CS- vs. CS+, indicating preserved differentiation between threat and safety. No group differences emerged during the extinction phase. Despite the preliminary nature of our findings, the pattern of results demonstrates interaction of different fear learning pathways in shaping the risk for the development of pathological fear and anxiety.

title: Shared and Differential Psychological Processes Associated With Treatment Response in Mindful Self-Compassion and Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy for Chronic Pain: An Exploratory Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Psychological treatments for chronic pain are effective, but the processes associated with therapeutic change, and whether these are shared across treatments or treatment-specific, remain unclear. This exploratory secondary analysis examined whether changes in pain acceptance, pain catastrophizing facets and self-compassion were associated with clinical outcomes in Mindful Self-Compassion (MSC) versus Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy (CBT).

METHODS: Data were drawn from a randomized trial comparing MSC (n = 61) and CBT (n = 59) in adults with chronic pain and elevated emotional distress. Processes and outcomes were assessed at baseline and post-treatment. Single and theoretically ordered multiple-mediator models examined whether changes in pain acceptance, rumination, magnification, helplessness and self-compassion were associated with changes in anxiety, depression, quality of life, pain interference and pain intensity.

RESULTS: Compared with CBT, MSC produced larger increases in pain acceptance and reductions in helplessness. These processes statistically accounted for improvements in self-compassion, depression, mental quality of life and pain interference; acceptance additionally accounted for reduced pain intensity, and helplessness for reduced anxiety. Rumination and magnification predicted improvements across treatments but did not explain between-group differences. Multiple-mediator models indicated that acceptance/self-compassion and helplessness/self-compassion pathways favoured MSC for depression, anxiety and mental quality of life, explaining up to 51% of change. No mediator accounted for physical quality of life.

CONCLUSIONS: MSC and CBT appeared to engage overlapping processes, with differential associations mainly involving pain acceptance and helplessness. Acceptance may be more relevant to functional and pain-related outcomes, whereas helplessness/self-compassion pathways may be more relevant to emotional recovery.

SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: This study identifies pain acceptance and reduced helplessness as candidate processes associated with treatment response in MSC and CBT, with acceptance more closely linked to pain-related and functional change and helplessness to emotional outcomes. These findings support more precise, process-based psychological treatment for chronic pain.

title: Auditory Biofeedback Gait Training in Individuals With Chronic Ankle Instability: Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic ankle instability (CAI) develops in a large majority of patients with lateral ankle sprain (LAS), who often experience recurring injuries, residual feelings of instability, and abnormal neuromuscular patterns. Specifically, gait alterations are common in those with CAI and considered a contributing factor to poor long-term ankle joint health. Yet, there are no evidence-based gait-training protocols targeted to improve biomechanics, which may improve long-term outcomes related to ankle joint health and patient satisfaction.

OBJECTIVE: This study protocol introduces a progressive auditory biofeedback (ABF) gait-training program aimed to improve short- and long-term lower extremity biomechanics and talar cartilage outcomes and reduce the frequency of ankle-giving-way episodes and recurring injuries.

METHODS: This study is a multisite randomized controlled trial (RCT) with a target enrollment of 100 patients with CAI into a control group (n=50, 50%) or an ABF gait-training program (n=50, 50%). Both groups will complete a progressive 6-week (12-session) protocol comprising walking, ruck marching, and running on a treadmill. Lower extremity kinematics and kinetics, talar cartilage characteristics (via ultrasonography), self-perceived dysfunction and instability, and number of recurring sprains will be assessed prior to intervention, immediately after intervention, and 6 and 12 months postintervention. Finally, the frequency of ankle-giving-way episodes in the 6 months prior to intervention will be compared to the frequency of episodes at the 6- and 12-month time points to determine a longitudinal difference in ankle-giving-way episodes.

RESULTS: The study was funded in September 2024 and prospectively registered through ClinicalTrials.gov on March 10, 2025. The first participant was enrolled in May 2025. As of August 2026, 118 individuals had been recruited and 19 participants enrolled. Recruitment will remain open until September 2027, and study completion is expected in September 2028. Data processing is projected to continue through September 2028, with the final report published in June 2029.

CONCLUSIONS: This study will be the first RCT of ABF gait training to assess the immediate and long-term effects on lower extremity biomechanics, ankle joint health, and patient-reported outcomes in patients with CAI. Results from this study will advance the knowledge of long-term joint health that may be associated with poor outcomes post-LAS.

title: Virtual Reality for Enhancing Self-Compassion and Reducing Burnout Among Mental Health Care Professionals: Protocol for a Pilot Feasibility Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Mental health care professionals working in high-demand clinical environments are frequently exposed to patient suffering and trauma, placing them at increased risk for burnout and secondary traumatic stress. Compassion-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CF-CBT) has shown promise in reducing psychological distress and enhancing self-compassion; however, traditional delivery methods may be limited by time, accessibility, and resource constraints. Virtual reality (VR) may provide an immersive and accessible approach for delivering compassion-focused interventions.

OBJECTIVE: The primary objective is to evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of a self-administered VR-enhanced CF-CBT (VR-CF-CBT) intervention for mental health care professionals. Secondary exploratory objectives are to estimate changes in self-compassion, burnout, and secondary traumatic stress (STS), as well as between-group differences that can inform the design of a future definitive trial.

METHODS: A 2-arm randomized controlled pilot trial will be conducted among mental health care professionals. Participants will be randomized to either a VR-CF-CBT intervention or an active comparison condition consisting of self-guided CF-CBT delivered via digital booklets. Participants will complete 8 brief sessions (approximately 10 minutes each) over a 4- to 6-week period. Exploratory clinical outcomes will include changes in self-compassion, burnout, and STS measured using validated self-report instruments. Primary feasibility and acceptability outcomes will include recruitment, retention, intervention adherence, session completion, participant satisfaction, and scores on the Acceptability of Intervention Measure, Intervention Appropriateness Measure, and Feasibility of Intervention Measure.

RESULTS: The study was funded in April 2026. As of October 2026, 38 participants had provided consent and enrolled. Recruitment for a second wave of participants is ongoing, and data collection is in progress. Enrollment and data collection are expected to continue through 2026, with data analysis and dissemination of findings anticipated by spring 2027.

CONCLUSIONS: This pilot study will provide information on the feasibility and acceptability of delivering CF-CBT through immersive VR to mental health care professionals. Findings will help identify whether modifications are needed before a larger trial and provide preliminary estimates to inform the design of future efficacy testing.

title: Serial or Parallel? Sublexical Scanpath Analysis of Eye-movement Sequences in Single Word Reading
abstract: Are the letters of a written word processed sequentially or in parallel? Despite an abundance of research on visual word recognition, the evidence in this longstanding debate rests almost entirely on indirect inferences from word-length effects and conventional whole-word eye-movement measures. We sought direct evidence on the serial-parallel question by investigating sublexical gaze-fixation sequences-so-called  scanpaths . This study is the first to apply scanpath analysis to fixation sequences within single words. Thirty-four Hebrew-speaking adult university students read aloud three-letter and five-letter real words and pseudowords while their eye movements were tracked. As expected, real words showed more parallel processing, whereas pseudowords displayed more sequential, letter-by-letter scanpaths. Surprisingly, longer words tended to elicit serial processing regardless of word familiarity. Our findings support the applicability of scanpath analysis in visual word recognition and its potential to open up new perspectives on word-recognition processes.

title: On bias in detecting bias: A signal detection analysis of attributions to gender discrimination
abstract: Discrimination is the unjust treatment of people based on their group membership, and detecting discrimination is a necessary first step in countering it. Attributions to discrimination have often been conceptualized in terms of signal detection theory, with researchers speculating about the role of sensitivity (i.e., observers' ability to recognize discrimination) and response bias (i.e., their tendency to judge that discrimination is present) in observers' judgments. Here, we take a first step toward moving beyond conceptual applications to empirical signal detection theory analyses of attributions to discrimination across five studies examining judgments about gender discrimination in corporate pay raise decisions. We find that prototypes (Studies 1-3) and their alignment with the actual pattern of decisions (Studies 2-4) inform observers' response bias, reflecting differences in their attribution of unfair outcomes to discrimination (Study 5). In contrast, the extent of harm caused by discriminatory outcomes exerts a small effect on sensitivity and a large effect on response bias (Studies 1-3), which reflects observers' determination of a fair standard for decisions (Study 5). Theoretically, the present work contributes to the causal analysis of central factors shaping attributions to discrimination. Specifically, we shed light on whether effects of these factors are mediated by response bias or sensitivity, and assess their causal origin in either the application of a merit standard or attributional processing. title: Confounds in Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging-Part I: Mechanisms
abstract: In this review, the first in a three-part series, we consider the origins of confounding in fMRI. We review the signal properties of an fMRI experiment and the intended sensitivity to neurovascular coupling, the hemodynamic response function, and the spatial-temporal biases imposed by the heterogeneous anatomy of the vascular system. We then explore the various mechanisms that can leave nuisance signals, often termed physiologic noise, in fMRI data. All mechanisms having a biological dependence are considered, including mechanical effects from head motion and respiration, blood gases, brain motion from the cardiac pressure wave, blood pressure, and scanner instabilities that couple with the participant's body.

title: Confounds in Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging-Part II: Modifiers
abstract: In the first part of this three-part series, we reviewed the mechanisms that cause nuisance signals in fMRI data. Here, in the second part of the series, we review "human factors" that modulate these confounding mechanisms. The modulators may be trait characteristics such as age or bodyweight, or they may be state dependencies that alter the relative contributions of nuisance signals in the fMRI data. A wide array of psychological (e.g., motivation/arousal, cognitive strategy, task engagement), lifestyle (e.g., exercise, sleep, and dietary habits), experimental (e.g., scanner anxiety, task-related movement), and situational (e.g., prandial state, time of day, menses) factors can affect the brain state directly as well as via changes in systemic physiology mediated by autonomic nervous responses.

title: Spatial Memory Guides Attention before Object Recognition: Evidence from Lateralized N1pc Responses
abstract: Visual search is facilitated when targets reappear within invariant distractor layouts (contextual cueing). Although contextual cueing can bias attention within 150 msec, it remains unclear whether this guidance relies on global spatial configuration or requires object identity. We recorded ERPs while participants searched for targets in repeated versus novel arrays. Critically, each trial began with a placeholder display that conveyed only spatial configuration, preceding the search display by 500 msec. Following learning, targets were relocated and swapped their locations with a distractor in the opposite visual field, such that the overall search layouts remained unchanged. ERPs time-locked to placeholder onset revealed an early poster contralateral negativity (N1pc, 140-160 msec) for repeated contexts, despite the absence of target-specific object information. After relocation, this effect reversed polarity, indicating persistent orienting to the learned target location. A second N1pc, followed by N2pc and CDA, emerged only after search onset. These findings show that learned spatial structure rapidly guides attention, whereas effective selection requires additional processing of object information.

title: Cognitive forecasting: How intuitive theories of attention shape anticipated risk preferences
abstract: How do people forecast their own and others' risk preferences? Although it is well established that affective forecasts shape decision-making, less is known about where these forecasts come from. Five studies demonstrate that people rely on intuitive theories of attention when forecasting future affect-such as dread and savoring while waiting for a risk to be resolved-with these affective forecasts in turn shaping willingness to take such risks. In Study 1, forecasts of the participant's own expectations and attention were systematically related to forecasts of positive and negative affect during a waiting period, which in turn predicted risk preferences. Studies 2a and 2b demonstrate substantial heterogeneity in intuitive attention-affect theories: some participants believed attention amplifies the emotional consequences of expectations, whereas others believed attention is uniformly affectively negative. These differences led to sharply divergent predictions about when attention should increase or decrease risk-taking. Study 3 shows that attention is also informative about expectations: participants differed in whether they believed attention signals optimism or pessimism, producing downstream consequences for affective forecasts and risk-taking. Finally, Study 4 reveals that many people endorse asymmetric causal models, viewing optimism as a cause of risk-taking, but risk-taking as a cause of attention. Together, these findings show that forecasts of risk preferences depend critically on people's intuitive theories about how cognition shapes affect and how affective utility is generated over time. By integrating affective forecasting, attention, and decision-making under uncertainty, this work highlights the role of metacognitive beliefs in shaping economic preferences.

title: Successful modal reasoning depends on WHAT went WHERE
abstract: Modal reasoning requires quantifying over possibilities (e.g., categorizing events as necessary, possible, and impossible). This suite of abilities matures during the preschool years, but toddlers perform better in some modal reasoning tasks than others. We propose that these mixed findings reflect a cognitive distinction: toddlers perform worse when reasoning about ambiguous locations of objects (WHERE) than when reasoning about ambiguous kinds of objects (WHAT). In Experiments 1 and 2, we directly compared these forms of ambiguity using matched tasks. Consistent with the hypothesis, toddlers performed substantially better when reasoning about ambiguous kinds than ambiguous locations. Experiment 3 revealed a similar asymmetry in language comprehension, with preschool children showing better comprehension of modal terms such as "can" and "have to" in a What-based task than in a Where-based task. Thus, modal reasoning emerges earlier than previously suggested, and diversity in results reflects differences in how kind and location information are represented and processed.

title: Metacognitive monitoring in Kenyan, Chinese, and U.S. children
abstract: Theories of cognitive development propose that cultural values shape metacognitive skills. However, cross-cultural research on metacognition remains limited and often relies on verbal assessments that may lack validity across cultural contexts. The present study examined metacognitive monitoring in Kenyan, Chinese, and U.S. children (N = 95; 6-10-year-olds; 46% female) using a non-verbal problem-solving task in which children assembled objects according to a model. Across all three cultural contexts, children exhibited various monitoring behaviors (e.g., checking the model), and the frequency of these behaviors increased with age. Cross-cultural differences emerged in the specific monitoring strategies children used: Chinese children engaged in more thorough monitoring than Kenyan and U.S. children. These findings highlight both culturally-recurrent and culturally-variable patterns in children's metacognitive monitoring.

title: Noncausal joint-action scenes facilitate Mandarin-speaking preschoolers' interpretation of intransitive verbs with conjoined subjects
abstract: Children learn novel verb meanings by integrating sentence-level cues with information from the surrounding event. Although sentence frames provide information about verb transitivity, success with intransitive frames varies across languages and tasks. In Mandarin, preschoolers have been reported to struggle with conjoined-subject intransitive sentences, raising the question of whether this difficulty reflects a limitation in syntactic bootstrapping or partly stems from how children construe the comparison scenes. In a forced-choice pointing task, Mandarin-speaking 3-, 4-, and 5-year-olds heard transitive or conjoined-subject intransitive sentences containing novel verbs and chose between a causal scene and a noncausal scene. Critically, the noncausal scene was either a parallel-action scene or a joint-action scene. In the joint-action scene, the two participants acted together in physical contact but without a causal asymmetry. Children at all ages reliably matched transitive sentences to causal scenes. For intransitives, 3-year-olds performed at chance in both scene conditions, 4-year-olds succeeded only with joint-action scenes, and 5-year-olds succeeded in both. Thus, performance with intransitives improved with age and was facilitated when the noncausal alternative was easier to construe as a single noncausal event. These findings suggest that previously reported failures with Mandarin conjoined-subject intransitives cannot be attributed solely to insensitivity to argument structure, but also depend on how candidate events are visually and conceptually represented. More broadly, the results are consistent with a multiple-factor view of verb learning, in which syntactic cues interact with semantic, and event-based information.

title: Self-report measures of mindfulness for children: convergent validity, predictive validity, and impacts of social desirability bias
abstract: Mindfulness-based interventions have shown promise in supporting psychological well-being in children. However, mindfulness is commonly measured using self-report questionnaires, a method that might be problematic due to its reliance on children's accurate self-perceptions of their own mindfulness and the potential influence of social desirability bias. In the current study, we examined the convergent validity, the predictive validity, and the influence of social desirability bias on three mindfulness self-report measures for children ages 9-13  years (N = 109). Results showed that children's self-reported mindfulness demonstrated good convergent validity and predictive validity, as higher levels of self-reported mindfulness were positively associated with higher levels of parent-reported executive functioning. Self-reported mindfulness also covaried with social desirability bias. However, controlling for this bias did not substantively affect the convergent validity nor the predictive validity of self-reported mindfulness. These findings suggest that children's self-reported mindfulness also captures social desirability bias, but this bias may not affect conclusions about mindfulness when assessed as a latent factor across multiple measures. Future work measuring children's mindfulness with self-reports should account for social desirability bias when possible, as well as explore objective methods of assessing mindfulness in children.

title: [Toward independent nursing consultations in child and adolescent psychiatry]
abstract: Faced with a shortage of child psychiatrists and an increase in demand for care, mental health organizations must reinvent themselves. The implementation of a collaborative protocol in child psychiatry - allowing trained nurses to conduct independent consultations, including prescription renewals - represents an innovative solution. This approach improves access to care and its quality by ensuring appropriate, enhanced, and personalized follow-up for each patient.

title: A "Question of Competency": Child Guidance, Pediatrics, and the Origins of Child Psychiatry in America
abstract: During the 1920s and early 1930s, American psychiatrists and other experts in the field of child guidance engaged in debate about which discipline had professional competency over children's mental health. Psychiatrists contested psychologists' claims to expertise, arguing that children's behavioral disturbances were medical problems of an emotional nature. As the child guidance movement gained steam through the proliferation of child guidance clinics, pediatricians protested their exclusion from it. Some hospital-based psychiatrists echoed their claim that the adoption of psychoanalysis at child guidance clinics without a hospital connection isolated psychiatry from scientific medicine. The authors examine the early work of some of these psychiatrists, who sought to collaborate with pediatricians in a hospital framework. They developed a medical model for the nascent discipline of child psychiatry, alternative to the model practiced at child guidance clinics. Eschewing psychoanalytic interpretations, they emphasized the interaction between physical and mental health problems from early childhood.

title: Instruments and scales for assessment, screening, and psychoeducational diagnosis of children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder: a scoping review
abstract:
ABSTRACT Objective: To investigate instruments and scales for psychoeducational assessment, screening, and diagnosis of children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder. Data source: This review followed the methodological procedures recommended by the Joanna Briggs Institute and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses - Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Its research question was, “What are the main instruments and scales for psychoeducational assessment, screening, and diagnosis of children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder in school?”. Data synthesis: The study included 16 articles that investigated instruments for psychoeducational assessment, screening, and diagnosis of children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder. The instruments found were the Psychoeducational Profile - Revised (PEP-R), Psychoeducational Profile 3 (PEP-3), and the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC-IV). This indicates a scarcity of instruments and scales for the psychoeducational assessment, screening, and diagnosis of children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder. Conclusions: The most used instruments to assess the psychoeducational profile of schoolchildren with autism spectrum disorder include the Revised Psychoeducational Profile (PEP-R) and the Psychoeducational Profile, 3 rd Edition (PEP-3), according to scientific literature. There is a scarcity of instruments and scales for the psychoeducational assessment, screening, and diagnosis of children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder, suggesting the need for further research on the subject.

INTRODUCTION Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder with a neurobiological basis, characterized by persistent impairments in communication and social interaction, associated with restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior. 1 Initial signs can be observed between 12 and 24 months of a child’s life, manifesting as significant developmental delays or regression of previously acquired skills. 2 The etiology of ASD is multifactorial and, since it does not present biological markers, the diagnosis is predominantly clinical, based on systematic observation and information provided by caregivers. It is also recommended that standardized instruments be used to qualify the diagnosis. 3 , 4 , 5 The assessment of a child with ASD is not limited to diagnostic conclusions, but is essential for defining their psychoeducational profile and guiding individualized therapeutic and educational interventions and strategies. 1 , 3 The assessment of the student’s psychoeducational profile aims to understand their learning, cognition, motor skills, behavior, and social relationships at school and in the ecological environment, integrating educational and psychological knowledge to obtain a complete overview of child development and offer the necessary references to assist in the development of an inclusive educational curriculum. 3 According to the literature, instruments such as the Psychoeducational Profile - Revised (PEP-R) and the Psychoeducational Profile - 3 (PEP-3) prioritize the measurement of development in multiple domains, including expressive and receptive communication, cognition, motor skills, social interaction, and characteristic motor and verbal behavior, identifying strengths and weaknesses to guide educational interventions. 6 , 7 Historically, children with ASD have sometimes been treated as “untestable” due to low adherence to testing situations, bonding difficulties, and expressive and receptive communication limitations, which hinder the applicability of conventional instruments. 7 Thus, the PEP-R and later the PEP-3 were conceived as benchmarks for understanding the repertoire of skills and needs of children with ASD, supporting the definition of the level of support and the development of an individualized educational and clinical plan, as well as the possibility of short, medium, and long-term follow-up. 7 The timely and thorough identification of ASD is a structural basis for implementing interventions capable of enhancing development and improving the quality of life of children and adolescents. However, the psychoeducational assessment of this population requires duly validated instruments and scales, sensitive to the specificities of the disorder and able to reliably screen, support diagnosis, and monitor outcomes with adequate adaptation to different cultural and educational contexts. Nevertheless, the literature still has a limited collection of validated measures for psychoeducational screening, diagnosis, and characterization, especially in specific settings. This weakens the standardization and reliability of practices and limits the conduct of interventions rigorously anchored in scientific evidence. This scoping review aimed to identify instruments and scales for screening, assessment, and psychoeducational diagnosis of children and adolescents with ASD at school and to provide an updated overview to support education and health professionals in choosing appropriate instruments, contributing to the development of contextualized and effective practices. METHOD This scoping review followed the guidelines of the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and presented its results according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses - Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). 8 The study had the following phases: developing the research question; identifying relevant studies; selecting studies; investigating data; and grouping, summarizing, and presenting the results. 9 The review used the Population, Concept, and Context (PCC) strategy 10 to include publications that covered topics related to: a) the population: people with ASD aged 5 to 12 years; b) the concept: psychoeducational profile; c) context: schools, thus answering the research question: “What are the main instruments and scales for psychoeducational assessment, screening, and diagnosis of children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder in school?” The review considered publications that met the PCC inclusion criteria, in any language, from the last 13 years. The search was limited to the last 13 years because this period coincides with the publication of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition - DSM-5 (2013), which introduced relevant changes in ASD criteria and classification, influencing the characterization of samples and the comparability between studies, and ensuring greater diagnostic consistency and up-to-date findings. Articles were searched on the electronic databases of Latin American and Caribbean Health Sciences Literature (LILACS); Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online (MEDLINE, USA), via the United States National Library of Medicine (PubMed); Cochrane, via the Brazilian Coordination for the Improvement of Higher Education Personnel (CAPES) Portal; Scopus, via CAPES Portal; Embase, via CAPES Portal; and Web of Science, via CAPES Portal, from April to June 2024. The search terms, selected from the Health Sciences Descriptors (DeCS) and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH), were autism spectrum disorder, psychoeducational diagnosis. The study also used free terms: synonyms, related terms, orthographic variations, abbreviations, acronyms, and keywords indispensable to the research: diagnóstico psicoeducacional, psychoeducational diagnosis, psychoeducational assessment, educational psychology, educational assessment. The consulted databases and their respective equations are described in Table 1 . MEDLINE data were excluded from the Virtual Health Library (VHL) of the Ministry of Health, as they were analyzed via PubMed. Duplicates were excluded as the search was finalized within each database. The review selected articles from the last 13 years, encompassing children aged 5 to 12 years, and excluded those that did not answer the research question, as well as review articles, doctoral theses, master’s theses, essays, conference proceedings, case studies, and expert opinion articles ( Figure 1 ). Two researchers identified and screened the articles by reading the titles and abstracts independently. The reference generator (Rayyan QCRI ® ) was used to organize research results, remove duplicates, and help with selection. Then, the researchers compared their analyzed data; in case of disagreement or incompatibility, they reanalyzed them until they reached a common result. Next, an evaluator read the selected eligible articles in full and excluded those that did not meet the article selection criteria. The following article data were extracted to an Excel ® spreadsheet: authors and year, design and country, sample (subjects, sex, age, and total sample size), diagnosis, instruments, and main results. RESULTS The initial database search resulted in 325 articles. After excluding duplicates, reading titles and abstracts, and applying exclusion criteria, 19 articles remained for full-text reading. Then, 11 articles were excluded because they did not meet the inclusion criteria. Eight articles remained and were included in the review after qualitative synthesis. Subsequently, other articles on psychoeducational profile and autism were manually searched on Google Scholar with the descriptors: psychoeducational profile and autism spectrum disorder, considering articles from the last 13 years, in any language. Hence, another eight articles were selected, read in full, and included in the study, and a total of 16 articles were selected ( Figure 1 , Table 2 ). Four of the studies selected for this scoping review were published in Brazil, five in China, and one each in the United States, Australia, Italy, France, Tunisia, Ukraine, and Portugal. Nine of the 16 articles selected for analysis were cross-sectional observational studies, three were case-control studies, two were randomized clinical trials, one was a retrospective observational study, and one was a longitudinal study. The articles were published between 2013 and 2024. China and Brazil had the highest number of publications on the psychoeducational assessment of children with ASD. The most frequently cited instruments for psychoeducational assessment were the PEP-R and PEP-3; one article cited the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC-IV). Thus, among the 16 selected articles, the identified assessment instruments were the PEP-R, PEP-3, and WISC-IV. Research describes PEP-R as an instrument that measures the developmental age of children with ASD or related communication disorders. 7 This instrument was organized into two scales: one that observes development and the other related to behavior, based on the CARS scale 7 and Creak’s criteria. 7 In Brazil, the PEP-R began to be used in 1992 for clinical purposes in its original, translated form. PEP-3, which replaced PEP-R, assesses schoolchildren’s psychoeducational profile. It identifies irregular and idiosyncratic learning patterns through a developmental impairment profile. 7 , 8 The test has ten subtests, six focused on developmental skills and four on maladaptive behaviors and is indicated for children aged two to 12 years. PEP-3 data provide information on developmental skill levels and diagnosis in children and adolescents and help determine the level of support for ASD (the latter identified in children up to seven years old). 7 The skills investigated include verbal and preverbal cognition, expressive language, receptive language, fine and gross motor skills, visuomotor imitation, expression of affectivity, social reciprocity, motor and verbal characteristics, behavioral problems, personal care, and adaptive behavior. Research also used the WISC-IV, albeit less frequently. It is a clinical instrument for assessing intelligence and problem-solving processes in children aged six to 16 years and 11 months, applied individually and organized into four indices: verbal comprehension, perceptual organization, working memory, and processing speed. 11 , 12 The PEP-R and PEP-3 can be applied by specialized professionals, including educators, occupational therapists, speech-language-hearing pathologists, and psychologists, provided they are trained in their use and interpretation. The WISC-IV, however, is meant to be used only by psychologists in clinical settings. Among the studies that cited PEP-R and/or PEP-3, five were published in China, four in Brazil, and one each in France, Tunisia, Ukraine, Portugal, and Australia. Two bilingual Brazilian translators adapted the PEP-R for Brazil, changing some items for cultural adaptation. After translation, reliability values for developmental and behavioral dimensions ranged from 0.80 to 0.97. 7 The articles that cited the PEP-R reported using it for assessing verbal and nonverbal behavior in children with ASD, 11 testing academic and social skills and activities of daily living, 12 and verifying child development in schoolchildren stimulated by caregivers in the family context. 13 Studies also reported using it to monitor developmental progress over two years, with assessments at the beginning and end of the period, finding associations between improvement in test domains and in daily functioning. 19 , 27 Other studies reported using it to assess motor development, speech, and cognition and to identify delays in general motor skills in individuals with ASD. 21 Studies that used the PEP-3 were found mainly in China - five of the six articles that cited it were Chinese. These studies described PEP-3 application for psychoeducational profiling, treatment support, and the formulation of long-term rehabilitation plans. 14 , 17 , 28 A study on the psychometric properties of a simplified Chinese version (sCPEP-3) was also described, reporting internal consistency, test-retest reliability, interrater reliability, convergent validity, construct validity, and factorial validity. 17 , 22 , 23 Furthermore, it was mentioned that the PEP-3 includes a caregiver report, which is absent in the PEP-R. 16 DISCUSSION The assessment of children and adolescents with ASD is a complex process that must be multidisciplinary, with clinical observation, interviews with primary caregivers, and standardized instruments, such as tests and scales. Because it is multidisciplinary, it requires a partnership between education and health professionals, allowing for a detailed analysis of the child. There was a greater concentration of international studies on the subject, with China and Brazil standing out in terms of the volume of publications. This pattern suggests a geographical asymmetry in scientific production and may reflect differences in the availability of instruments, the tradition of using the TEACCH/PEP model, and investment in psychoeducational assessment.
