title: Automated screening of autism via a pretrained vision-language model in naturalistic caregiver-child interactions
abstract:
Early autism screening is essential for timely intervention but remains constrained by specialist dependence, costly protocols, and limited accessibility. We present Autism-CLIP, a vision-language model that automates screening from 3-min naturalistic caregiver-child interaction videos recorded in toddlers aged 15–24 months. By integrating contrastive learning, large language model–generated supervision, domain-specific architecture, and hybrid training, Autism-CLIP aligns visual behavioral cues with autism-related assessment outcomes, enabling annotation-free inference. In multicenter evaluation, Autism-CLIP achieved an AUC of 0.903 in the internal cohort ( n = 103) and 0.873 in the external cohort ( n = 102), outperforming conventional machine learning methods. Attention mapping highlighted clinically relevant markers, including gaze aversion and limited social reciprocity. Requiring only smartphone-captured videos without manual coding or controlled settings, Autism-CLIP offers a scalable, low-cost approach to broaden access to early autism screening and support prioritization of clinical resources.

Here, the authors develop Autism-CLIP, a vision–language model for automated early autism screening using 3-min home videos of toddlers aged 15–24 months.

Introduction Autism, affecting 1 in 31 individuals in the United States 1 , and with a pooled prevalence of 0.70% among 6–12-year-old children in China, is characterized by social communication challenges and restricted/repetitive behaviors that impair daily functioning 2 . Early screening of autism is critical: neurodevelopmental trajectories in the first two years of life are marked by heightened neural plasticity 3 , 4 , offering a pivotal window for interventions that can substantially improve long-term outcomes 5 , 6 . During this period, subtle behavioral markers of autism—such as reduced joint attention, diminished eye contact, and delayed responsiveness to social cues—often emerge 7 , 8 . Yet, a significant proportion of children with autism remain undiagnosed before the age of 2, with only 49% having received their first evaluation by age 3 1 , underscoring systemic barriers in current screening paradigms. Conventional autism screening relies on clinician-administered tools like the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) 9 , 10 , which demand specialized training, costly resources, and controlled clinical environments. While machine learning (ML) has advanced automated analysis of structured assessments (e.g., shorten ADOS assessment 11 and pose estimation in ADOS videos 12 ), these methods remain tethered to standardized settings and clinician oversight, limiting scalability in low-resource communities. Recent innovations in mobile health platforms, such as gamified apps capturing gaze patterns or vocal prosody 13 – 15 , demonstrate improved ecological validity but retain operational complexity. For instance, tools requiring specialized-sensor setups, or user training and systematic implementation by primary providers, to balance accuracy with real-world feasibility 16 , 17 . Critically, none address the urgent need for scalable, caregiver-friendly screening in children under 2 years—a gap perpetuating diagnostic delays. Naturalistic approaches, which analyze unstructured caregiver-child interactions in familiar environments, offer a promising alternative. Prior work using the Systematic Observation of Red Flags (SORF) has shown that manual coding of home or brief parent-child interaction videos can distinguish autistic from non-autistic toddlers, including in 10-min interaction samples from children aged 15–24 months 18 , 19 . However, these approaches still depend on trained human coders and manual behavioral scoring, which limits scalability. Early machine learning models, trained on handcrafted behavioral features (e.g., eye contact, social smiles 20 , 21 ), still required manual labeling by raters. A clinically viable solution must therefore overcome four barriers: (1) compatibility with ubiquitous mobile devices, (2) usability without prior training, (3) elimination of manual annotation, and (4) robust performance in children under 2 years. Advances in computer vision provide a pathway. While traditional convolutional/recurrent neural networks (CNNs/RNNs) excel at temporal video analysis, vision-language models (VLMs) like CLIP 22 —pretrained on vast image-text pairs—enable zero-shot classification by aligning visual features with semantic concepts. However, autism screening poses unique challenges: complex semantic information, prolonged video durations, and small domain dataset sizes demand domain-specific adaptation of these frameworks. In this study, we present Autism-CLIP, a pretrained VLM fine-tuned on 3-min naturalistic videos of toddlers (15–24 months) interacting with caregivers (Fig. 1 ). By integrating diagnoses and clinical assessment scores (e.g., ADOS-T) as supervisory signals using Large Language Model (LLM) and CLIP architectures, designing domain-specific predictive networks, and employing hybrid supervision strategies, Autism-CLIP bridges the gap between generic action recognition and autism-specific phenotypic analysis, automating screening of diagnostically salient behaviors (e.g. gaze aversion) without manual coding. In multicenter validation (internal n = 103; external n = 102), Autism-CLIP achieved an AUC of 0.873 (95% CI: 0.796–0.937) and sensitivity of 0.857, outperforming state-of-the-art ML models. Attention mapping further localized autism-related behaviors (e.g., atypical social engagement), enhancing interpretability for clinical translation. This work advances the field by (1) demonstrating the first pretrained VLM adapted for autism screening in naturalistic settings, (2) validating performance in children under 2 years, i.e., a cohort underrepresented in prior ML studies, and (3) eliminating dependencies on structured tasks or manual annotation. By enabling analysis of brief, smartphone-captured videos, Autism-CLIP democratizes access to early screening, aligning with global priorities for equitable neurodevelopmental care (Supplementary Table 1 ), offering a unique approach compared to existing methods. Results Participants and demographics The study was conducted across three branches of the Third Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University. The participants include an internal training dataset and an external validation dataset. Participants of internal dataset were recruited from children attending outpatient clinics specializing in developmental disorders and child healthcare at the Child Development and Behavioral Center of the Third Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University (Tianhe District Hospital and Lingnan Hospital), between September 2021 and December 2023. Out of 117 toddlers, 103 were enrolled in the study (Table 1 and Supplementary Table 2 ). Fourteen toddlers (6 with autism, 4 with developmental delays, and 4 neurotypical) were excluded due to poor video quality, video containing more than one child or more than one caregiver, non-cooperation during assessments, or failure to complete assessments within the follow-up time window (Supplementary Fig. 1 ). Of the 103 toddlers in the internal cohort, 46 overlapped with participants reported in our previous SORF-based manual-coding study 19 . These participants were drawn from the Longitudinal Chinese Autism Study of Early Development (LCAS-ED), a cohort study focusing on infants at high familial or elevated likelihood of autism. Participants of external dataset were recruited from children visiting outpatient clinics specializing in developmental disorders and child healthcare at the Zhaoqing Hospital of the Third Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University between March 2024 and March 2025. The external validation cohort was newly recruited for the present study and all 102 toddlers were enrolled in the study (Table 2 , Supplementary Fig. 1 ). Model output and classification framework The machine learning architecture generates continuous autism likelihood scores ranging from 0 to 1, quantifying the algorithmic confidence in autism classification. This probabilistic output undergoes threshold-dependent dichotomization using an empirically derived cutoff of 0.5 for clinical decision-making. Operationalized through this binary classification schema: Scores >0.5 classify individuals into the autism category; Scores ≤ 0.5 assign participants to the nonautism control group, which encompasses both neurotypical populations and those with developmental delays unrelated to autism. This operational framework strategically preserves methodological flexibility by maintaining tunable sensitivity parameters for different implementation phases. The continuous scoring system enables dynamic threshold adjustment during subsequent clinical validation studies or real-world deployments, accommodating evolving diagnostic criteria while preserving inherent measurement fidelity. Model performance We trained and evaluated the proposed Autism-CLIP model using 3-min videos, clinical assessments and diagnostic results collected from Chinese children cohorts. The proposed Autism-CLIP achieves high accuracy in classifying autistic and nonautistic (development delay and neurotypical combined) groups with an AUC of 0.903, sensitivity of 0.866, and specificity of 0.806 (Fig. 2a ). It also demonstrated robust results in classifying autistic and development delay groups, achieving an AUC of 0.890, and classifies autistic and neurotypical groups with an AUC of 0.912. Subgroup analysis When stratified by gender, age, and the caregiver-child relationship in the video, the Autism-CLIP model consistently demonstrates strong performance in classifying autistic versus nonautistic groups. With all AUC values exceeding 0.85 (Table 3 ), the model’s classification ability remains robust across various demographic and caregiver-related factors. These results indicate that the effectiveness of our Autism-CLIP model is not significantly impacted by these stratifying variables. Performance results based on the Youden Index are presented in Supplementary Tables 3 and 4 . External validation 102 children were recruited as external cohort (Table 2 and Supplementary Table 5 ). Each child underwent a 3-min video recording, which was uploaded to a private server for analysis. These videos were independently analyzed by the Autism-CLIP model, which achieved an AUC of 0.873 for distinguishing autistic from nonautistic (Fig. 2b , Tables 4 and 5 ). Notably, the model achieved superior performance in differentiating autistic from neurotypical groups, showing an AUC of 0.886 and a sensitivity of 0.857. These findings collectively demonstrate that Autism-CLIP is a promising tool for accurate autism identification, even when using brief video recordings. The external dataset evaluations utilized the model checkpoint from the fold with the highest AUC during the 10-fold validation on the internal dataset. Performance results based on the Youden Index are presented in Supplementary Table 6 and Supplementary Table 4 . Interpretability analysis Analysis of the contribution weights from video frames reveals distinct behavioral patterns that help explain the likelihood score for each child. Specific pixel blocks within the video frames are found to either positively or negatively influence the output likelihood score, providing insights into the model’s diagnostic decisions (Supplementary Fig. 3 ). This analysis serves two main purposes: (1) offering potential explanations for the Autism-CLIP model’s decision-making process, and (2) highlighting unique behavioral patterns associated with autism or typical neurodevelopment. In the internal data analysis, the Autism-CLIP model primarily focuses on the faces (including eyes and other facial features) of both children and caregivers, as well as the caregivers’ upper limbs (Fig. 2c , d ). This pattern may suggests that the model places significant emphasis on eye contact, facial orientation, facial expressions, and other facial features, as well as the interactions between the child and caregiver—key factors in identifying autism-related behavioral patterns. Comparison with state-of-the-art models We evaluate our approach against state-of-the-art action recognition frameworks, including VideoSwin 23 , UniFormer v2 24 , MViT v2 25 , and X-CLIP 26 . All models were pretrained on Kinetics-600 27 and fine-tuned on our internal dataset, with performance further assessed on both internal and external dataset to examine capabilities. For natural-setting video classification (Table 6 ), traditional vision-based architectures VideoSwin, MViT v2, and UniFormer v2 exhibited AUC values below 0.8. In contrast, X-CLIP achieved a substantial improvement with an AUC of 0.89 in internal dataset, demonstrating the advantage of CLIP’s multimodal architecture over vision-only models in this task. This performance gap arises from the autism screening context, which demands robust generalization to handle diverse real-world scenarios. However, X-CLIP’s performance significantly declined on external validation data, suggesting limitations in its cross-domain adaptability. The performance results using 0.5 as the threshold are shown in Supplementary Table 7 . Our proposed Autism-CLIP, initialized with CLIP ViT-L/14, outperformed all baselines with an AUC of 0.90 in internal dataset while maintaining relative stability in external dataset. This improvement stems from four factors: (1) The foundation in CLIP’s pretrained vision-language framework provides rich semantic representations; (2) Hybrid supervision integrates both diagnostic labels and additional information derived from standardized assessment scales; (3) Domain-specific architecture design enhances the model’s ability to discern subtle behavioral cues critical for autism screening. (4) LLM reduces the difficulty of model learning by refining complex textual information. The results highlight that Autism-CLIP’s hybrid learning paradigm better addresses the challenges of limited labeled data and domain shift compared to purely vision-based methods or CLIP derivatives using single-modality supervision. Ablation study Table 7 summarizes the ablation study results. The full Autism-CLIP architecture (Row 1) achieves the highest performance metrics. Removing the LLM module (Row 2) forces the model to generate descriptive text by directly concatenating sentences from Supplementary Tables 8 and 9 , producing excessively verbose outputs that disrupt text encoder focus. This simplification reduces AUC to 0.80 and sensitivity to 0.77, demonstrating the LLM’s significant role in refining label semantics while maintaining information density. The architecture without the text encoder (Row 3) exhibits comparable performance degradation (AUC 0.83), indicating the text encoder’s essential function in supplying autism-specific contextua

title: Online gaming for autistic youth: Exploring the impact on participation from the perspectives of autistic adolescents and their caregivers
abstract:
Abstract Introduction The rise in the number of adolescents diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder has highlighted the need for strength‐based approaches to support them. The accessibility of online gaming has made it a popular avenue for autistic adolescents to socialise and connect with others while enhancing skill development. This study aimed to explore online gaming from the perspectives of autistic adolescents and their caregivers, including the impact gaming may have on daily participation and functioning. Methods This study employed a mixed methods research design. Both autistic adolescents and their caregivers completed online surveys comprising a combination of Likert‐scale and open‐ended questions. The survey responses were descriptively and thematically analysed. Consumer and Community Involvement Survey questions were reviewed by volunteer staff (including autistic staff members) of a local autistic community coding club to ensure readability and accessibility of the survey. Results In total, 45 participants (23 caregivers and 22 autistic adolescents) responded to the survey. Themes relating to online gaming were identified, including social communication, emotion regulation, and skill development while also highlighting caregiver concerns of online safety and excessive screen use. Most autistic adolescents reported feeling happy when playing online games and most caregivers agreed online gaming supported their child to build better relationships with others. Over half of autistic adolescents agreed that online gaming helped them feel more confident in social situations with others. Conclusion Allied health professionals, including occupational therapists, may utilise online gaming, incorporating strength‐based learning and skill development, when working alongside autistic adolescents and their caregivers to facilitate social participation and promote online safety.

PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY Online gaming is becoming more common, giving autistic young people a way to make friends and learn new skills. This study explored how online gaming affects autistic teenagers, from both their own perspective and their caregivers'. The researchers collected information through online surveys from 22 autistic adolescents and 23 caregivers. The study found that online gaming helped many autistic teenagers feel happier, more confident, and better at talking to others. Many caregivers noticed that gaming helped their child build relationships. However, some caregivers were worried about online safety and too much screen time. Occupational therapists could use online gaming to help autistic youths develop social skills.

Key Points for Occupational Therapy Online gaming utilises the unique preferences and interests of autistic adolescents which promotes strength‐based skill development. Autistic adolescents' development of social communication, fine motor, and problem‐solving skills can be supported by online gaming. Concerns of online safety, emotional regulation, and excessive screen use should be considered by allied health professionals. 1 INTRODUCTION Autism is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition characterised by differences in reciprocal social communication, interaction and response to sensory input, and the presence of restricted or repetitive behaviours, interests, and activities (American Psychiatric Association, 2022 ; Hodges et al., 2020 ). It is estimated that 1 in 100 children are diagnosed with autism globally (Zeidan et al., 2022 ). Expanding awareness and understanding of autism has contributed to an increase in the rate of diagnosis, emphasising the need for deeper exploration into alternative mediums to provide strength‐based support to autistic adolescents (American Psychiatric Association, 2022 ; Hodges et al., 2020 ). Living in a predominately neurotypical society, there is increased pressure for autistic individuals to adapt their communication skills to participate in society (Mitchell et al., 2021 ). Adolescents may experience increased social pressure in different social contexts, where there is often a lack of understanding in communication between neurotypical and autistic individuals (Chen et al., 2015 ; Deckers et al., 2014 ). Stigmatisation and negative reception of behaviours misinterpreted by neurotypical peers may contribute to higher levels of social anxiety and reduced social participation of autistic adolescents (Briot et al., 2020 ). Expression of autistic characteristics has traditionally been discouraged and autistic adolescents may consequently ‘mask’ their true selves, negatively impacting their mental wellbeing (Cage & Troxell‐Whitman, 2019 ; Hull et al., 2017 ). In comparison with their neurotypical peers, autistic individuals may experience higher incidences of anxiety, depression, and suicidality, attributing to discrimination, social isolation, and reduced likelihood of receiving appropriate health care and support services (Croen et al., 2015 ; Shattuck et al., 2011 ). Strength‐based approaches focus on harnessing an individual's strengths and interests to build skills and positive experiences, diverging from a deficit‐focussed mindset (Lee et al., 2024 ). They challenge traditional notions of autistic traits by re‐evaluating them as potential strengths. Embedded in the social model of disability, a strength‐based approach takes a holistic view, emphasising that societal structures, not individual abilities, create barriers (Lee et al., 2020 ). Interventions can be adapted to suit autistic adolescents by leveraging their unique strengths and interests, including circumscribed interests, to increase engagement and participation (Dunn, 2017 ). The positive outcomes of this approach are credited to creating safe social environments and keeping activities interest‐based (Jones et al., 2021 ). Utilising the interests of autistic adolescents promotes a sense of accomplishment and builds confidence, empowering them to engage in different activities or challenges (Koegel et al., 2012 ). One example of strength‐based interventions is online gaming. Video games, online gaming, and technology interventions have become increasingly popular through the rise of the internet and more accessible technologies in clinical, educational, and community settings (Fam, 2018 ; Kaplan et al., 2022 ; Odom et al., 2015 ). Online games can provide social skills training, cognitive and executive function training, treatment of mental health conditions, and an alternative mode of presenting educational material to adolescents with processing difficulties (Beaumont et al., 2019 ; Bocci et al., 2023 ; Crouch et al., 2023 ; Rashedi et al., 2022 ; Zayeni et al., 2020 ). Studies show adolescents are attracted to video and online games as they are motivationally fun, social, immersive, and provide a sense of achievement (Snodgrass et al., 2017 ). However, some autistic adolescents use online games to escape from dysphoric moods and problematic relationships within the real world (Snodgrass et al., 2017 ). This can lead to negative repercussions within their daily life if not adequately addressed, including behavioural and lifestyle changes (Granic et al., 2014 ; Kaplan et al., 2022 ). Traditionally, research into online gaming interventions focussed exclusively on the perspectives of caregivers or autistic adolescents (Mazurek et al., 2012 ; Rashedi et al., 2022 ; Willis et al., 2022 ). However, there is frequently a discrepancy between these two views, with many caregivers voicing concerns about screen time and its effects on their children (Fam, 2018 ; Kaplan et al., 2022 ; Rashedi et al., 2022 ; Snodgrass et al., 2017 ). This contrasts with the experiences of autistic adolescents, who describe online games more positively, attributing these to outcomes such as self‐confidence, conversation skills, emotion recognition, and conflict resolution (Afsharnejad et al., 2022 ; Einfeld et al., 2018 ; Płatos et al., 2023 ; Snodgrass et al., 2017 ). There are limited studies exploring the perspectives of both populations and the impact online gaming may have on participation and functioning in daily activities. This study aims to bridge this gap in the literature by exploring both autistic adolescents' and caregivers' viewpoints of online gaming relating to everyday participation and functioning. Exploring the lived experiences of both autistic adolescents and their caregivers within the community can add to the growing body of research regarding the benefits and challenges of online gaming and provide recommendations to allied health professionals utilising and developing online gaming interventions. 2 METHODS 2.1 Study design A mixed methods research design was used, with both qualitative and quantitative results converged in the discussion (Hunter & Brewer, 2015 ). Surveys with a variety of questions, including Likert scales and open‐ended questions, were used to collect data, providing complimentary perspectives on the content while also offering depth and breadth of the topic. Likert scales were used in the adolescent and caregiver surveys to encourage the selection of responses that best represented how they felt about online gaming, particularly its impact on social skills. Data were collected from autistic adolescents and their caregivers using online surveys hosted on Qualtrics ( 2024 ). Data were analysed using a thematic analysis approach to uncover themes of similar perspectives or shared meanings from the participants (Armstrong et al., 2021 ). 2.2 Participants Participants were required to meet the following criteria: (1) adolescents aged 10 to 18 years, (2) with a primary diagnosis of autism, or (3) the primary caregiver of an autistic adolescent. A total of 45 participants (22 autistic adolescents; 23 caregivers) completed the surveys. Participants were recruited from a strength‐based coding club that promotes social interaction among autistic adolescents in Western Australia and from relevant autistic Facebook groups and communities. Autistic adolescents were offered a $10 online voucher as a token of appreciation for their time spent completing the survey. 2.3 Data collection This study was approved by Curtin Human Research Ethics Committee (HRE2017‐0147‐99). All participants were provided with an information sheet detailing their potential involvement in the research and offered the opportunity to ask any questions prior to giving their informed consent to participate. Caregivers filled out and signed an external assent form if their adolescent did not complete the survey with them present. Questions relating to the research topic were prepared and curated with a team of autism researchers, and data were collected using online survey platform, Qualtrics (Briot et al., 2020 ; Płatos et al., 2023 ; Qualtrics, 2024 ). Coproduction design ensured survey questions prompted in‐depth exploration of relevant aspects of online gaming (Armstrong et al., 2021 ). Questions were refined with the parent of an autistic child before being trialled with coding club facilitators (including autistic young adults) to ensure the suitability and engagement of the surveys for autistic adolescents. Researchers handed out flyers with a QR code to caregivers attending the coding groups or dropping their adolescents off. The information flyer with QR codes and hyperlinks to the surveys was posted to Facebook and relevant Facebook groups by the research team. Individuals interested in participating in the study completed the Qualtrics survey (Qualtrics, 2024 ) via the QR code on the flyers or hyperlinks. 2.4 Data analysis Demographic data, multiple‐choice responses, and Likert scales were exported from Qualtrics to Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Office 365, 2021a ) and summarised using descriptive statistics. Researchers downloaded open‐text data to Microsoft Word (Microsoft Office 365, 2021c ) for cleaning, coding, and analysis. The six‐step thematic analysis involved (1) researchers familiarising themselves with the data, (2) generating codes, and (3) identifying themes, providing a rich description of each theme; (4) remaining members of the team subsequently reviewed the codes, and (5) after several meetings with the whole team, (6) the findings were then written up (Braun & Clarke, 2006 ). 2.5 Rigour To address credibility, research participants were emailed the recommendations the research team compiled based on the findings which constituted member checking (Varpio et al., 2017 ). The research team documented the research process and data with an audit trail stored throughout, de‐identified data, including removing personal names, stored this data in a protected drive, and uploaded it via Microsoft Teams (Microsoft Office 365, 2021b ). To ensure rigour and trustworthiness, the research team followed these criteria: credibility (member checking), transferability (thick description), dependability (audit trail), and confirmability (research supervisors were involved in confirming results) (Nowell et al., 2017 ). 2.6 Positionality statement M.H.‐E., S.G., and B.M. are registered occupational therapists and active members of an autism research group exploring strength‐based approaches among other areas of research of importance to the autism community. T.I., I.F., Z.S. and J.L. were final‐year occupational therapy students at the time of the study who had received approximately 18 months of research training and were supervised by senior researchers within the autism research group. 3 RESULTS 3.1 Participant demographics and perspectives on online gaming A total of 23 caregivers and 22 autistic adolescents completed the online survey. Caregivers were mostly female (73.9%) with the majority aged between 35 and 54 years (87%). Their children were mostly male (90.9%) and ranged in age from 10 to 15 years with most being 12 (26.1%) or 13 (30.4%) years old. Additional participant demographic information is included in Table 1 . Over a third (36.5%) of caregivers believed that their child played online games with their friends from school, and only 11.5% thought their child played games with unfamiliar people online. Over a third (34.8%) of caregivers stated there was an improvement in their child's ability to regulate their emotions, and a further 43.5% reported no change. Caregivers' responses on the number of hours their child spent online gaming indicated 60.9% spend 5–20 hours per week, and 17.4% stated their child spent more than 30 hours. Some caregivers (43.5%) were neutral to the statement ‘I have seen a reduction in social anxiety or stress related to social situations in my child’ (Figure 1 ), while a further 30.4% disagreed with the statement. title: [Russian early childhood psychiatry: challenges and prospects]
journal: Zh Nevrol Psikhiatr Im S S Korsakova
abstract:
This article examines the main challenges In Russian early childhood psychiatry. It outlines the developmental stages of Russian "micropsychiatry," which addresses children from the first year of life to age four, and notes its close relationship with pediatrics, neurology, and early childhood psychology. The increasing prevalence of mental disorders among children and adolescents in recent decades underscores the need for early diagnosis, rehabilitation, comprehensive treatment, and prevention within national policies aimed at strengthening the mental health of the younger generation. Establishing a system for early detection and comprehensive intervention for developmental disorders in children within primary healthcare settings has therefore become a priority. Early childhood psychiatry currently faces clinical-diagnostic, classification, terminological, interdepartmental, therapeutic-corrective, and organizational-methodological challenges, which this article examines along with proposed solutions.

В статье обсуждаются основные вопросы и задачи, которые стоят перед психиатрией раннего детства на сегодняшний день. Изложены этапы становления отечественной «микропсихиатрии», которые охватывает возраст с первого года жизни до четырех лет, подчеркивается ее неразрывная связь с педиатрией, неврологией и психологией раннего детства. Рост психической патологии у детей и подростков, отмечаемый в последние десятилетия, свидетельствует о необходимости диагностики и реабилитации этих расстройств в раннем возрасте, их комплексной терапии и профилактики в контексте государственной политики, нацеленной на укрепление психического здоровья подрастающего поколения. title: Working memory and language development have a bi-directional longitudinal relationship in autistic preschoolers
abstract:
Background Among neurotypical children working memory and language development are closely related, but the longitudinal relationship between these factors is unknown in autism. This study had the goal of evaluating potential bidirectional relationships between these domains. Methods A longitudinal design included language and visuospatial working memory assessments across three time points with 160 autistic preschoolers. Time points were one year apart. A cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) using Full-Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) was used to evaluate longitudinal associations between performance on a working memory task (i.e., the Hide and Seek Task) and language scores (i.e., verbal development quotient). Results Cross-lagged associations were significant for paths from working memory at the first time point to language at the second time point (β = .31, p = .01) and from language at first time point to working memory at the second time point (β = .40, p < .001). Cross-lagged paths from the second to third time point were not statistically significant in either direction. Conclusions This study provides evidence of a bidirectional relationship between working memory and language in autistic toddlers and preschoolers among younger autistic preschoolers. These results highlight working memory as a potential early assessment and intervention domain for improving language outcomes in autism as well as the role of language delays as a factor related to reduced working memory skills later in development.

Introduction Understanding the early neurocognitive development of autistic children can clarify etiology and inform intervention. Working memory is the ability to hold information in mind while updating it to problem-solve [ 1 ]. Language includes speech, gesture, sign, writing, and enables communication, social interaction, and engagement with cultural and environmental contexts [ 2 ]. Both working memory and language underly foundational aspects of child development, including the acquisition of new knowledge, social communication, and adaptive functioning across everyday contexts. Difficulties in either domain can therefore have cascading effects on learning and developmental outcomes. In autism, working memory and language abilities are frequently characterized by persistent delays or differences relative to same-age peers, though the extent and quality of these difficulties varies considerably across individual children and is sensitive to modality and task demands [ 3 – 7 ]. There are several potential theoretical relationships between working memory and language development. Diamond [ 8 ] suggested that working memory supports language development by allowing children to link speech or speech sounds they hear with other information that is not well-synchronized such as gestures or labeled objects. Conversely, language skills including inner speech may allow children to develop cognitive skills including working memory. Specifically, language supports the development of self-regulation and of reflective and abstract thinking [ 9 – 13 ]. Language may also enable children to represent things that are not currently present in their memory. Of course, it is possible that a third factor could underlie the development of both language and working memory, or that the relationship between working memory is bi-directional with mutual influence in early development [ 14 ]. Indeed, there is some evidence for a bi-directional longitudinal relationship between language and executive function batteries that include working memory tasks in young neurotypical children [ 15 – 17 ]. Evidence suggests that working memory is an early developing component of cognitive function [ 18 – 21 ]. For neurotypical children, the capacity to actively hold information in mind typically emerges between 9 to 12 months of age [ 20 ], and working memory abilities increase in their complexity to include manipulating and updating information around 15 months [ 18 ]. Working memory capacity continues to increase during the preschool years [ 19 , 21 ], a period that also coincides with rapid language development. Neurotypical children are also acquiring receptive language within their first year, and expressive language expands through toddlerhood and into their preschool years. Numerous studies have examined the relationship between language and working memory across varying developmental levels and age groups. Among young neurotypical children, early working memory predicts later language skills, particularly vocabulary [ 22 – 26 ]. For example, verbal working memory ability at age four predicted vocabulary a year later [ 25 ], working memory at 30 months predicted vocabulary size at age three [ 22 ], and verbal working memory at age two predicted both receptive and expressive language at age four [ 26 ]. Conversely, early language ability predicts working memory and other aspects of executive functioning among neurotypical children [ 27 – 30 ]. For instance, verbal ability at age three predicted executive function performance on a battery that included working memory tasks at age four [ 30 ], and significant correlations between earlier language and later executive function as well as earlier executive function and later language were reported across two-, three-, and four-year assessments [ 27 ]. However, a second study examining these relationships over the same time period found evidence of a direct relationship for language on later executive function but not for executive function on later language [ 16 ]. These studies document the potential influence of language on later working memory and of working memory on later language early in neurotypical development, but most investigations examined executive function generally rather than isolating working memory and not all studies tested potential bidirectional relationships. No research has specifically investigated the longitudinal relationship between working memory and language in autistic children during the preschool period. Several studies have explored the concurrent relationship (i.e., at cross-sectional time points) between working memory and language in autism. Among school-aged children, working memory and language were not related in an autistic group despite a relation in a neurotypical group [ 31 , 32 ]. In contrast, working memory relates to both structural and pragmatic language in autistic groups [ 33 , 34 ], and a group of autistic children with language impairment had lower verbal working memory ability than a group of autistic children without language impairment [ 35 ]. School-aged autistic children may be less likely than neurotypical children to use verbal strategies to support their working memory performance [ 31 , 32 ]. More recent work found autistic children with structural language impairment were less likely to use verbal mediation during a planning task that involved working memory compared to autistic children with normal language and neurotypical peers suggesting the relation between working memory and language may differ within autism depending on a child’s language profile [ 36 ]. Among preschoolers between the ages of 2–4 years, verbal ability related to working memory performance and this relationship was stronger among autistic children than neurotypical children [ 37 ]. These authors used lab-based tasks to create a working memory composite and measured language using a composite of receptive and expressive language. Similar results were reported for 2- to 8-year-olds using parent report of real-world working memory ability and parent reported communication, pragmatic, and receptive-expressive social communication skills [ 38 ]. Investigating the potential longitudinal relationship between working memory and language is particularly important due its clinical implications. A deeper understanding of how these domains influence each other during the preschool period could help to inform early interventions, promote school readiness, and support better outcomes across a variety of domains that involve language and working memory. The current study aims to identify whether a bi-directional relationship exists between working memory and language development in autistic preschool-aged children. Specifically, we tested the bi-directional longitudinal relationship between visuospatial working memory and language in a combined sample of autistic 2- and 4-year-olds at three time points that were one year apart. To our knowledge, this was the first longitudinal evaluation of these relationships in autistic preschoolers. Due to the mixed results in neurotypical preschoolers, we did not have a priori hypotheses about the directionality of the relationship between these domains in autism. Methods Study design Autistic children were enrolled at age 2 or 4 years and participated in a baseline (T1), 1-year (T2), and 2-year (T3) follow-up. Cohorts were combined to provide adequate power for a cross-lagged longitudinal model. At each time point, children completed language assessments and an executive function battery that included working memory assessment. At baseline, children completed a clinical evaluation to determine eligibility after written consent was obtained from each child’s parent or legal guardian. The protocol for the study was reviewed and approved by the Boston Children's Hospital Institutional Review Board in accordance with the Belmont Report, federal, and state regulations guiding human subjects research. Participants The sample included 160 autistic children who were followed for 2 years. At baseline, there were 94 2-year-olds and 66 4-year-olds in the sample; 37 of the children were girls (23%). Children were recruited as part of a larger study examining the development and trajectory of executive function and social development in autistic and non-autistic children. Children were eligible for the study if they were 2–2;11 or 4–4;11 years at enrollment and able to participate in English. The mean age of the sample was 40.42 months (SD = 12.60, 24–60). All participants completed an assessment of global cognitive functioning using the Mullen Scales of Early Learning (MSEL; [ 39 ], at their initial visit. Toddlers who were 30 months or younger were required to have a Visual Reception age equivalent of at least 12 months to participate in the study. Toddlers and preschoolers who were 31 months or older were required to have a Visual Reception age equivalent of at least 18 months. These age equivalents ensured the valid use of autism diagnostic measures; minimum age equivalents for the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, Second Edition (ADOS-2; [ 40 ] are 12 months for the Toddler Module (used with children 30 months and younger) and 18 months for Module 1 (used with children 31 months and older). Minimum age equivalents also supported the valid use of experimental measures of executive function but may exclude children with more significant cognitive delays, limiting sample representativeness and the generalizability of findings to the broader population of children with autism. The mean score at baseline for the Mullen Early Learning Composite was 68.22 (SD = 19.71, range = 49–122). The Early Learning Composite is a standard score with a normative mean of 100 and standard deviation of 15, and scores between 85 and 115 are considered within the average range. We also computed a developmental quotient [(mean mental age/chronological age) × 100] for the nonverbal (Visual Reception, Fine Motor) and verbal (Expressive, Receptive) subtests. Developmental quotients for children who are developing at the expected rate would fall at 100, with higher scores reflecting more advanced development relative to age expectations and scores below 100 reflecting a developmental level below age expectations. Means were 74.18 (SD = 18.92, range = 25.00–116.98) for the nonverbal developmental quotient and 62.11 (SD = 27.64, range = 8.00–128.70) for the verbal developmental quotient. Autism diagnosis was also required for eligibility. Children were eligible if they met DSM-5 [ 41 ] criteria for autism spectrum disorder based on the ADOS-2 [ 40 ] and the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R, [ 42 , 43 ]). Diagnosis was determined by licensed psychologists who were research reliable on the ADOS-2 and ADI-R. Because electroencephalography was collected as part of the larger study to examine neural and behavioral development of cognition, exclusionary criteria focused on factors that would limit the validity and comparability of neural and behavioral assessments. These criteria included parent report of a history of seizures or seizure medication, medical disorders or medications impacting the central nervous system, prolonged prenatal substance exposure, and significant sensory, motor, or physical conditions that limited participation in the planned tasks. Parent report of demographic characteristics including child sex, race, ethnicity, caregiver educational level, and household income was collected via a study-specific background questionnaire. Children under 5 years old completed the Receptive Language and Expressive Language subtests of the MSEL [ 39 ]. Children 5 years or older completed the Verbal Comprehension and Naming Vocabulary subtests of the Differential Ability Scales, Second Edition (DAS-II, [ 44 ]) unless they could not obtain a valid score for either verbal subtest. The MSEL provides a valid and reliable assessment of language from 0–68 months [ 39 ] and the DAS-II Early Years provides a valid and reliable assessment of language from 30–83 months [ 44 ]. Each test includes one receptive and one expressive subtest. title: [Autism, selective mutism and mild intellectual disability explained by 17q12 microdeletion syndrome]
abstract: The patient had presented symptoms during preschool years with motor coordination difficulties, deviant reactions to sensory stimuli and separation anxiety. A language stagnation had occurred at the age of 1.5 to 2 years. At school start, she became completely mute during school hours but spoke at home. At assessment at the Child Neuropsychiatric Clinic at the age of 10, autism, selective mutism and ADHD/ADD were diagnosed. Her intellectual level corresponded to borderline intellectual functioning, and a similar test result was evident also at the age of 14 years. When transition to upper secondary school was planned, the cognitive assessment showed a mild intellectual disability. Then, medical investigations, including genetic SNP array, was carried out. This analysis showed a 17q12 microdeletion syndrome. Then, specific medical investigations were carried out due to the various medical conditions that need to be checked and followed up in patients with 17q12 microdeletion syndrome.

title: Autism with social anxiety is associated with acquiescent behaviors and enlarged amygdala volume
abstract:
Social anxiety (SA) frequently co-occurs with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), but it remains unclear whether SA in ASD reflects greater symptom severity or a distinct subtype. Across two complementary studies, we characterized the behavioral and neural correlates of SA in ASD using a naturalistic social navigation task measuring affiliative and power-related behaviors. In Study 1 (ASD = 575; controls = 357), autistic individuals with SA exhibited significantly reduced task-derived power behaviors (e.g., compliance with others’ requests) compared to those without SA—a pattern not observed in non-autistic individuals. In Study 2 (ASD = 72; controls = 72), individuals with both ASD and SA showed enlarged amygdala volumes relative to both ASD without SA and non-autistic individuals. These behavioral and neural differences found in Study 1 and Study 2 were not observed in ASD with co-occurring depression or generalized anxiety disorder. Moreover, in Study 2, larger amygdala volume in the ASD group was associated with reduced task-derived power behaviors, indicating a neural signature linking social-behavioral differences and anxiety-related features. Together, these findings point to a distinct ASD phenotype marked by social anxiety, altered interpersonal dynamics, and amygdala enlargement, with implications for diagnosis and tailored intervention.

Introduction Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition that affects approximately 1–2% of the population [ 1 , 2 ]. Anxiety was noted as a feature in Kanner’s 1943 description of autism, alongside core symptoms such as social communication and interaction difficulties and restricted, repetitive behaviors [ 3 ]. Research estimates that 30% to 50% of individuals with ASD (mainly cognitively unimpaired) experience social anxiety [ 4 – 6 ]—four times the rate in the general population [ 7 ]. Assessing social anxiety in the context of autism is challenging because certain autistic behaviors—such as reduced social approach—can resemble the behavioral criteria used to diagnose social anxiety, making differentiation difficult [ 5 , 8 – 10 ]. Despite its prevalence and considerable phenotypic overlap [ 11 ], the social-behavioral and neural features that distinguish social anxiety in ASD remain poorly understood, and research in autistic adults is particularly limited. Social anxiety symptoms may limit the benefits of social skills interventions [ 12 , 13 ], which may increase the challenges of employment and social life. Understanding social anxiety in ASD is crucial for improving diagnosis, developing effective treatments, and enhancing support for this population. The hallmark features of social anxiety disorder are fears of negative evaluation and avoidance of anxiety-provoking social situations [ 14 ]. While social fears are associated with social anxiety in both autistic and neurotypical (NT) individuals [ 4 , 15 , 16 ], the nature of these fears may differ. NT individuals with social anxiety often show intact or heightened perspective-taking yet underestimate their own competence [ 17 ]. In autism, however, social fears frequently stem from core social-cognitive difficulties—such as confusion in social situations or intolerance of unpredictability—rather than prototypical fears of rejection or embarrassment [ 9 , 10 , 18 ]. Although autistic individuals with social anxiety display greater social avoidance than those without [ 5 ], this avoidance may arise from mechanisms distinct from those in NT populations. Many autistic individuals value peer approval and desire social connection [ 19 – 21 ], yet difficulties interpreting social cues can make interactions distressing and promote motivational avoidance [ 18 ]. Consequently, social anxiety in autism is often inferred from behavior rather than explicitly reported internal fears [ 11 ], and may present differently than in NT individuals, contributing to limited treatment response [ 22 , 23 ]. These differences highlight the need to identify social-behavioral phenotypes that disentangle social anxiety from autism-related social difficulties and more precisely capture how social anxiety manifests within autism. To quantify the social-behavioral profile of social anxiety in autism, we employed a naturalistic experiment for assessment of implicit social behavior [ 24 ]. Our task was designed to capture social behavior tendencies on the dimensions of power and affiliation [ 25 – 27 ], which define a 2D social space—a cognitive map that supports flexible social behavior across abstract domains [ 28 ]. The affiliation-power model of social space has been used to study social anxiety, social motivation and depression (e.g., [ 29 – 32 ]). Our naturalistic task specifically captured high-level behaviors including social motivation, reciprocity, compliance, and communication—embedded within realistic decision-making scenarios, and the items corresponding to the two social dimensions have been validated and examined across multiple samples [ 24 , 30 , 32 – 36 ]. In our previous work, we found that autistic adults showed lower affiliative behaviors and reduced social distance (a combined measure of affiliation and power in the 2D social space) compared to NT individuals [ 35 , 36 ]. These results indicate that the affiliation-power model could reflect meaningful social-behavioral phenotypes of ASD. Therefore, this model is suitable for examining whether social anxiety further reduces task-derived affiliation and/or power behaviors. Studies estimated that 49% to 80% of autistic adults experience interpersonal victimization [ 37 , 38 ]. Difficulties recognizing manipulation or anticipating consequences may also lead to compliance in some contexts [ 39 ], suggesting that social anxiety in autism may diminish their ability to navigate interpersonal demands rather than increasing assertive or dominant behaviors. Beyond the limited work on social-behavioral features, neural correlates of social anxiety in autistic adults have been scarcely examined. Across species, the amygdala—particularly its medial divisions—acts as a central hub of the social behavior network, transforming diverse social cues into adaptive affiliative, defensive, or competitive responses [ 40 – 42 ]. Rather than merely generating emotional valence, the amygdala assigns social meaning and orchestrates downstream behavioral mechanisms, making it a core integrator of social perception and social action [ 41 , 42 ]. Converging cellular, molecular, and neuroimaging evidence further highlights the amygdala as a biologically vulnerable system in autism [ 43 , 44 ]. Transcriptomic work shows that numerous ASD-susceptibility genes are expressed in the developing amygdala and exhibit cell-type–specific dysregulation [ 45 ]. Neurochemical studies similarly report reduced NAA/Cr ratios—an index of neuronal integrity—in the amygdala–hippocampal region, correlating with autistic symptoms of greater social and emotional impairment [ 46 ]. Postmortem findings reveal atypical developmental trajectories, with an early surplus of neurons followed by decline into adulthood [ 47 ], and longitudinal MRI work identifies enlarged basolateral nuclei and altered subnuclear growth associated with social-communication symptoms [ 48 ]. Furthermore, at the circuit level, specific amygdala microcircuits regulate social evaluation, social-threat learning, and anxiety in social contexts [ 49 – 51 ], suggesting a mechanism through which amygdala abnormalities may contribute to social anxiety–related difficulties in autism. This aligns with the alternative view that amygdala dysfunction in ASD may relate more to heightened fear and anxiety than to social-cognitive deficits per se [ 52 ]. Together, these discussions point to a structurally and functionally atypical amygdala in ASD, underscoring the need to characterize amygdala structure in autistic adults and determine how it relates to individual differences in social–behavioral features and social anxiety. If amygdala structure is particularly altered in autistic individuals with social anxiety—and if social anxiety in ASD presents with distinct social-behavioral features—then the amygdala may encode social behaviors that are especially salient to social anxiety in autism. In the existing literature, most studies examining amygdala volume and anxiety in ASD focus on children or adolescents. Several reported enlarged amygdala volumes in autistic youth with anxiety compared to autistic peers without anxiety or NT controls [ 53 – 55 ], although smaller volumes [ 56 ] or null findings [ 57 ] have also been documented. Enlarged amygdala volume has also been observed in NT individuals with social anxiety [ 58 ]. Yet few studies have specifically investigated amygdala structure in relation to social anxiety in ASD [ 59 ], and, to our knowledge, none have examined this question in autistic adults or its links to affiliation-power behavioral profiles—a significant gap this work seeks to address. Here, we examined self-reported social anxiety diagnoses as an index of vulnerability and investigated their association with task-derived social behaviors and amygdala volume in autistic adults. In Study 1, using a large online sample (ASD = 575, NT = 357), we tested whether task-derived affiliative and power behaviors differed between autistic adults with and without social anxiety and NT controls. We predicted that autistic individuals with social anxiety would show distinct social-behavioral profiles compared to both other groups. In Study 2, using an in-person neuroimaging (ASD = 72, NT = 72), we compared amygdala volume across autistic adults with and without social anxiety and NT controls. We hypothesized that amygdala volume would be enlarged in autistic individuals with social anxiety. Finally, we examined whether amygdala volume was associated with autism-related social behavior phenotypes captured by our task. All comparisons were conducted using independent participant samples across studies. Figure 1 provides an overview of the study design and research questions. Methods Participants Study 1 - online behavior sample We recruited a large sample of ASD participants through Simons Powering Autism Research (SPARK) Research Match program, a project supported by Simons Foundation. All registered SPARK participants self-attested to having received professional diagnoses of ASD. The eligibility criteria were: (1) ages 18 to 30, (2) Social Communication Questionnaire [ 60 ] total score >9. Among 956 participants who consented, 675 individuals completed all surveys and the social task. The sample size after excluding 100 participants with an “ASD validity flag” (criteria include diagnosis rescinded, or diagnosis before 15 months of age, repetitive behavior scale-revised score <10, unknown diagnosis source, etc.) identified in the SPARK phenotype dataset was 575 (409 females). IQ was measured by cognitive tests from TestMyBrain ( https://www.testmybrain.org ). All participants provided written informed consent and received compensation for their participation. Neurotypical (NT) controls were from the US and recruited from Prolific ( www.prolific.com ), a platform that helps researchers recruit participants for their online research. The exclusion criteria were: (1) neurodevelopmental diagnoses, including ASD, dyslexia, attention deficit disorder or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, (2) mild cognitive impairment or dementia, (3) history of neurological concerns such as epilepsy, traumatic brain injury, Parkinson’s disease, seizures, or multiple sclerosis, (4) other chronic diseases such as diabetes, heart disease or stroke, and (5) first language is not English. IQ was measured by ICAR (The international cognitive ability resource https://icar-project.com ). Because no prior studies have examined the association between task-derived power/affiliative behaviors and social anxiety in ASD, an a priori power analysis was not feasible. We therefore relied on the large online dataset we collected. Autistic individuals without intellectual impairment were shown to experience more social anxiety [ 11 ]. Among the final ASD sample of 575, 200 had self-identified cognitive or language delays (such as intellectual disability, specific language impairment). Our sample showed a similar rate of cognitive delays among ASD individuals as reported in the latest systematic review [ 2 ]. We matched NT samples to ASD samples excluding individuals with self-reported cognitive or language delays. From a total sample size of 696 NT participants, we selected 357 participants who matched our ASD sample based on sex, age, and education using the “MatchIt” package in R. Among these 357 NT individuals, 25 (7.08%) declared SA diagnoses, consistent with the general US population [ 7 ]. Study 2 - onsite imaging sample ASD participants were recruited through physical flyers around New York City, email listserv announcements, local research registry and word of mouth. The eligibility criteria were: (1) ages 18 to 50, (2) meeting DSM-5 criteria for ASD, (3) having an IQ over 60 (assessed onsite by the Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence and Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Adults [ 61 , 62 ]), (4) having no history of neurological concerns like epilepsy or traumatic brain injury, and (5) no substance or alcohol abuse disorders and no recreational drug use. ASD screening was conducted by licensed clinicians using the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, 2nd edition (ADOS-2 [ 63 ]), supplemented with developmental and clinical history as needed, to inform DSM-5 criteria. We intentionally over-recruited females to ensure better representation of this underrepresented group in autism research. NT participants were recruited through announcements posted on physical flyers around New York City and email listservs with the eligibility criteria of (1) age between 18 and 50, (2) IQ > 60 (assessed via The Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence; WASI-II), (3) no 1st degree relatives with idiopathic ASD, (4) no history of neurological concerns (e.g., epilepsy, TBI), and (5) no recreational drug use 24 h prior to MRI visit. Since no prior studies in autistic adults were available to inform a power estimate, we utilized our onsite sample, which has a sample size comparable to that of earlier studies conducted in children (e.g., [ 53 – 55 , 59 ]). title: [Guideline for intervention and rehabilitation in children with autism spectrum disorder (2026 edition)]
journal: Zhongguo Dang Dai Er Ke Za Zhi
authors: National Health Commission of the People's Republic of China
abstract:
On September 22, 2026, the National Health Commission released the "Guideline for intervention and rehabilitation in children with autism spectrum disorder (2026 edition)". The guideline applies to intervention and rehabilitation services for children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) under 18 years of age. It establishes eight basic principles, namely early intervention, individualized intervention, comprehensive intervention, evidence-based practice, long-term and high-intensity intervention, primary-level care as the mainstay, family participation, and social inclusion and support, and specifies that the optimal treatment window is before 6 years of age and that intervention should be provided for at least 20 hours per week. It covers health education, intervention for developmental deficits, intervention for challenging behaviors, family intervention, digital and intelligent intervention and rehabilitation, and follow-up.
